The *Mātṛkācakraviveka*:
First Section, composed by Svatantrānandanātha.

Indeed, here [is] the vital breath of the venerable Lord Paramaśiva, whose right and left sides constitute the states of waking and deep sleep, and whose lower part is fashioned from the nature of dream.

For the sake of favoring the world that wallows amidst various internal and external conflicting doctrines, manifested by the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*)— which flows spontaneously and consists of the wonder of both knowledge and ignorance—
the great Siddha named Svatantānanda, impelled by Śiva, [acted] by virtue of his own inherent perfection.

And because it is the source of the entire body of speech, desiring to define the nature of the ultimate reality— free from confusion by dispelling all doubts through the instruction on the meaning of the great *mātṛkā* mantra, which is of vast measure— he first [describes] the Blessed One’s [form], which consists of the meaning of the great mantra.

He contemplates the Great Power of Mahādeva—which consists of the lineage transmission (*pāramparyapravṛtti*)—for the sake of attaining the desired goal, beginning with the words "jāgrad" (waking) and so forth. The state of the continuous awareness and cognition of jars, cloths, and other objects upon the cessation of deep sleep is "waking" (*jāgrad*); deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the insentient slumber; these two have been produced in succession by those [states].

That [state] by which the right and left sides [are distinguished]. Because it consists of activity (*kriyā*), the waking state has the nature of the right side; indeed, the right side of the body is experienced as being primarily characterized by action (*karman*). Sleep, consisting of the nature of slumber, has the nature of the left side; indeed, the left side is inactive and feminine in character. Regarding the phrase "in dream," etc.:
We contemplate the Mistress of Prāṇa, the Supreme Śakti of Paraśiva, whose face and heart-region are formed by the states beyond the Fourth (turyātīta). || 1 ||

When sleep has not yet ceased, the mental differentiation is *saṃsāra*; that very state (*svabhāva*) is a particular condition (*avasthāviśeṣa*), by which the inferior portion—the *yonibhāga*—is fashioned. This occurs during the intermediate stage between deep sleep and waking, which is appropriate for the middle part of the dream.

It is called the *yoni* (womb) because it is the locus from which conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises. Thus, one should understand that deep sleep is the embryonic stage of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), dreaming is the stage of birth, and waking is the stage of growth. Having thus contemplated the triangle—which consists of these three states of the individual soul (*jīva*)—as situated within the wheel of the body, [one perceives] that which resides therein.
He contemplates the triangle of Śiva with the words "the fourth" (*turya*) and so forth. The fourth is the fourteenth [state].

It is the transcendence of the pervasion of the object of consciousness (*cetya*). The state of the fourth is the stage of contemplating the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*) of this [Self], which has consciousness as its cause, during the three states of the individual soul (*jīva*). Even there, although...

The occurrence of the three states arises due to the three states of waking and so forth, which are the objects of consciousness’s pervasion; nevertheless, because consciousness possesses all-pervasiveness and lacks differentiation due to its unity, the fourth state (*turya*) is said to be of a single nature.
That which transcends the fourth is the "transcendent fourth" (*turyātīta*), which is the repose within the pure, inward-turned consciousness untouched by the stain of transmigratory existence.

By these two, it is sequentially fashioned with the parts of the mouth and the heart. The state of being the "mouth" (*mukhatva*) is said of the Fourth (*turya*) because it swallows the objects of cognition (*cetya*) manifested during the stages beginning with waking; for the mouth is characterized by the activity of chewing. Ati-turya (the state beyond the Fourth) is described as the "heart" (*hṛdayatva*) because it is the vital breath of all the stages.
And thus, [this refers] either to the four-cornered wheel consisting of the four states beginning with waking, or—
due to the identification of even the fourth state (*turya*) as being threefold under the influence of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of waking and so forth—
to the six-cornered wheel produced by the union of two triangles of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*).

One should effect the realization of the existence of Paramaśiva’s Mistress of Vital Breath (Prāṇeśvarī), who resides in the form of the body at the center in the region of the heart— the seat of the hub of the wheel— throbbing as the power of vital breath (prāṇakalā) whose nature is repose beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), consisting of either four or six limbs. By this, the five states are transcended.

By accepting that the state of Supreme Śiva (paramaśivadaśā) is somehow of an undivided nature and universal, the superiority of Śiva is stated. Although that state of Supreme Śiva is possible through the phrase "the Mistress of Breath" (prāṇeśvarīm), nevertheless, its existence is dependent upon the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), which is the very essence of consciousness; thus, the excellence of Śakti is maintained.

Thus it should be understood. By the phrase "we reflect," it is indicated that in the contemplation of every action, including even salutation and the like, there is nothing but pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone. || 1 ||
(3) [She is] she whose states of waking and sleep are delineated by touch and sound,
and who has awakened from the deep sleep indicated within.
With our minds, we enter that state of deep sleep which arises during the waking state described as "heat" (ūṣman), the mother of the entire collection of mantras. || 2 ||

Now, he states that this very Supreme Śiva-Śakti—who consists of the five limbs (avayava) comprising the five stages (pañcāvasthā), who is the unified totality (samaṣṭi) of all established doctrines, and who is embodied as the Great Mantra Mātṛkā—is expressed by the following: "The consonants," and so forth. The consonants (*sparśa*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* pertain to the subjects of creation and dissolution; the vowels (*svara*) begin with *a* and end with the visarga.

The meaning is that because there is an abundance of contraction and expansion during pronunciation, they are "like sounds" (nādakalpāḥ), that is, they are indeed *nādas*. *Svara* means *nāda*. By means of the *sparśas* and *svaras*, she is that by which the states of waking and sleep are respectively delineated and awakened;
the meaning is that she manifests waking through the *sparśas* and sleep through the *svaras*. Regarding the passage beginning with "the semi-vowels" (*antaḥstha*), etc.:

The *yaralava* are called *antaḥstha* because they stand within (*antaḥ*)—that is, in the middle (*madhya*)—between the vowels (*svara*) and the consonants (*sparśa*). By these [letters], the state indicated or awakened is the "awakening arisen in deep sleep" (*suṣuptyudita*); that is, it arises precisely in the state of deep sleep, and not like the awakening at the end of sleep in the waking state, which consists of the recognition of objects such as pots and cloths—that is to say, it is what is meant by "dream. That [state] is [described].

The meaning is that it makes known the state of dreaming within the internal consonants (*antaḥstha-varṇa*). Regarding "the sibilants" (*ūṣman*) and so forth: *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the sibilants; this is a technical term. Alternatively, it refers to the commencement of the transformation into sibilants and the like, characterized by the abandonment of contraction once again by the dull consonant groups (*sparśa-varga*) which had previously assumed a contracted form.

Those phonemes in which there is a specific effort are called *ūṣman* (aspirates); they arise and emerge only in the waking state (*jāgaradaśā*). That state of the individual soul (*jīvāvasthā*) which occurs after waking and before sleep—known as the "yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*)—is the fourth state (*turya*). *Bālā*, the collection of mantras, is Śrīvidyā, Parā, and Mahārtha-Śāmbhavī.

The meaning is that she is the *mātṛkā*— the mother and the causal source— of the collection of mantras, both those pertaining to the other world such as the *caraṇavidyā* and others, and those pertaining to this world such as the five-syllabled and eight-syllabled [mantras]. We contemplate her with our minds as the root of everything, because she is the cause of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
And because it is a great means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that completely cuts through doubts regarding the object of ultimate reality produced by various commitments (*samaya*),

the meaning is that we become single-mindedly focused upon it. Here, in the description of "Heat" (*uṣman*), the intention is to indicate the manifestation of the fourth state, which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*), whose nature is the composite syllable (*kūṭākṣara*) in the form of the letter *kṣa*.
The object of knowledge is without remainder. || 2 ||
The two efforts that serve as indicators of the states of waking and deep sleep do so by way of the presence or absence of the recourse to contraction.
The wise have understood the two states of contact and openness as they occur in the consonants and vowels; let us now examine them. (3)
It has been stated that the states such as waking and so forth are made known by colors such as sparśa and the rest.
Since there must be some relationship between the signified (jñāpya) and the signifier (jñāpaka)—whether through denotation (abhidhā), indication (lakṣaṇā), or another means—one might ask:
what is this relationship here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "saṅkoca... [meaning] "in the resorting to contraction."

"Appropriation" (*parigraha*) is grasping; "avoidance" (*varjana*) is its relinquishment. Their state is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is to say, a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*).
By way of that—that is, by means of its mode or similarity—is the meaning.
There are two indicators (*gamaka*) or signifiers (*jñāpaka*) for the states of waking and deep sleep respectively. Respectively: [the verse continues].

Regarding the attainment of the phonemes through touch and tone, there are two articulatory efforts (*prayatna*): contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) and openness (*vivṛtatā*). Contact is the articulatory effort for the production of a phoneme consisting of the mutual impact between the upper and lower portions of the throat, palate, and so forth. Openness is the state of that same pair of [articulatory] regions of the throat and so forth when they are not in contact.

Furthermore, there is the effort of separation (*vighaṭṭana*). The very contact between the regions of the throat and so forth is *spṛṣṭatā* (contact), while the very separation is *vivṛtatā* (openness). The efforts characterized by the grasping of contraction and the relinquishing of that [contraction] serve as indicators of the waking and deep sleep states due to their similarity; the sense is that they are manifestors through representation (*abhinayāt*). For example:

The meaning is that just as the closing of the fingers and so forth is the manifestor [of that state], so it is here. When the stage of perceiving jars, cloths, and so on is active, the self possesses a state of contraction; however, in the stage of rest, which is deep sleep, there is a state of fullness—this is to be known through direct experience. Therefore, between waking and deep sleep, by means of the two—the collection of touch and the collection of sound—...

The similarity between states, consisting of contraction, grasping, and the abandonment [of those], is indeed accepted by discerning people. The intention is that this very similarity is what brings about the relationship between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifestor (vyañjaka).
By the qualifying phrase "known by the wise," [the author indicates] both the phonemes (varṇas) and their states.
Since the two efforts— which serve as the primary cause for the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor—
are accessible only to those who possess discernment, it follows that even though the phonemes themselves are not the conveyors [of meaning],
the similarity of states consisting in contraction and expansion is rooted in effort. This is the case even when the phonemes alone constitute the conveyors.
We examine how the attainment of a state by two efforts is metaphorical;
thus, we ourselves also pursue this very investigation of effort, and no further means of realization than this has been taught. || 3 ||
The contact [articulation] has the *y*-class as its object and is conjoined with openness; openness resides in the *ś*-class and is accompanied by contact.

I remember these two efforts, which serve as indicators of the states of deep sleep and the fourth state (turya), corresponding respectively to the incomplete and the complete fulfillment of the whole.

Now, he establishes the relationship between the internal stops (*antaḥstha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*) regarding their function as indicators of the fourth state (*turya*) while they are in a state of sleep, beginning with the words "contact" (*spṛṣṭi*) and so forth. The meaning is that contact (*spṛṣṭi*)—which pertains to the *ya*-class—is a degree of articulation (*prayatna*) characterized by openness (*vivṛtatva*), thus constituting a mixed effort (*miśraprayatna*). In this context, regarding contact...
The predominance belongs to openness (*vivṛtatā*), while its subordinate status arises from following that [contact].

Thus, when the effort for the articulation of the *ya*-class is incomplete due to the mixing of contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) and openness, it is "slightly contacted" (*īṣatspṛṣṭatva*); this is the distinction. Regarding the effort for the articulation of the *śa*-class, [there is] openness.

It should be understood that due to the lack of totality caused by the confusion of the state of being touched (*spṛṣṭatā*), there is indeed a slight opening. For this very reason, these two efforts serve as indicators, respectively, for the states of sleep and the fourth state (*turya*), which consist of incomplete non-fulfillment and complete fulfillment— that is, incomplete contraction and fullness— since sleep is of the nature of slight contraction.

The meaning is that the slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*) and the slight opening (*īṣadvivṛtatā*) of the *tūrya* tone, which is slightly full in form, are manifested through similarity as before. It is understood right here that the grammarians' statement— that the articulation (*karaṇa*) for the *sparśa* consonants is "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*), while that for the semi-vowels (*antasthā*) is "slight contact" (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*)— is correct.

The claim that [the phonemes] are "opened" by the *ūṣman* sounds and the vowels is to be disregarded because it contradicts the experience of the *ūṣman* sounds and the vowels. Regarding the phrase "I remember": by means of his own internal reflection, he intends to instruct the person being taught. || 4 ||
In the state of non-conceptualization, which is deep sleep, fulfillment is indeed complete;
likewise, in the waking state, the abode of worldly existence, there is likewise a lack of fulfillment.
In the fourth state (turīya), which is the locus of the conjunction of waking and deep sleep,
as well as in a dream similar to them, there is simply the incompleteness of those two.

Now, he establishes through experience that the states of waking and so forth possess the connection with bliss, such as contraction and expansion, by means of the verse beginning with "pūrṇa" (complete). The sense is that in the state of non-conceptuality (*avikalpapada*), which is the level of the non-discursive (*nirvikalpaka*), there is a resting of both the external and internal senses. And this is the qualifying attribute.

Fulfillment (*pūrti*) has been stated as the cause of completeness. Experience is the proof that the very absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) indicates the state of being full and free from defects (*nirāghaṭa-pūrṇabhāva*). Because it is the state of non-conceptualization, fulfillment is indeed complete and entire in deep sleep; likewise, it is so in the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—the station of transmigratory life—which is untouched by the repose consisting in the non-recollection of jars, cloths, and so forth.

The meaning is: "the locus for the arising of intense conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, this qualifying attribute is stated as the cause for the completeness of the state of contraction (*saṅkoca*). Experience itself is the proof that the very arising of intense conceptualization bestows great contraction. [This occurs] in the state where waking and deep sleep coexist, in the mixed state, and in the fourth (*turya*) state.

In the fourth stage (daśā): although there is an extension of the deep sleep characterized by repose in consciousness (*cid-viśrānti*) in the fourth state, nevertheless, that [repose] is also connected with the waking state; thus, because it is touched by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is a persistence of the waking state, and this constitutes precisely its mixed nature. And it is the same in such a dream.

Although in the mixed state, because dream is dominated by conceptualization, the union of waking and deep sleep is of a single form for both, nevertheless, with the intention of expressing the mere commonality of being "mixed," the similarity of dream to the Fourth State (turya) was stated. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": in those two [waking and dreaming], there is incompleteness due to their lack of fullness, whereas in the Fourth State, there is none.
The completeness of fulfillment and the incompleteness of non-fulfillment are to be applied respectively in the case of dreams. || 5 ||
Indeed, dream is but waking accompanied by deep sleep,
and the fourth state (*turya*) is but deep sleep persisting within waking.
This being so, there is likewise a distinction between dreaming and waking,
and similarly, a distinction between the fourth state and deep sleep.

Having established, by means of the aforementioned types of phonemes such as *sparśa* and others, the relationship between the signifier and the signified based on similarity— characterized by the contraction and so forth of the waking state (*jāgrat*) and the rest—

the twofold nature of each of these states, namely waking and deep sleep, is presented according to their forms as knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). Among those, [the nature of] dreaming is...

That state which is known as the waking of consciousness (*jñāna-jāgrat*) is the waking of action (*kriyā-jāgrat*); that which is the fourth (*turya*) is the deep sleep of consciousness (*jñāna-suṣupti*). That state which is known as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the deep sleep of action (*kriyā-suṣupti*). Therefore, dream is merely a variety of waking, and the fourth state is merely a variety of deep sleep; such is the fourfold set of states.

He teaches the nature of these two groups as the basis for the knowledge of their true essence and so forth, starting with the words "dream is that which follows upon deep sleep," and so on. Now, an objection may be raised: "Dream is indeed just waking;
for just as jars, cloths, and other objects are perceived in the waking state, they are likewise perceived here [in the dream state]. This is the only distinction, namely, that in the dream..."

The persistence of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) in the waking state and its cessation therein [is the difference]; and the fourth state (*turya*) is indeed deep sleep itself. Likewise, because rest is perceived there, this is the only distinction: that in the fourth state the waking state persists, whereas in deep sleep it ceases. Thus, due to the slightness of this distinction, the states of dreaming and the fourth are considered varieties of waking and deep sleep respectively.
The sense is that it should be understood thus. || 6 ||
Indeed, when [the state] has arisen internally as the nature of gnosis, it is designated by the specific names "sleep of awakening" (*bodhasupti*) and "the fourth" (*turya*).
When these two, having arisen externally as the nature of action, are well-known as "awakening" and "sleep," respectively. || 7 ||
He clarifies the dependence of dream and the fourth state upon waking and deep sleep with the words "by the nature of cognition" (*jñānātmanā*).
The intended meaning of the subject matter under discussion is that the differentiation of phonemes (*varṇabheda*) consists precisely in the form of cognition. Regarding "by the nature of cognition":
*bodha* (waking) and *supti* (sleep) constitute "waking-and-sleep"; the first [term] refers to the internal, within the inner enclosure.

When [the two states] arise as the nature of knowledge— that is, in the form of knowledge— they respectively receive the specific names "dream" and "the fourth" (*turya*). Alternatively, when they arise in the external sphere of the external senses in the form of action—
that is, as activity— they are designated as "waking," "deep sleep," and "waking-deep sleep" for the states of waking and deep sleep.

The meaning is that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs through what is known as established convention (*prasiddhākhyā*). By this, it should be understood that internal sensory coordination is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), while external sensory coordination is of the nature of action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, both the process of manifestation (*saṃsṛti*) and repose (*viśrānti*) first involve internal sensory coordination, and only subsequently [external].

The distinction is that [the state] descends into the manifestation of the external senses. The underlying sense is that every entity, being of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, possesses the form of both knowledge and action.
And thus, there is the waking of knowledge, the waking of action, the deep sleep of knowledge, and the deep sleep of action; furthermore—

The essential meaning is that one should contemplate the revolution of the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), whose navel is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), as it emerges from the four states beginning with the waking of knowledge. || 7 ||
(8) Indeed, the manifestation outside in the waking state is the creation of duality, while the manifestation within in the dream state is the other condition; thus there are only these two states.
In the state of non-dual creation, deep sleep—which is the ground of both the arising and the resting of the two-fold creation—attains the designation of the Fourth (turya). || 8 ||
Now, he demonstrates, as appropriate, how the four states of waking and so forth have the nature of saṃsāra— consisting of difference and non-difference— and their repose therein,
beginning with the words "waking is external," etc. Emission (*sṛṣṭi*) is saṃsāra in the form of active engagement (*pravṛtti*), because it is the emission of differentiation.

The outward manifestation of the transmigratory process, which functions through the form of differentiation, appearing within the sphere of the external senses, is the waking state; the inward surging of that very same creation of differentiation, vibrating within the sphere of the internal senses, is the dreaming state— this constitutes the two states.

It should be understood that the state of the bound soul (*paśu*) is the ground of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus, both [the waking and dreaming states] constitute the tenfold [manifestation], which is precisely the twofold state of waking and dreaming; this is the creation of non-differentiation (*avibheda-sṛṣṭi*). Non-differentiation is the absence of differentiation, which is dissolution (*saṃhāra*); it is the adoption of the path of the cessation of duality through the orientation toward rest. In the creation of that [non-differentiation]...

This path attains the designation "turya" (the fourth) because it is the fourth in relation to the three states ending with waking; thus, the word *turya* is indeed a synonym for the fourth. It demonstrates the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) by the phrase "of the two-fold creation. Of the two-fold creation...

The "birth" (janir) of that which consists of both difference and non-difference is its arising; the "rest" (viśramaḥ) is its dissolution. That state is the plane of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Because deep sleep will be demonstrated as being characterized by the repose of both difference and non-difference, it constitutes the ground for the emergence and dissolution of the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva. This is what is meant: [The text continues:]... [the state] which is the locus of the arising and dissolution of the world-process of the individual soul and Śiva, by virtue of its being established as the nature of the repose of both difference and non-difference. [the state] which is the locus of the arising and dissolution of the world-process of the individual soul and Śiva, by virtue of its being established as the nature of the repose of both difference and non-difference. The individual soul (*jīva*) transmigrates through the three states by way of differentiation, beginning with deep sleep and ending with the waking state. By that same triad of states, which is characterized by non-differentiation beginning with the waking state and ending with deep sleep, and which partakes in what is called the Fourth (*turya*), Śiva rests. Although he follows the path of rest while still subject to the fetter (*pāśa*) through *māyā*, [he remains as such].

He does not reflect. Thus, Śiva also, though devoid of the distinctions that are merely synonyms for will, knowledge, and action, undergoes transmigration as if through the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking;
and he rests by means of the path of cessation beginning with the waking state—which is the synonym for the fourth (turya) state—and ending with deep sleep. Even though [this is so] in Śiva...

Because the paths of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) are non-different and of a single nature, the conventional designation "the Fourth" (*turya*) exists; nevertheless, it is the path of withdrawal alone that possesses the primary status for this convention—this is the great instruction.
This will be further established in the subsequent passages where it is stated that "the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the non-dual world is equal to the dualistic world."
In those words, there is the derivation of their grammatical formation.
The creative emission (*visarga*) is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is externally projected as the consciousness of Śiva;
Śiva, swallowing that [nature] with his own self, is this very *bindu*.
Regarding the names "those who enjoy rest from saṃsāra," the two transmigrating beings are Paśu and Śiva—that is, the bound soul (paśu) and Śiva. || 9 ||

Having thus taught the nature of the ten states (*daśā*), and intending to define the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as Śiva who presides over them, he establishes the technical definitions of *bindu* and *visarga*— which are established by the tradition of the Mantra-samaya— as being useful for the present subject,
beginning with the words "emitted externally" (*sṛṣṭā bahiḥ*). [The term] "by the consciousness of Śiva" (*śivacitā*) refers to that consciousness which is conventionally designated as "Śiva."

By means of the principle of manifestation (*prakāśa-tattva*), [things appear] "externally," as if external, but not externally in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). For an all-pervading reality, existence is established only when it is grounded upon the foundation of manifestation; if it were external to that, its existence would not be established. Created and then emitted—emission, too, is merely a wonder (*camatkāra*). Its nature (*prakṛti*) is its very essence (*svabhāva*).

It should be understood that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is [the essence]. Or rather, reflective awareness is the very nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*). For without this nature, even when there is the coloring by an object, manifestation would result in insentience (*jāḍya*), like a crystal or similar objects; thus, the fact that [manifestation] possesses its own self-consciousness has been proclaimed by the authors of the scriptures as the sole convention of Mantra.

Immediately following initiation (*dīkṣā*), only those who have mastered the scriptures and established tenets of the authoritative consciousness (*saṃvit*) are qualified for the instruction of the meaning of mantra, which is of the nature of the supreme secret.

Therefore, in this exposition on the discernment of the meaning of mantra, we have set forth only the essential core of the doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvinmata*); thus, there is no lack of effort [on our part]. For illumination (*prakāśa*) indeed...
Vimarśa— which is one's own essential nature, resting within one's own self,
conveyed by various scriptural terms such as *parā*, *prakṛti*, *svātantrya*, *māyā*, and *avidyā*,
and which constitutes the seed of the universe— is at times, when there is a desire to manifest the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [manifested] precisely upon the wall of one's own self.
The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), denoted by the term "emission" (*visarga*) because it is as if emitted outward, possesses the form of the object and devours the subject;

for this very reason, it becomes the knower (*pramātṛ*). And that same subject, though consisting of consciousness, becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) when its sovereign power is eclipsed and it falls into the state of being an object of knowledge. However, when that light of Śiva [awakens]...
When there is a desire to withdraw the manifold world (*prapañca*), [the Supreme] swallows that Nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), by means of its own Self;

at that time, because the root *bhū* signifies non-interruption (*aviccheda*)—in the sense that "it exists" (*bhavati*) without being interrupted—it becomes designated by the term *bindu*. Furthermore, for the Indians, the *bindu* is the cause of non-interruption.

This is the conventional usage; the intended meaning is that [the Self] possesses an undifferentiated nature. Thus, it is taught that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essence is the object of knowledge (*vedya*) has the nature of emission (*visarga*), while the light (*prakāśa*) whose essence is the knower (*vedaka*) has the nature of the point (*bindu*). He states this very point in the words: "of those who experience rest within the cycle of transmigratory existence."
Vimarśa (reflective awareness) has the nature of transmigration (*saṃsaraṇa*), while Prakāśa (light) has the nature of the dawn (*aruṇa*).

Regarding these two aforementioned lights—vimarśa and prakāśa—the terms *visarga* and *bindu* are conventionally defined as their designations. Now, from a general perspective, regarding the manifold world (*saṃsāra*) which is elevated by the *visarga*:
He states the subject matter: "of transmigrating beings" (saṃsāriṇām) || 9 ||
Transmigration belongs to the bound soul (paśu) and is dualistic in nature; it is non-dual in form for the supreme Śambhu, who is beyond becoming.
Since even the three-fold transmigratory existence becomes mixed [with liberation], that which partakes of rest is indeed the supreme abode here, the Bindu. || 10 ||

It has already been demonstrated that those who are not common to the categories of *paśu*, *śiva*, and *paraśiva* are indeed transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) in general. Now, he demonstrates that *paśu*s and the others specifically occupy particular domains within transmigration by distinguishing them, stating:
"it becomes dualistic in nature. In that context, [this occurs] through the reflection (*vimarśa*), which is a synonym for emission (*visarga*), assuming the form of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The sense is: "because of the unfolding of the wonder of differentiation. That "transmigration" (saṃsaraṇa) belongs to Śiva, who is beyond becoming (abhava);

it should be understood that its nature as such arises there because of the grasping of the wonder of non-duality through the form of *vidyā*, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The phrase "the transmigration of the supreme Śambhu" is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. It is "mixed" (*miśra*).

It should be understood that therein, within the form of both duality and non-duality, there is the acceptance of the wonder of simultaneously demonstrating the single secret of difference and non-difference by means of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which possesses the dual nature of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Here, in this third stage, by the employment of the term "Supreme Śambhu" (*para-śambhu-pada*), even within the established doctrine of resting in the Trika, [this state is indicated].

Great esteem has been indicated. His inclusion among the transmigrators who preside over the third state was performed for the sake of the fourfold purpose through faith. Therefore, he discerns the state of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), whose nature is pure inward-turned repose and which is untouched by the stain of transmigratory existence:
"Having three forms," and so forth. The sense is that from which and wherein even the threefold cycle of transmigration comes to rest—that supreme, unsurpassed abode is extracted as the *bindu*.
This is because, although it possesses the nature of full awareness (*pūrṇavimarśa*), which is the material cause of the entire cycle of transmigration in the fourth stage...
Nevertheless, because even at the stage of the Great State of Rest (*mahāviśrāntipada*),
the slightest scent of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arising from the connection with the various levels of the three stages has not yet subsided,
the fifth state alone— which transcends that and is characterized as the Supreme Sky (*paravyoma*)— is the true goal.
The ultimate philosophical tenet is that the reality of the partless Great Bindu (*niṣkalamahābindutattva*) is purified by the fivefold tradition (*pañcamāmnāya*).

In this regard, the following is indicated: the three states of the bound soul (*paśu*), such as deep sleep and so forth, which are of the nature of duality, as well as the state beyond those, which occurs within the Śiva-like fourth state (*turya*) characterized by duality.
When it has been established that [the reality] is denoted by mantras consisting of vowels, consonants, and so forth, within this [system of] five decads,
there are three decads whose nature is the world characterized by the mixture of difference and non-difference; these are the forms of the single resting place for the entire world,
belonging to the fourth decad (or contained within the fourth decad).

Yoga occurs in the fourth [state], yoga in the tenth stage, and yoga in that which transcends it, namely the stage of the Great Bindu (mahābindu); such is the distinction between them. The path of the Siddhas declares that the entire collection of stages is subsumed within the stages of the threefold worldly existence, its repose in that single essence, and the great repose that transcends it. Therefore, this is the instruction:
It is heart-pleasing to the wise; enough, therefore, with this excessive elaboration. || 10 ||
For the realization that the *bindu* is secondary is of a non-dual nature; it becomes the Śiva-body, whereas the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is the state of duality.
From that [state] of the soul's restraint comes its true nature; through emanations, this is the worldly activity of the great ones. || 11 ||

According to the logic already stated, since the *bindu* is characterized by indivisibility (*apariccheda*), and since limitation (*pariccheda*) can arise through contact with conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), the term *bindu* is accepted as being applied to Śiva—even when his characteristics are incomplete—by way of metaphorical usage (*gauṇanyāya*). Thus he says, "metaphorical," and so forth. *Vṛtti* means consciousness (*saṃvitti*).

It is of a non-dual nature (*abhedarūpā*). This qualification refers to the quality (*guṇa*) consisting of non-duality, which serves as the basis for the conventional usage of the term "secondary bindu" (*gauṇabindu*);

the distinction is that it becomes a secondary bindu by virtue of possessing that quality. That consciousness (*vitti*) is Śaiva—that is, the body or essential nature (*tanūḥ svarūpaṃ*) belonging to Śiva.
In this way, the state of being the *bindu* (the point/essence) should be inferred even for one who presides over the mixed cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

It should be understood that the state of being the *bindu* is ascribed to Śiva himself due to the intention to emphasize the abundance of his worldly manifestation (*vyavahāra*). Likewise, even though the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses limitation, he has indeed attained the state of being the *bindu* by virtue of his nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*). Now, regarding him—
He states that because it pervades the *caitya*, its nature as *visarga* (emission) is also possible—beginning with "the locus of division" (*bhedapada*) and so forth.

The "locus of division" (*bhedapada*), meaning the place of differentiation, refers to the object of knowledge (*vedya*); however, the word [denoting it] makes known the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva, whose nature is consciousness (*vitti*). It is the concealer (*saṃvaraka*) of the soul; therefore, its very nature is such that if it belongs to this [soul].

The sense is that *saṃvara* (the act of covering/concealing) is its very nature (*svarūpa*). Even the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is a *saṃvara*—that is, it is pervasive—and therefore it becomes its nature; this is the meaning. Consequently, by virtue of having the form of the knowable, the individual soul (*jīva*) would become the object of the linguistic usage of the term "emission" (*visarga*), just like the knowable itself. [This applies] to the great ones.
"Of those who know the mantra-samaya" means this aforementioned manner of conduct (*vyavahṛti*), that is, practical behavior (*vyavahāra*). || 11 ||

The *caitya* is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the state of transformation through reflection; this is a property of consciousness (*cid-dharma*), arising from the emergence and dissolution of consciousness.
There is not even a trace of consciousness that does not have a reflected form;
therefore, it is a phenomenon, and consciousness arises from the power of reflective awareness.

Now, regarding the statement that there is a mutual devouring of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*) within the states of the individual soul (*paśu*) and Śiva, the author speaks— anticipating the question of what the cause for this is— beginning with "the object of worship" (*caityam*), etc.
The established doctrine of the secret *Āgama* is that the universe is the transformation of Light (*prakāśa*) and Awareness (*vimarśa*), which are synonyms for Śiva and Śakti.
Although it has been accepted by the ancients that the world is indeed a manifestation of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), nevertheless,
since the very nature of *vimarśa* cannot be established without *prakāśa* (light), even while *vimarśa* manifests in the form of the world,
it illuminates the aspect of light within that world with one half, and its own portion as the knower therein with the other half.

The aspect of light (*prakāśāṃśa*) is the object of knowledge (*vedya*), while the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśāṃśa*) is consciousness itself. This being so, that which is synonymous with the object of knowledge—the "caitya"—is the state of the transformation of reflective awareness; and upon close examination, it is indeed reflective awareness itself. Furthermore, this reflective awareness is an attribute of consciousness, an attribute of light. Why? Because it arises from light alone through the birth and dissolution of consciousness.

It dissolves back into that very same source; for since no entity whatsoever can have existence without manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), and since manifestation is dependent upon light (*prakāśa*), it must necessarily be admitted that its cause is light.
Furthermore, it is logical that the emergence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of sound-form, arises from the ether (*ākāśa*) and dissolves back into the ether itself.

That very sky is the Light; thus, by one who is eager for exposition, [the concepts of] ornamentation and so forth are taught out of compassion. Now, in another view, he states that even Light is an attribute of reflective awareness (vimarśa), saying: "It does not exist at all. That consciousness, even as the Light, would be of an unreflected nature if...
If its nature were unindicated by the reflection "this is such-and-such," it would not exist at all;

for if even an object that has not been reflected upon as "this is such-and-such" were to possess existence, it would follow that even things like a hare's horn would exist. Therefore, every object requires reflection when it ascends into the field of cognition; this applies to manifestation (*prakāśa*) as well.

He states—beginning with "Therefore, dharma arises"—that since deliberation (*vimarśa*) is the cause of the existence of a being (*sattva*), the quality of deliberation must necessarily be admitted [as its essential nature]. || 12 ||
(14) When the status of property and property-bearer is equal in the case of consciousness and its object,
their mutual stepping into each other's positions is their intrinsic nature.
Enveloped by consciousness, this sacrificial animal becomes the shrine; and by enveloping the shrine, even consciousness attains the state of Śiva. || 13 ||

He states the relevance of the discussion regarding the mutual relationship of attribute and substrate between *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) in the passage beginning with "of consciousness and its object" (*cic-caityayoḥ*).

In the manner described by the word "thus" (*iti*), when the relationship of attribute and substrate between consciousness and its object is equal, there occurs a mutual stepping into each other's positions; this is the innate nature (*svabhāva*) and the natural function (*naisargika-vyāpāra*) of the substrates. Of the substrates...

The sense is that this is due to the pervasiveness of the state of the subject-object relationship (*dharmapadavyāpti*). Furthermore, since it is possible for a single state to arise through the mutual succession of consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*caitya*), he says here:

"Enveloped by the object," and so forth. "This consciousness, enveloped by the object, becomes this beast"—by this direct reference to "this" before him, he demonstrates the state of wretchedness attained through the loss of one's own power. Now...
Enveloping and pervading the *caitya*, consciousness attains the renown of being "Śiva. || 13 ||
When the nature [of reality] is stilled through the equality of consciousness and its objects,
the intermediate state, which is a fusion [of the two], is the form of the Supreme Śambhu.
Through the mixing with various objects of worship, this [subject] is thus threefold:
the substratum (dharmin), that which is appropriate for each, and likewise the reflective awareness (vimarśa). || 14 ||

Now, he correctly teaches the nature of the third principle, the state of equal pervasion between consciousness (*citi*) and its objects (*caitya*), as it is a subject of dispute, beginning with the words "between consciousness and its objects," and so forth:
when the intrinsic nature of consciousness and its objects is stilled— that is, rendered motionless— by virtue of their equal pervasion.

The remainder [of the sentence] is that, by virtue of plunging into the nature of rest, that middle state—which is called "mixed"—becomes motionless and takes on the form of the Supreme Śambhu. The word *tu* (but/however) expresses the distinction from both Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*). By the phrase "the middle state," [the author indicates] the status of this particular state.
Although it is the third, its status as the "middle" is also accepted because it is fitting that it be a union due to possessing the dual nature of both Śiva and the individual soul (jīva);
this is taught when one considers the simultaneity of the activities of the jīva and Śiva, which consist of worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and renunciation (nivṛtti).

That very state, being conceived as a term of equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) because it is the root of both the tranquil state (*stimitadaśā*) and its opposite, pervades both sides and attains mastery over the specific qualities belonging to both sides. Just as a tree branch, which serves as the foundation for many twigs and roots, [exercises control] over those things connected to the twigs.

Just as this flowering and fruiting branch of a tree possesses ownership over its flowers, fruits, and so forth, in that same way, for the subject who perceives through the mixed state, there is a simultaneous realization of the activities of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), but not by ascending to the level of conceptual construction (vikalpaka) as if [the two] were merely the Śiva and the jīva. Were it otherwise, for one established in the third state...

Since there is an absence of even the majesty of entering into the essential nature of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) for one who, within the series of Śiva and jīvas of the Great Reality (mahātattva), is greedy to accept other activities for the sake of its own utility, any excellence—even if rooted in courtesy—would exist only in relation to those two; therefore, enough with this insistence on untimely dispute. Thus, here is this [conclusion]:
The intended meaning of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been stated thus: "One should not engage in discourse through erroneous understanding.

Now, strengthening the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth by means of a conclusion regarding the threefold division, he says: "Consciousness and the object of consciousness... This subject (*dharmin*), which has become manifest as a direct experience due to its mixed nature as reality, is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of the contemplation of duality.

Thus, "dharma" here refers to that which possesses it, namely the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). It is described as having three forms (*trirūpa*) from the perspective of the frequent usage of the term "mantra," but this is not because there is a fourth or fifth state; rather, it refers to the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the aforementioned nature, which takes the form of duality and so forth.

Intending to show that there is a threefold nature of the subjects (dharmin) due to their threefold nature, he says: "and appropriate to each. This appropriateness consists in the dualistic awareness of the individual soul (jīva), the non-dualistic awareness of Śiva, and the awareness consisting of both in the case of Paramaśiva.
The mind (*citti*) and the object of worship (*caitya*) are both that essence of reflective awareness (*vimarśatattva*);
for there is no ultimate difference between knowledge and action.
Knowledge would have the quality of grasping solidity as its action; knowledge itself would be that which possesses the support of rarefaction, and action alone [would be otherwise]. 15.

Thus, having clearly established here the nature of Śiva as the subject engaged with objects—the nature of Śiva as the threefold living soul (jīvatraya)—he explains His extremely essential nature as knowledge and action, beginning with "Consciousness" (citiḥ) and so forth. Consciousness is indeed *citi*; and that is indeed non-dual knowledge, as in [the cognition] "the jar is known."
For even though jars, cloths, and so forth are distinct, they are experienced as non-distinct due to their being of a single nature;

whereas the activity consisting of the form of the *caitya* is indeed of a distinct nature, because it is experienced in the form of distinction through the mutually exclusive essential natures of the *caityas*, such as jars and cloths.

Thus, he states that there is no ultimate difference between consciousness (*cit*) and its object (*caitya*), or between knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), in the words beginning with "for not of those two" (*na hi tayoḥ*). The intention is this: this appearance of difference between consciousness and its object is not ultimate; rather, it is based upon erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*), which is a synonym for *māyā*.
Regarding the distinction between the reality (*tattva*) and consciousness (*cit*), he says "knowledge" (*jñāna*), etc. Knowledge is illumination;

the sense is that it assumes the quality of solidity through the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Just as sound is the solidity of space, so too is reflective awareness the solidity of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); such is the relationship between illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

The intended meaning is that there is no real distinction between [consciousness] and water or a jar, as in the case of water and a jar. Now, one might object: let there be no distinction between *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) like that between water and a jar; however, it is impossible to deny the distinction between action—which consists of various forms such as jars and cloths due to its nature as an object (*caityātmikā*)—and light, which is of the nature of cognition. This is also true for reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is of the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*).
If it is argued that jars, cloths, and so forth are indeed distinct by virtue of having forms such as a broad base and a belly,

[we reply that] at the stage of discernment, no essential nature whatsoever remains for any object— such as a jar or a cloth— that exists apart from its own verbal designation and conceptual reflection (vimarśa) in the form of words like "jar" or "cloth."
Having established the non-difference of action from knowledge— since those whose darkness of illusion has been dispelled by the glance of the Guru have correctly understood [the truth]—

he now establishes the non-difference of knowledge from action, beginning with the words "Knowledge would be... That very action, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), assumes a state of fluidity through the abandonment of solidity.

It grasps the state of rest, which is the quality of thinness (viralimāna). This means that knowledge attains a state of absolute identity with light. Thus, the conclusion is that action is the external form of knowledge, while knowledge is the internal form of action; therefore, the two have the same essential object. || 15 ||
The form of cognition is not established without action,
and likewise, there is no apprehension of that action without it.
Therefore, the very state of their being twins is considered the established Siddhānta; indeed, the calculation of priority and posteriority here is merely the Pūrvapakṣa.

Now, demonstrating the *Yāmalasiddhānta*— which is established on the basis of the simultaneous realization of knowledge and action as being of equal primacy within the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and which is accepted as proven because it constitutes the very heart of the Mantra— he [the author] sets forth the root of the acceptance of this doctrine:

He restates what was previously mentioned— that knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), which are synonymous with manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are mutually causal— beginning with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). For, since without action, that is, without reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*) of knowledge is not established, and likewise, without that knowledge, [the nature of] that action is not established.
The non-apprehension of duality is not established; therefore, the state of being a pair—the simultaneous establishment of those two, namely knowledge and action—is indeed proven.

The sense is that this is "proven" (siddha) because it is connected to the perfected ones (*siddha*) due to its being the heart of mantra. In this context of investigating the establishment of knowledge and action, the conceptualization of priority and posteriority is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Whether it be in the form of the object and the subject, the primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa), the body and the self, the word and its meaning,

or even through various synonymous modes, the assertion of a temporal sequence between action and knowledge merely adopts the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), because such a sequence is impossible to establish.
The intended meaning. || 16 ||
One half is action, the other half is wisdom; the desire for equality between these two is the Middle Way.
Will alone is the seed; through its internal and external movement, knowledge and action are indeed the root and the sprout here. || 17 ||
Now,

[this occurs] through the Will (icchā), which is the unified form of both [knowledge and action], and which possesses the nature of both female and male, [arising from] the fitness of the relationship consisting of the single essential nature of the mutual inseparability of knowledge and action.

Intending to show the relationship of identity with the essential nature of the supreme Śiva-tattva as conceived by those who know the secret (rahasyavid), he demonstrates this connection through a single form in the passage beginning with "Half is action" (ardhaṃ kriyā). The intention is that action constitutes the right half of Śiva; for the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is accepted as the right path. Thus, this...

The established rule is as follows: knowledge (*jñāna*) is the other half, the left, because the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*) is accepted as belonging to the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*). [Objection: But is it not the case that Śaiva is the right-hand practice (*dakṣiṇācāra*) and Śākta is the left-hand practice (*vāmācāra*), according to the teaching of the Siddhas? [Response: This refers to ritual action (*kriyā*).

Since it consists of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it must be accepted as having the essential form of *Śakti*; and since knowledge (*jñāna*) consists of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*), it has the essential form of *Śiva*.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can action (*kriyā*) be the right-hand [path] and knowledge the left-hand [path]?"—it is true that this [confusion] belongs to those who are devoid of service to a true Guru who awakens one to the essence of the secret covenant (*samaya*).

The union (*saṅghaṭṭa*) is difficult to transcend; however, having set aside the state of Śiva characterized by the heavy side-glance of the Great Goddess (*mahāgurukaṭākṣa-śivatā*), it is here analyzed and taught as follows: it should be understood that the natures of Śiva and Śakti, who consist of knowledge and action respectively, have their own natures colored by one another through mutual passion.

Śiva’s nature is knowledge; when it is colored by activity, which has an insentient form, it becomes white through the whiteness of the insentient. Śakti’s nature is activity; when it is colored by non-insentient knowledge, it becomes ruddy through the radiance of the non-insentient sun. These two are mixed together.

Because of the union of both colors, that form becomes like gold; thus, in the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*) and the left-hand practice (*vāmācāra*), which consists solely of the activity of contemplating the nature of Śakti— the threefold aspects of will, knowledge, and action— corresponding to the three feet mentioned by Śambhu as synonyms for the threefold nature of Śiva and the others.

Thus it is established; this is the Kaulika Upaniṣad. This very object of knowledge has been elucidated by the author of the Sūtras through the presentation of the left and right halves as pertaining to knowledge and action.
He now states the arrangement of the parts according to his own will within the stages where knowledge and action are mixed:

"Equality of these two" means that the equality (*samatva*)—the state of equal pervasion (*samavyāptikatva*)—of these two, namely knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), is what one should desire; furthermore, the definition of will (*icchā*) should be understood here as well. "In the middle" means between the right and the left; this refers to the *icchātattva* (the principle of will).

He establishes that the previously explained nature of Supreme Śiva possesses the state of being the seed of both [powers], since it is the fundamental form of the two aspects consisting of knowledge and action, by means of the passage beginning "Desire alone is the seed. By the use of the particle *eva* (alone),
he demonstrates that even the triad of aspects— knowledge, action, and so forth— is essentially the nature of the three deities (*trimūrti*) which will be described hereafter.

Although it is logically consistent that these two are mutually foundational, nevertheless, according to the Madhyamika perspective, it has been taught by discerning great yogis that it is *icchā* (will) alone— which is a synonym for *suṣumnā*—
that is accepted as having the nature of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). This is because will alone is immovable, according to the principle previously established.

It has a steady nature; this specifically supports its status as a seed. For a seed remains motionless, while the root and the sprout alone extend inwardly and outwardly. Through internal movement, by way of an extension in the form of cessation, knowledge is the root that extends to the lower part of the seed; through external movement, it is the growing part.

In this context, activity (kriyā) is the sprout within the seed through the expansion of its active form; the word "and" (ca), by expressing a conjunction, indicates that the seed possesses its complete definition. || 17 ||
Knowledge, action, and will— which possesses the single flavor of both— constitute the triad of principles whose nature is eternally united.

"Knowledge" is the means of measurement, "the object of measurement" is the result, and "the knower" is the agent; for these are indeed different names for the various aspects of the single action. 18.

He states— beginning with "knowledge, action," etc.— that because will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) share a single objective through the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, the conventional usage of the terms "subject," "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) also occurs. Knowledge, action, and will— which is of a single flavor consisting of the synthesis of those two— are thus [the nature of the Lord].
The three principles possess a nature that is eternally united; they are mutually inseparable.

This qualification, by way of expressing the similarity between desire and the other [powers] and the subjects (pramātṛ) and so forth—whose nature is eternally united in the form of a triad—establishes their identity of purpose. Of desire and the others...

In response to the inquiry as to which [entity] among the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the others possesses oneness of referent with which [other entity], he says "of knowledge," and so forth. "Of knowledge" means [the relation] of the act of knowing; "the object of measurement" (*meya*) refers to the act; "of the other term" means of the term other than the act of knowing and the act [itself]; that is to say, of desire (*icchā*).
Furthermore, the distinction in designation arises from the difference in names, such as "the knower" (*mātṛ*), for those things possessing designations, such as desire and the rest.
The intended meaning is that, upon close examination of the knower and the other factors, there is indeed a distinction. || 18 ||
Knowledge and action are mutual roots; desire is the root of both of them, for indeed, that pair is the root of this [world].
This triad is considered the threefold form, possessing the nature of the three qualities (guṇas) by virtue of being the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. || 19 ||

With the intention of demonstrating how desire and the others arise from the triangular state of mantra, samaya, and siddhi, he establishes that each one has the other two as its root, beginning with "And knowledge... and so forth.
Knowledge and action are mutually rooted because their essential nature consists of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

The meaning is: "according to the principle previously established. Desire (*icchā*) is the root of those two—knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)—and the fact that the mixed category (*miśratattva*) has both as its root was also previously established;
for that desire, which consists of the mixture of knowledge and action, those two are the root of the third category.
The sense is that it is logical that accomplishment (siddhi) has the accomplishment of knowledge and action as its root.

This very triad of will and the rest, according to the aforementioned method, is the mutual root of the three forms of Being (sanmūrti) in the nature of Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha. Thus, the Great Power (Mahāśakti), appearing in the form of will and the rest, manifests itself.

The meaning is that this is the view of those who know the reality (*tattvavid*). Since even the three forms (*mūrti*) are mutually the source of one another, the existence of [the powers] such as Will (*icchā*) is established. When the triad of Will and the others is established as the three forms, it brings about the creation and so forth by depositing the principle of Mahat and the rest. This is the triad of Will and the others.

By virtue of being the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, its nature consists of the three *guṇas*. Within the sphere of the phenomenal world (*saṃsāra*), which is either differentiated or mixed, creation occurs in the principle of Will (*icchā-tattva*), maintenance in the principle of Knowledge (*jñāna-tattva*), and withdrawal in the principle of Action (*kriyā-tattva*). Thus, because this triad of Will and the others is the cause of creation and the rest, it possesses a nature of the three *guṇas* according to the sequence of creation and so forth.

The meaning is that the nature of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) is precisely the triad of desire and so forth, which constitutes the very essence of the three qualities (guṇas).
Because it consists of these three, everything is threefold in form; likewise, the states such as deep sleep and so forth are also three.
Sleep arises from the dullness resulting from action; the continuum is knowledge; and desire is another state that is a mixture of these two.

Therefore, he says— "By means of these three as their primary nature," and so forth— stating that in *saṃsāra*, every single entity exists in a threefold form precisely by way of being of the nature of desire (*icchā*) and the rest.
When all things whatsoever are examined in such forms as the three worlds, the three castes, and the three Vedas, they are found to exist solely in a threefold manner.

The meaning here is that the very fact of consisting of the triad beginning with will (*icchā*) is the reason. Now, he states that the three states under discussion—sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, including creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest—are also essentially composed of will and the other powers, by saying "sleep and the rest.
Thus, even the states of sleep and so on are essentially composed of will and the rest; this is the intention of the author of the Sūtras.

The secret object of knowledge (*rahasya-prameya*), which constitutes the intended meaning of what was stated generally, is now taught as it was originally composed by the Primordial Creator (*Ādikṛt*); for its application is seen in what follows, and because it has been transmitted through the lineage from the mouth of the Guru.
This is done because, in the state where sleep and the other [states] are mutually rooted in their nature as will (*icchā*) and so forth, they possess equal primacy.

When the three corners of the triangle are reached, a state of mutual beginning, middle, and end may be conceived; and this being so, the states of will, knowledge, and action, established as beginning, middle, and end, are each individually conceivable.
For instance, in the transmigratory world of duality, deep sleep is the will, because it consists of resting within the form of duality.

And because it is the locus for the commencement of the differentiation of saṃsāra, the "locus of commencement" is the path (mārga) struck by desire and so forth; it is a dream, because it is a state of slight contraction of knowledge (*jñāna*). Desire is the locus of commencement, while the stage of knowledge (*jñānadaśā*) is the locus of some accomplishment of what has been commenced; it is the state of waking, because it is a more distinct state characterized by the contraction of activity (*kriyā*).

Because that which has been commenced is brought to completion, there is the act of cessation; this is the direct path (*ṛjumārga*). Thus, it should be understood that every exertion is established within the triad of words: "he wills," "he knows," and "he acts. Furthermore, when there is an exertion toward the act of resting, the will of awakening [arises] upon the accomplishment of one exertion, while another [remains].

Since a pause in its activity is possible in the middle of its engagement, a state of rest characterized by desire exists within the waking state; this should be understood to apply similarly elsewhere as well.
Dreaming is cessation, because of the partial unfolding of knowledge; deep sleep is action.

Because it is a state of rest resulting from the continuity of activity, the nature of will, activity, and cognition has been described here individually for both deep sleep and waking; now, another state is being described. Because it consists of both conceptual and non-conceptual forms, dream—which is a state of rest that is not insentient—is the state of Light (*prakāśapada*).
Deep sleep is the state of rest for the insentient; the locus of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is dreaming, because it consists of the process of mutual appropriation between these two;
and waking cognition is the light within the waking state, as it takes the form of the commencement of activity that renders the insentient conscious.

In the objective aspect (vedyāṃśa), which appears as external to oneself, there occurs "insentient deep sleep" due to the assumption of insentience; this is because of the complete recollection of the act of becoming insentient, an act that was previously desired through [the state of] activity. Now, regarding this insentient nature, when it is once again made manifest, it becomes non-insentient.

Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is precisely the exertion of the activity of becoming (*bhāva-kriyā*), because it consists in the commencement of an activity that is not yet inert (*ajaḍībhāva*). Waking (*jāgrat*) is knowledge (*jñāna*), [characterized by] the emergence of a certain non-inertness in the object (*vedya*) which is touched by the light of the knower (*vedaka*). Dream (*svapna*) is activity (*kriyā*), consisting entirely of that which has both an inert and a non-inert form.

This is due to the continuous connection with the activity of non-inertness. In this way, it should be understood that for each of dream and deep sleep there is the nature of will and the nature of action, while for the waking state there is the nature of knowledge.
By this very same method, one should also understand the process of mutual existence between the states of waking and dreaming, as well as between the positions of the inert and non-inert subjects.
According to the method to be explained, by virtue of being a fusion of the *bindu* and *visarga*,

and by penetrating the intermediate stage of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) which consists of resting in both the insentient and the sentient, the nature of Will (*icchā*) must be applied to each [of these]. Since deep sleep, though consisting of rest, is composed of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the designation of it as "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is entirely unobjectionable.

The individual soul (*jīva*), by plunging into deep sleep (*suṣupti*), becomes Śiva even while knowing that state of rest; and Śiva, by plunging into that same state, becomes the individual soul while knowing its insentience (*jaḍatva*). Thus, it is entirely logical that deep sleep occupies the middle position [between the states of waking and dreaming]; this is a flawless and sound conclusion. This applies likewise to the triad of states beginning with sleep.
By the practice of any [of these] whatsoever, through the state of reverse and direct order,

even the samādhi of the mutual relationship between the three stages of the flow of the words and Śiva-Śakti is accomplished; thus, for one who [practices] within the three sections of the Mātṛkā which awaken the three states beginning with deep sleep...

Since the reversal [of the sequence] of even a single [syllable] through some method is indeed traditional, that investigation of all the procedures should be thoroughly studied. As it was said by the author of the *Laghustotra* in the introduction to the *Bālā-mantra*, which consists of a collection of *mātṛkās*: "Whether it follows the established order or exists in a reversed order..."

Even in the context of the worship of the Śrīcakra— which consists of the three groups of wheels (such as the fourteen-spoked wheel) that are reflections of the three states beginning with deep sleep— there occurs, by means of the commencement of any one of those groups,
a flow of the three groups of wheels in both reverse and direct order, with reference to the three seed-syllables.

It has been explained that the complete investigation of this entire process belongs to the eminent teachers, as it is precisely the accomplishment of right experience through meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
and that this object of knowledge is the very life-breath of the great mantra and yantra.

Establish that dreaming, waking, and deep sleep possess the nature of will, knowledge, and action by means of the well-known path, beginning with "deep sleep is action," and so forth. Regarding their status as action, insentience (*jāḍya*) is stated as the reason; for action indeed consists in an external connection [with objects] through the form of direct experience, which is distinct from memory.
Since it does not become non-inert like the internal reflection of the form of that cognition, the inertness of action is established by experience. || 20 ||

In this context, the existence of the two forms— the shrine (*caitya*) and the embodied being (*city*)— which have their bodies mutually merged, occurs in three states, beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
It should be contemplated as being conjoined with both worldly engagement and renunciation,
through the vision of its abiding within the fundamental structure of the Śrīcakra.

He clarifies the dual nature of deep sleep and the other states— consisting of both the insentient and the sentient— as indicated by the previously stated method, beginning with the words "of those whose bodies are mutually merged. Indeed,
the three states beginning with deep sleep belong to Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), which are respectively synonymous with consciousness (cit) and the object of consciousness (caitya).
The very nature [of consciousness] is the locus of the worldly transaction of wandering through and resting within saṃsāra.

Its inherent character is the mutual absorption of *cit* (consciousness) and *caitanya* (the object of consciousness)—terms synonymous with *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Indeed, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of *vimarśa* resides invariably within *prakāśa*, and the latent impression of *prakāśa* resides within *vimarśa*.

Because these two possess a nature consisting of mutual dependence, by means of this very distinction between insentience and sentience, within each of their own essential forms during the three states such as deep sleep and so forth, that which is insentient [is present] in the sentient, or that which is sentient in the insentient, remains latent in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) and manifests in turn.

The purport of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding the phrase "of the *caitya* and the *acitya*," the intention is that because the word *caitya* is placed first, due to the predominance of *māyā*, there is first the manifestation of the states of the individual soul (*jīva*), which are synonyms for the *caitya*.
Thus, existence (*bhava*) consists of activity and cessation respectively pertaining to the *caitya* and the *acitya*—that is, the *jīva* and Śiva—and for this very reason, it is of two forms.
Samsara is to be contemplated as intertwined and mutually merged within the three states, such as deep sleep (suṣupti) and the rest.

Regarding the determination of this "intertwining" (śleṣa), characterized by the mutual merging of the states of the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva, he states the root source in the passage beginning with "Śrīcakra," etc.
The "cakra" is the nine-triangle yantra distinguished by intertwining; the "root-mantra" (mūlamanu) and the "Mātṛkā" [alphabet] are those two.

"Arrangement" (saṃsthiti) refers to a specific configuration; by observing—that is, by reflecting upon—that arrangement, one perceives the structure of the Śrīcakra within each of the three groups [of triangles], beginning with the fourteen-spoked [lotus]. In each group, there is a junction of two triangles;
through that junction, those [triangles] abide in a triple form for each individual group.

The realization of the successive manifestation of the states of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) through the determination of their mutual interpenetration is the fundamental abiding in the Root; it is the movement of the three sections in both direct and reverse order, and by means of that,
the regulation consisting of activity and cessation of the states of the individual soul and Śiva which are mutually interpenetrated.
The distinction is that it is the practice of manifesting [the deity] in succession. || 21 ||
Desire is deep sleep; awakening that does not produce external [perception] is knowledge; and for the insentient, activity becomes waking.

Indeed, the states beginning with will (icchā) and ending with deep sleep (suṣupti)— ranging from the waking state situated in the fourth (turyastha) up to the limit of deep sleep— are the non-inert aspects of Śiva.

Now, by means of the arrangement of mantras established through the sequence of articulatory efforts— namely, the slightly opened (*vivṛti*), the touched (*spṛṣṭi*), the slightly touched (*spṛṣṭīṣat*), the slightly opened (*iṣadvivṛti*), and the fully opened (*vivṛti*)—

one should understand the two paths of activity and cessation belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva, which range from deep sleep up to waking for the former, and from waking up to deep sleep for the latter.
The manifestation of the state full of contraction (saṅkoca) becomes heart-stirring for those who share the conventions of the connoisseurs (sahṛdaya).
Desiring to make that convention understood by resorting to that path, he establishes the nature of desire and the rest as being sleep and so forth, beginning with "Desire is deep sleep," etc.

The intended meaning is that deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the various forms of desire, and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) are [the states of the individual soul]. Awakening (*prabodha*) produced neither externally nor internally is dreaming (*svapna*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) is waking (*jāgaraṇa*), the state of wakefulness. Action (*kriyā*) is the designation of the inherence (*samavāya*) of desire and the other qualities in the inert living being (*jīva*). This refers to the one established in the fourth state (*turyastha*), and so forth. Indeed, this was stated previously.
When the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are perceived as non-different, there is the conventional usage of the term "the Fourth" (*turya*). With this intention, it is said here:

"the state of waking and so forth situated in the Fourth. This means that the state of waking—which is of the nature of non-difference and pertains to the conventional usage of the Fourth—starting from its beginning up to the boundaries of deep sleep, constitutes the deep sleep of one who abides in the Fourth; these [states] have that [deep sleep in the Fourth] as their limit.

The meaning is that waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are non-differentiated. Since non-inertness is already established by the state of the Fourth (turya), the further qualification "non-inert" (ajaḍa) should be understood as being applied by way of its being the foundational substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). The states of Śiva consist of [the powers of] Will and so forth.

An objection may be raised: "Was it not previously stated that Śiva consists of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and is oriented toward activity (*pravṛtti*), while the bound soul (*paśu*) consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and is oriented toward withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)? How, then, can it be said here that the fourth state (*turya*) is of the nature of withdrawal for Śiva? To this it is replied: The bound soul who is oriented toward withdrawal is indeed designated as Śiva.
And Śiva, being oriented toward manifestation, is designated as the "bound soul" (paśu); such is the faultless path of instruction of the Great Guru, the author of the Sūtras. || 22 ||
The movement of the *bindu* is said by the teachers to be inward-facing, while the movement of the *visarga* is said to be outward-facing.
The former reaches the middle state of deep sleep from the midst of waking,
while the latter reaches deep sleep from the midst of that [middle state].
Now,

reminding us of the previously established method— that the mutual manifestation of Jīva and Śiva as distinct from one another due to their being outward-turned and inward-turned is indeed logically sound— he says: "Antarmukhī," and so forth.
The Guru has stated that the movement of the *bindu* is inward-facing (*antarmukhī*), while the movement of the *visarga* is outward-facing (*bahirmukhī*).

Since it was previously established that these two possess the natures of resting (*viśramaṇa*) and transmigrating (*saṃsaraṇa*), they need not be explained here; this should be understood accordingly.
