And how can there be the state of *visarga* for the subject of non-duality in the external state of the fourth-wakefulness (*turya-jāgrat*)?

To this, he says: "Even in duality. Even in duality—that is, within the transmigratory world of difference—the *bindu* is the presiding deity of the group of short vowels in the state of non-differentiation.
In the non-dual cycle of emanation (*visarga*), the long vowels are the presiding deities over the internal and external boundaries.

In the dream state of duality and in the waking state of the Fourth (*turya*), they are perceived as the locus of knowledge and action respectively—specifically, the internal state as the locus of knowledge and the external state as the locus of action—in the form of the letters *e* and *o*. This is the meaning. These two...
By the power of the context— that is, by the power of the context which consists of both difference and non-difference— the *bindu* and the *visarga* do not attain that nature of the *bindu*,
which is non-differentiated, nor that nature of the *visarga*,
which is differentiated; rather, they clearly manifest that nature which consists of both non-difference and difference.

Because of the negation, "one does not attain the very manifest nature," it is understood that one indeed attains some nature. This is the meaning: the *bindu* situated in the state of the dream of duality does not clearly attain its nature as non-duality due to the force of the context of duality, but it certainly attains something [of it].
For one who is awake from the state of pure differentiation, there is non-differentiation within the dream due to the touch of non-duality;

by virtue of that touch, it becomes a specific state. Likewise, even the emission (*visarga*) established in the waking state of the Fourth (*turya*) does not clearly attain a nature of differentiation through the power of the context of non-duality; rather, it attains nothing at all.

It should be understood that because the pure state, which is non-different in form from the fourth dream-state (turiya-svapna), comes into contact with differentiation through the fourth waking-state (turya-jāgrat), a distinction indeed exists. || 10 ||
The *bindu*, the *kalā*, and the *visargakalā* are the *guṇas*; furthermore,
*sarga*, *kalā*, and the *bindukalā* are constituent parts [of these].
The Bindu is indeed the fire of eight kalās, the consumer of the Visarga;
but the Sarga is the Moon, the firm Bindu of sixteen kalās. || 11 ||

Now, demonstrating that in this state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the *bindu* and the *visarga*, as well as their respective powers (*kalā*), is identical due to their mutual interpenetration, he explains the nature of the original form (*bimba*) of the *bindu* and *visarga*:

"It should be understood that [this occurs] when there is the conceit of the pervasion of the *visarga*. Now, *sarga* is *visarga*, and its powers (*kalā*) are also [to be understood in the same way].
It should be understood that [the mantra] becomes a limb (*aṅga*) of the *kalās* of the *bindu* when there is the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *bindu*.
Now, as to how many *kalās* belong to the *bindu* and how many to the *visarga*, he says: "The *bindu*-fire," and so forth.
The *bindu*-fire is the *bindu* in the form of fire. It consists of exactly eight *kalās*: the five short vowels, the two [diphthongs] *e* and *o*, and *aṃ*.
One *kalā* is its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*). Thus, there are eight *kalās* of the *bindu*.
There are eight *visarga-kalās* that constitute the limbs (*aṅga*) of the *bindu*. To the question of how the *bindu* possesses eight *kalās*, he says:
"the drinker of the *visarga*" (*visargapāyī*), meaning it drinks the *visarga* which has the form of the moon. [The *bindu*] is the fire within the *bindu*, accompanied by the *kalās*.

The meaning is that the *visarga* assumes a single form; thus, there are exactly eight *kalās* of the *bindu*. "Firm *bindu*" (*dṛḍhabindu*) means that even during its own pervasion, the *bindu* is not severed, because upon its cessation, the unity of the nature of the *visarga* is established.
The *indu*, which is the *visarga* in the form of the moon, possesses sixteen *kalās* together with the *kalās* of the *bindu* as its constituent parts.
The construction is as follows: the five long vowels, along with the forms of the letters *ai*, *au*, and *ahaḥ*, and the sixteen digits of the visarga. || 11 ||
From the *bindu* there are seven *kalās*, and from the *visarga* there are also seven; by virtue of this sequence, [there arises] the fourteen-spoked [wheel].
The Bindu, fire, and the creation situated within the eight-petaled lotus;
and within that, the sixteen-petaled lotus. || 12 ||

Now he demonstrates the mutual union of the *bindu* and the *visarga*, as well as their respective digits (*kalās*), within the fourteen-spoked wheel (*cakra*) situated in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the Great Yantra—beginning with the words "of the *bindu*" and so forth. There are seven digits of the *bindu* and seven digits of the *visarga*; in both cases, it should be understood that these are exclusive of the digits of the constituent parts.
By virtue of the sequence and the conjunction of these two groups of seven, it results in fourteen spokes;

this is the remainder [of the sense]. Within that—that is, inside those fourteen corners—is the point (bindu), which, according to the previously taught method of contemplating sleep, resides within the fire of the eight-petalled lotus. Of this...

And within the Bindu, which has the form of an eight-petalled lotus, there is the Visarga situated in the sixteen-petalled lotus; here too, the process previously explained should be kept in mind. || 12 ||
The fire, consisting of the short vowels, indeed occupies the eight-petaled portion; the moon, whose nature consists of the long measures, occupies the sixteen-petaled lotus portion.
In the case of the Moon and Sun, who consist of eight digits multiplied by three, there is a conjunction in the Fire [triangle] with the Bindu, which consists of eight petals multiplied by four.
Thus ends the second section, the Investigation of Deep Sleep, in the Investigation of the Wheel of the Mother-Syllables (Mātṛkācakra).
Now, in another manner, the *bindu-kalā* is distinguished. Thus, demonstrating the sixteen petals of the *visarga*,

he shows the three stages consisting of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *bindu* and *visarga* within the group of vowels— beginning with "short" (*hrasva*), etc.— wherein "fire" (*anala*) is the *bindu*.
The moon, which is the *visarga*, takes the form of short vowels and resides within the circle of an eight-petalled lotus;

it possesses the nature of long measures (*mātrā*) and rests upon the circle of a sixteen-petalled lotus. The meaning is that it is supported by the circle of the sixteen-petalled lotus, which consists of the sixteen measures found within the eight long vowels. This is because each vowel possesses two measures.

Although among the sixteen-mātrā-perfected long vowels and consonants, eight mātrās consist of the *bindu*— since the rule for the placement of the *visarga* requires it to be accompanied by the *bindu*— nevertheless, because the *bindu* can exist as a distinct object separate from the form of a short vowel, [the phoneme] consists of sixteen *mātrās*.

There is the conceit that the eight long vowels are the distinct domain of the *visarga*. And thus, by this, the solar nature (*arkatva*) of the *bindu*—which presides over the state of non-difference between the *visarga* and the *bindu* of the Moon and Sun—is also indicated, because the non-dual fragment has a single presiding subject. This is because the attainment of the aesthetic wonder of differentiation has been described.

The sun is that which brings about the mastery over the world with remainder; fire is that which brings about the mastery over the world without remainder. Therefore, the sense is that both [the moon and the sun] are designated as the "point" (bindu) of non-duality. Of those two—the moon and the sun, whose forms are the visarga and the bindu, and which consist of twenty-four digits (eight multiplied by three)— [The verse continues: The moon, which is the supreme nectar, is the essence of the eightfold [powers]; it is the supreme bliss, the supreme lord, and the supreme reality. It is the supreme Śiva, the supreme Śakti, and the supreme soul. It is the supreme light, the supreme void, and the supreme consciousness. It is the supreme time, the supreme space, and the supreme direction. It is the supreme mantra, the supreme mudrā, and the supreme yoga. It is the supreme dharma, the supreme jñāna, and the supreme vairāgya. It is the supreme aiśvarya, the supreme śānti, and the supreme śāntyatītā. It is the supreme creation, the supreme maintenance, and the supreme dissolution. It is the supreme awakening, the supreme dream, and the supreme deep sleep. It is the supreme fourth state (turya), the supreme beyond-the-fourth (turyātīta), and the supreme all-pervasive (vyāpaka). It is the supreme guru, the supreme disciple, and the supreme lineage. It is the supreme initiation, the supreme consecration, and the supreme transmission. It is the supreme truth, the supreme liberation, and the supreme goal. It is the supreme peace, the supreme joy, and the supreme rest. It is the supreme ocean, the supreme mountain, and the supreme tree. It is the supreme lotus, the supreme lion-throne, and the supreme throne. It is the supreme palace, the supreme temple, and the supreme city. It is the supreme wheel, the supreme mandala, and the supreme yantra. It is the supreme syllable Om, the supreme Hrim, and the supreme Hūm. It is the supreme A, the supreme Ā, and the supreme Aḥ. It is the supreme Ka, the supreme Kha, and the supreme Ga. It is the supreme Gha, the supreme Ṅa, and the supreme Ca. It is the supreme Cha, the supreme Ja, and the supreme Jha. It is the supreme Ña, the supreme Ta, and the supreme Tha. It is the supreme Dha, the supreme Na, and the supreme Pa. It is the supreme Pha, the supreme Ba, and the supreme Bha. It is the supreme Ma, the supreme Ya, and the supreme Ra. It is the supreme La, the supreme Va, and the supreme Śa. It is the supreme Ṣa, the supreme Sa, and the supreme Ha. It is the supreme Kṣa, the supreme A, and the supreme Visarga. It is the supreme Bindu, the supreme Nāda, and the supreme Śakti. It is the supreme Vyāpinī, the supreme Samanā, and the supreme Unmanā. It is the supreme Mūlādhāra, the supreme Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the supreme Maṇipūra. It is the supreme Anāhata, the supreme Viśuddhi, and the supreme Ājñā. It is the supreme Lalanā, the supreme Rasanā, and the supreme Avadhūtī. It is the supreme Iḍā, the supreme Piṅgalā, and the supreme Suṣumnā. It is the supreme Gaṅgā, the supreme Yamunā, and the supreme Sarasvatī. It is the supreme Gaurī, the supreme Lakṣmī, and the supreme Sarasvatī. It is the supreme Umā, the supreme Pārvatī, and the supreme Śivā. It is the supreme Durgā, the supreme Kālī, and the supreme Tārā. It is the supreme Tripurā, the supreme Bhairavī, and the supreme Vārāhī. It is the supreme Cāmuṇḍā, the supreme Mahālakṣmī, and the supreme Siddhalakṣmī. It is the supreme Gaṇeśa, the supreme Kārttikeya, and the supreme Nandin. It is the supreme Brahmā, the supreme Viṣṇu, and the supreme Rudra. It is the supreme Īśvara, the supreme Sadāśiva, and the supreme Śiva. It is the supreme Śakti, the supreme Śaktimān, and the supreme Śiva-Śakti-saṃghaṭṭa. It is the supreme unity, the supreme duality, and the supreme non-duality. It is the supreme oneness, the supreme manyness, and the supreme all-inclusiveness. It is the supreme beginning, the supreme middle, and the supreme end. It is the supreme birth, the supreme life, and the supreme death. It is the supreme past, the supreme present, and the supreme future. It is the supreme cause, the supreme effect, and the supreme instrument. It is the supreme knowledge, the supreme object of knowledge, and the supreme knower. It is the supreme subject, the supreme object, and the supreme consciousness. It is the supreme silence, the supreme speech, and the supreme song. It is the supreme dance, the supreme music, and the supreme offering. It is the supreme worship, the supreme devotion, and the supreme surrender. It is the supreme grace, the supreme mercy, and the supreme protection. It is the supreme refuge, the supreme support, and the supreme shelter. It is the supreme light, the supreme darkness, and the supreme radiance. It is the supreme heat, the supreme cold, and the supreme balance. It is the supreme hunger, the supreme thirst, and the supreme satisfaction. It is the supreme pleasure, the supreme pain, and the supreme equanimity. It is the supreme friend, the supreme enemy, and the supreme indifference. It is the supreme teacher, the supreme disciple, and the supreme transmission. It is the supreme scripture, the supreme commentary, and the supreme realization. It is the supreme liberation, the supreme bondage, and the supreme freedom. It is the supreme heaven, the supreme earth, and the supreme underworld. It is the supreme mountain, the supreme river, and the supreme forest. It is the supreme village, the supreme city, and the supreme kingdom. It is the supreme kingdom of heaven, the supreme kingdom of earth, and the supreme kingdom of hell. It is the supreme Brahmaloka, the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, and the supreme Kailāsa. It is the supreme Śvetadvīpa, the supreme Pātāla, and the supreme Rasātala. It is the supreme Sumeru, the supreme Mandara, and the supreme Kailāsa. It is the supreme Meru, the supreme Kula, and the supreme Kula-krama. It is the supreme Kula, the supreme Akula, and the supreme Kula-Akula-saṃghaṭṭa. It is the supreme Kaulika, the supreme Kaulinī, and the supreme Kaula. It is the supreme Kula-yoga, the supreme Kula-mudrā, and the supreme Kula-mantra. It is the supreme Kula-tattva, the supreme Kula-jñāna, and the supreme Kula-vairāgya. It is the supreme Kula-aiśvarya, the supreme Kula-śānti, and the supreme Kula-śāntyatītā. It is the supreme Kula-sṛṣṭi, the supreme Kula-sthiti, and the supreme Kula-saṃhāra. It is the supreme Kula-bodha, the supreme Kula-svapna, and the supreme Kula-suṣupti. It is the supreme Kula-turya, the supreme Kula-turyātīta, and the supreme Kula-vyāpaka. It is the supreme Kula-guru, the supreme Kula-śiṣya, and the supreme Kula-santāna. It is the supreme Kula-dīkṣā, the supreme Kula-abhiṣeka, and the supreme Kula-krama. It is the supreme Kula-satya, the supreme Kula-mokṣa, and the supreme Kula-prayojana. It is the supreme Kula-śānti, the supreme Kula-ānanda, and the supreme Kula-viśrāma. It is the supreme Kula-samudra, the supreme Kula-parvata, and the supreme Kula-vṛkṣa. It is the supreme Kula-padma, the supreme Kula-siṃhāsana, and the supreme Kula-pīṭha. It is the supreme Kula-prāsāda, the supreme Kula-mandira, and the supreme Kula-nagara. It is the supreme Kula-cakra, the supreme Kula-maṇ

The eight *kalās* of the *bindu*, which is the self of those [vowels], multiplied by three, constitute twenty-four *kalās*. The *visarga* consists of sixteen *kalās*, in the form of the measures (*mātrā*) of the long vowels. Together, both possess twenty-four *kalās*. In these two, which consist of the eight parts of the protracted (*pluta*) vowels, there are eight protracted syllables formed by twenty-four measures (*mātrā*).
They are accomplished because the *pluta* vowel has three morae (*trimātra*).
In that Great Bindu, which is Fire, this [state] exists because it pervades both the positions of difference and non-difference.
The Great Bindu is indeed fire alone; it is not even a locus for the conventional usage of the sun.
In that fire, there would be the union (*yukti*), that is, the conjunction (*yoga*), of those two, the moon and the sun, because the *pluta* vowel is the resonance (*nāda*) within the nose.
Of this state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), which consists of that [fire],...
It has been taught that the Great Reality (mahātattva), which is the motionless ground of the movement of both worldly engagement and withdrawal, is eternal.
It possesses a single form composed of three aspects: non-differentiation, differentiation, and their mixture.
The power of Śiva, consisting of the meaning of the groups of vowels, shines within the hearts of the great-souled ones.

Having contemplated the form of the supreme phoneme (*varṇa*), which is meaningful, consisting of the two parts— the *bindu* and *visarga*— and possessing a central line that indicates the state of their essential identity (*sāmarasya*).
And this mortal [mantra], though merely recited, is the root of all spiritual accomplishments. || 1 ||
The form of the letter *i* should be worshipped as the seat of the throbbing *bindu* within, and externally, above that, as the eightfold nature of the *visarga*.
And then the image of the letter *ma* in reverse order. || 2 ||
In the center is the full point (bindu) which indicates the mixed words; at the top of that is the point of the fragments of the words "cit" and "acit";
and it has the form of the moon and fire within the orb of the letter *ī*.
One should place the sandals of Śrī upon the heads of the supreme Śiva. || 3 ||
The eternal sixteen-fold essence, the digit of the vowels, whose form is the perpetual triangle, is a single wave of the substance of flavor for those who have directly realized the void.

For one who worships correctly through this [mantra], the meaning of the host of divine syllables— the ground of fulfilled purpose— shall flash forth in his heart by the grace of Ambikā, even though it was previously hidden.
By the sage Śivānanda, who abides by the command of his teacher,
the word has been explained in the second [chapter], the "Discrimination of the Wheel of Mātṛkās."
Thus ends the second section.
Now begins the third section:
Thus, the causal state of the universe has been investigated; this sequence of effects arises from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Having rested in the Self, which is called the Supreme, during sleep, the reflective awareness then vomits forth the universe in the state of awakening. || 1 ||

Now, beginning a new section (*skandha*), in order to demonstrate the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections, he introduces the subject matter (*prameya*) of the subsequent section by first stating the purport of the preceding section,
beginning with the words "of the universe" (*viśvasya*). In this manner, [he describes] the universe in its form as both rest (*viśrānti*) and saṃsāra.
The state of the cause-and-effect form has been described as the state of resting in the causal stage.

The meaning is that dreamless sleep, which is the nature of resting, is the universe in its causal form, while dreams and so forth, which constitute the form of transmigratory existence, are the universe in its effect-form. Such is the sequence of effects; when it is the sequence of causes, then—
The meaning is that the sequence of the effect also follows from the identity of form between cause and effect.

The sequence of the cause consists of the attainment of the three levels—such as the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—and the pervasion of the insentient and sentient; in the same way, the sequence of the effect is the sequence of the levels of the object of knowledge and so forth, which resides within the effect. This is the effect.

The ellipsis implies that the universe arises from *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). *Vimarśa* is the reflective awareness of the universe, which consists of the verbal nature [of consciousness] rooted in the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) that "this is such-and-such. Therefore, the universe, in its form as an effect, has *vimarśa* as its root. In what form does this *vimarśa* abide during the repose of deep sleep?

Regarding this, he says "rested" (*viśrāntam*), and so forth. "Vimarśa" [refers to] sleep, at the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "In the speech called Parā"—that is, in the speech conventionally designated as *parā*. "In the self" means in one's own form, which is the nature of *parāvāk*.
"The universe rested" means it was dissolved. "Then," that is, immediately after deep sleep.

Even in the state of awakening (*vibodhapada*), during the phase of emergence (*vyutthānadaśā*), he "vomits" or emits [the universe] outward; by this, it is indicated that the existence of the universe is essentially grounded in *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Because it is of the nature of its play (*vilāsa*), it is the play of *vimarśa*.
Even while being absorbed within *vimarśa* itself, in the state of awakening, it manifests clearly through the internal and external senses.
The sense is that [the world] emerges from the womb of *vimarśa*. || 1 ||
The supreme Speech (Parā-vāṇī), indeed consisting of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*, accompanied by the scent of contraction, is also asleep in the ether.
Contraction itself is the speech of the ether of consciousness and unconsciousness; that ether contracts within primordial nature (prakṛti) and within reflective awareness (vimarśa).

It has been stated that *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) abides in the repose of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) by way of the form of the "beyond" and the "this-side. Regarding the question of what the locus and what the essential nature of the supreme speech (*parā vāk*) is within the state of repose consisting of the vowels from *a* to *u*—which represent the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—the author says: "Speech," and so forth. [This refers to] the supreme speech (*parā vāṇī*).

Indeed, by means of this [form of the letter *ṛ* and *ḷ*], it is stated that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the nature of the supreme word (*parāvāk*), possesses the character of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It should be understood that even in states of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), reflective awareness is of the nature of a means of valid cognition;
for the senses, which are themselves of the nature of means of valid cognition, consist of synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and [reflective awareness] is that synthesis.

Since [the process] culminates in the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the very nature of reflective awareness is the sense organs themselves; this is the distilled discernment. Furthermore, regarding the fact that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), consisting of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*, is the nature of reflective awareness as the supreme speech (*parāvāk*), he provides another justification for their contraction even during the act of movement.
The sense is that even in sleep, which is of a general nature, it possesses its full essence.

The presence of contraction is perceived in the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ* in comparison with the vowels *i* and *u*, because they are experienced as having a degree of grossness similar to that found in consonantal phonemes. Now, [one might ask] regarding the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*)...

If contraction (*saṅkoca*) is its very nature, then indeed the validity (*pramāṇatva*) consisting of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*, which are characterized by the state of contraction, is established; thus he demonstrates that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Parāvāk has contraction as its nature, [beginning with] the words "contraction" (*saṅkoca*). Of the sky of consciousness and non-consciousness (*cidacidgagana*)...
The repose within the sky, which consists of the equilibrium of consciousness and unconsciousness, is indeed contraction.
In the state of the reflective awareness of speech (*vāṇī-vimarśa*), that very nature, having come to rest, is experienced in its fullness.
In whatever manner that same nature assumes the ground of inquiry (*anusandhāna-bhūmikā*), so [does it manifest].

It contracts by way of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of the manifestation of both the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). Indeed, the contraction of the sky occurs through the form of sound. It is thus established that there is a contraction of the reflective awarenesses in the form of sound within the sky, which is of the nature of repose. Now, [one might ask: what of that which abides in fullness?
For what reason does that sky of repose attain a state of contraction through the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)? To this he says:

"That void" (*tadvyoma*). That void—the sky of repose—contracts when reflective awareness is its *prakṛti*, its very nature. The assumption of a state of contraction by the nature of reflective awareness is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the principle of repose.
The meaning is that there is no cause whatsoever for this. || 2 ||
When fixed upon its own dharma— which flows by its own inherent nature and consists of the very form of speech—
even the supreme ether attains existence.
The reality of non-discrimination, which is eternally embraced by sentient beings, wonderfully reaches even the sky, which is its true nature (dharmatā). || 3 ||

Now, demonstrating that even the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the seed of the world in its form as effect, possesses the nature of being the seed of the world in its causal form, he explains its greatness with the words beginning "dharma" and so forth: "in that which flows by its own natural impulse," meaning it has the habit of flowing spontaneously and not through the instigation of another; for if it were so [dependent], then there would also be a need for an instigator of that [instigator].

Since impulsion is impossible without a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of the formative intention (*saṅkalpa*), and since that reflective awareness itself cannot proceed without another reflective awareness— leading to an infinite regress— one must admit that reflective awareness possesses an inherent spontaneity (*svarasavāhitva*) as its ultimate state. Therefore, within the nature of speech which flows spontaneously, it is indeed a property of consciousness (*ciddharma*) residing in consciousness itself.

And because of the dissolution into the Source (janana-laya), according to the principle previously established, when one is fixed in one's own nature which is the very form of reflective awareness (vimarśa)—that is, in Dharma—even the supreme Sky, which consists of the equilibrium of consciousness and unconsciousness and is the reality of repose, attains existence; for there is no state that does not enter the limit of reflective awareness. Thus, even that [supreme] consciousness does not truly exist [independently].

Because, by the aforementioned activity, even the principle of repose (*viśrānti-tattva*) lacks the establishment of its own essential nature; therefore, for the sake of existence— that is, for the establishment of being— the sky (*gagana*), which consists of the equilibrium of consciousness and the unconscious, and even the sky of repose, must always and invariably possess the quality of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), namely, the state of being embraced by the principle of reflective awareness.
It attains its true nature (*dharmatā*). The meaning is that it is wonderful and marvelous how various things possess one another as both attributes (*dharma*) and substrates (*dharmin*).

This point, established previously, has been recalled here in order to demonstrate the power of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) within the system of the scriptures, which hold that *vimarśa* is the root of the world in every respect; thus, there is no fault. || 3 ||
Therefore, the Supreme Mother alone is to be worshipped;
for she is the dual form of the supreme ether, having transcended all dullness.
And this [power] binds living beings by means of the elevation of the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa), and it liberates them when raised from the "I-portion" (ahamaṃśa). || 4 ||
Therefore, because it is the root of everything, one should worship the very principle of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); thus he says, "Therefore," and so forth.

Because it is the root even of repose—that is, its cause—and because it is the mother of all as the root of everything, the supreme *vimarśa-śakti* alone, which is the *mātṛkā* of all, is to be worshipped. The particle *eva* (alone) is to be understood as having this [exclusive] sense.
He states the conclusion. He unveils that very contemplation with the words "of the void" (*vyomnaḥ*), and so forth. The sense is:

"of the supreme void," which is considered as the object of worship. Its "form devoid of inertia" means its nature is free from the suspicion of inertia that might otherwise be suspected due to its lack of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśatā*). For this is indeed the Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*).

The sense is that the supreme void (*paramagagana*), which is intended as the object of worship by virtue of its nature as volition (*cetanā*), is the locus of the portion of consciousness (*caitanyakalā*);

for this very reason, it is more venerable than the unmanifest portion of consciousness (*avyaktacaitanya*). By this, the identity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) with light (*prakāśa*) is established. Through the statement that reflective awareness is the supreme object of worship, [the supremacy] of that which consists of it [is also established].

The specific suitability for worship of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) has been established. This point is manifested by the arrangement of the wheel of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacakra*), which takes the form of a fourfold square consisting of the primary positions suitable for the initial worship of the Great Machine (*mahāyantra*); it is thus elucidated as being worthy of worship.

The passage beginning with "She binds" (*badhnāti*) and so forth establishes that this very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the root of the engagement in worship and the sole agent of both bondage and liberation, exists within the elevation of the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*)— that is, between the two parts of its own nature, the "this" and the "I," which consist of difference and non-difference. This supreme [power], whose form is reflective awareness, [resides] therein.

It binds living beings through the elevation of the "this" (idam) aspect. Whenever there is the cognition of the form of "this" regarding any object, or even when there is the cognition of the form of "I" (aham) regarding the mere body, that very elevation of the sense of "I" is indeed bondage. And it liberates living beings from that elevated sense of "I" by means of the transformation of the cognition of "this."
The sense is that liberation consists precisely in the intensification of the realization of "I-ness" (ahantā) everywhere.
Of these two—bondage and liberation—the Supreme Power (parāśakti), whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa), is indeed the root; for she flows by her own inherent savor.
Whosoever’s heart she flows through with the predominance of "this-ness" (idantā) and the subordination of "I-ness," that person is bound.
The meaning is that whoever, in whose heart the sense of "I-ness" flows with intensity while the sense of "this-ness" is subordinated, that person becomes liberated. || 4 ||
The nature of that [consciousness], which consists of the manifestation "this" and "I," exists in a state where the two aspects are both equal and unequal.
By virtue of the association with that property, the subject likewise possesses three forms, its established nature being the union of the shrine (caitya) and consciousness (citi). || 5 ||

By the preceding sūtra, it was indicated that these two cognitions—*idam* (this) and *aham* (I)—are both constituent parts within the nature of the Supreme (*parā*), whose form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). With this sūtra, he clarifies that very point: "In three ways," and so forth.
The nature of that Supreme [consciousness] consists of that twofold manifestation which is *idam* and *aham*.

The meaning is that it is "threefold" because it is characterized by three parts. To the question "What are those parts?", he says: "of both parts," and so forth. The connection with "threefold" is as follows: it is due to the equality of the two parts consisting of the manifestations in the forms of "this" and "I.
Equality between the parts of "this" and "I" constitutes one part; when there is inequality between them, [the other two parts arise]. Regarding "this":
When there is an intensity of vibration, one part consists of the intensity of the vibration "I," and another part consists of the intensity of the vibration [of the object];

these two parts, having come together through a state of equality, become three parts. Here too, as in the case of the similarities between the insentient and the sentient, each of those situated within the whole is divided into parts without [the need for] a formal partitioning.

The status of being a "part" (aṃśatva) for those whose essential nature consists of equanimity and so forth is a metaphorical designation (upacāra). Having thus reflected upon the reflective awareness (vimarśa) which constitutes the property (dharma), he recalls the threefold nature (trirūpya) of the substratum (dharmī)—even though it was previously established—by means of its similarity to the formal procedure (prakriyā), in the passage beginning with "taddharma... and so on. This refers to that [substratum] which possesses the aforementioned threefold character by virtue of its connection with those properties.

By virtue of its connection with the property (*dharma*) whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the substratum (*dharmī*) likewise possesses three aspects; thus, [the text] indicates the substratum characterized by these three forms with the word "caitya. The meaning is that its established form consists of the union of the *caitya* and consciousness (*citi*), that is, the *caitya* which possesses pervasion (*vyāptimat*) and the consciousness which possesses pervasion, through the merging of both.

The distinction is as follows: by virtue of the association with the intense reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*), the subject (*dharmin*) is of the nature of the pervasive object (*caitya*); by virtue of the association with the intense reflective awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), the subject is of the nature of the pervasive consciousness (*cit*). And in the state of association with a reflective awareness that is tranquil due to the equality of "this-ness" and "I-ness," the subject is of the nature of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between consciousness and its object. || 5 ||

In the abode of rest, within its own substratum, there is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of both consciousness (*cit*) and the object of cognition (*caitya*); even though it is itself the substratum in the state of phenomenal existence (*bhavapada*).
Making these two rest solely upon its own support, it sports by its own spontaneous power both internally and externally.

Now, with three verses beginning with "viśrānti," he demonstrates the wonder of the supportless manifestation of the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) of the sovereign power of Lord Paramaśiva—the [power] which has its own resting place (*nijāśraya*). *Vimarśa* is the agent;
"in the abode of rest" means in the state of rest, that is, in deep sleep. Of its two own resting places...

Because consciousness (*cit*) and its object (*caitya*) find rest in silence, it is logically established that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of both consciousness and its object is supported by and dissolved therein. In the state of becoming (*bhavapada*), which is the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārapada*), [the subject] himself becomes the support;

for the state of becoming is rooted in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and since conceptual construction is essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), within that state every object, such as the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, [is subsumed].
Since it is rooted in *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) alone, both consciousness (*cit*) and its object (*caitya*), as well as the two subjects, are dependent upon *vimarśa*.

Likewise, even for the two substrata, *vimarśa* is the support; thus, this pair consisting of consciousness and its object, while making these two substrata their own inherent support—that is, their very own locus—remains within the internal boundary, not outside.

And externally, as well as beyond the boundary, she sports according to her own spontaneous sequence—whether from the outside toward the inside, or from the inside toward the outside—and by such other modes of natural flow. || 6 ||
In a dream, there manifests a form whose nature is internal and devoid of external senses; then,
upon waking, there appears a form whose nature consists of external instruments, both internally and externally.
In this case, it undergoes some contraction with respect to the preceding word, but it assumes that [contraction] to an even greater degree with respect to the following word. || 7 ||

"Regarding the passage beginning with *svapna* (dream): in a dream, that which has no external sensory form—consisting of the nature of the mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*)—manifests within the internal sphere. The sense is that it displays the world-form as its own play.
Furthermore, the word 'dream' is also indicative of the phenomenal world (*prakṛti-saṃsāra*), for there too [the world appears] in the form of the mind and intellect."

Because of the emission of the universe through *vimarśa*. Then, immediately thereafter, upon awakening—that is, upon the cessation of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—in that awakening which consists of the pure waking state, there appears externally the form of the causes, namely the nature of the organs of knowledge and action such as hearing and speech. Thus, it manifests externally, in the outer sphere.

The connection [is as follows]: here, within the pair of terms consisting of "dream" and "waking," the first term, "dream," assumes a certain degree of contraction. Because the full reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which exists in a state of uniformity through rest in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), undergoes a slight contraction in its subsequent term, "dream," the same applies to the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*) by virtue of that [contraction].

He describes that very contraction of the waking state in the phrase "but in the subsequent state. In the subsequent state—that is, in the waking state which follows the intermediate dream—he undergoes (*ādadhāti*), meaning he accepts, that contraction to an extreme degree, that is, excessively. || 7 ||
It bestows pervasion upon the external field at the limit of the contracted state, but not within the full internal abode.
Even beyond this, the insentient reflective awareness (vimarśa), having attained the wonder of Māyā, bestows a most complete rest.

He demonstrates the manifestation of the bound soul (*paśu*) within the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of a perverted perception brought about by the grasping of the wonder of *māyā* through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) residing at the limit of contraction—on the external stage that is the supreme level of the state of contraction.
This he expresses with the words "contraction" (*saṅkoca*). On the external stage, which is the supreme level of the state of contraction, at the ultimate limit of contraction...

In the state of waking (*jāgratpada*), it bestows pervasion and superimposes fullness. Through the clear and direct perception of jars, cloths, and so forth, one reflects that the light of waking itself is full, because within the full [reality], contraction is merely slight when compared to the waking state. In the inner abode, in the internal sphere, [is] dream (*svapna*).

This is the meaning. Here, one does not establish the pervasiveness or fullness [of the dream-light], but rather contemplates the inferiority of the dream-illumination compared to the waking illumination. Since even objects such as jars and cloths that were directly perceived vanish upon the onset of the waking state, the dream-illumination is indeed comparable to the lightless state of deep sleep.

The meaning is that he proceeds [to another state]. Even from this dream, he proceeds to a state of rest that is more complete and perfectly full—a state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—which is "smaller" than this dream, being a locus of contraction (*saṅkocapada*), because nothing at all, such as a jar or a cloth, is perceived therein; this is the intended sense.
Thus, he states the cause for the appearance of the contrary in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), beginning with the word "māyā. Māyā...

The meaning is that, having attained a state of wonder (*camatkṛti*), the insentient (*jaḍa*) becomes *vimarśa* itself in a reversed form. Nowhere is there a reality (*tattva*) other than *vidyā* and *māyā*; rather, it is *vimarśa* itself appearing with the predominance of "this-ness" (*idantā*) that is called *māyā*, and that same [vimarśa] appearing with the predominance of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) is called *vidyā*.
It should be understood that it is designated as such. || 8 ||
67) When the pair of breaths is separated by two desires, in the group of *ya*-letters during sleep, one should indeed observe the state of insentience.
For here, motherhood belongs to the mind, which is embodied as the letter *la*;
indeed, it is well known that a dream is a mental wandering. || 9 ||

Now, although the first discernment of the waking state is appropriate— since the waking state follows deep sleep (suṣupti), which is the world of mere will, and precedes dream and waking, which are the worlds of knowledge and action respectively, and because this section concerns emission (visarga) where action predominates— nevertheless, knowledge is primary here because it constitutes the creative act of origination.
Performing the initial discernment of the dream of the cycle of existence (*jñāna-saṃsāra*), he describes the state of dreaming— which takes the form of slight contraction—
within the *ya*-group, which possesses slight contraction, according to the procedure for the placement of vowels (*svarapada-prakriyā*) between the two desires: "icchā" and so forth.

The two letters *ya* and *va*, which are the contracted forms of *i* and *u*, possess the nature of the insentient and the sentient Will (*icchā*). By these two Wills, the pair of measures (*mānayugam*)—
consisting of the letters *ra* and *la*, which are the contracted forms of *ṛ* and *ḷ*, and embodying Action (*kriyā*) and Knowledge (*jñāna*)— is interposed, that is, placed in the middle.

The meaning is as follows: in that group of *ya*-letters (*yavarga*) where there is a pair of measures (*pramāṇa*), the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) in dream—which is inert—must indeed be observed as the state of the dream of duality; for there is a connection of similarity between the dream-state of the *yavarga* and [the waking state] due to their both being slightly contracted in form. Here, within this dream, [one should consider] the mind, which is the embodiment of the letter *la*.

Thus is the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*). Indeed, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) stands in the place of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In the dream-like cycle of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the mind alone is the means of knowledge, and not the ears and other senses; for it is an empirical fact that the sense organs do not function independently in relation to their respective objects. What [is the nature] of the mind?
To explain its own nature, he says that there are two forms of the ear and the other senses: an external form and an internal form.

Just as when the ear and the others are closed externally, they function internally, at that time the internal form of the ear and the others is called the mind (*manas*); whereas when they are opened externally, they function externally.

At that time, it should be understood as the conventional usage of "ear" and so forth. This is because, internally, the term "mind" (manas) is used for the interior of the ears and other [senses]. The letter *la*, which occupies the place of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), is indeed the mind; likewise, the letter *ra*, which occupies the place of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), is the intellect (*buddhi*). It should be understood that the internal form of even the organs of action is the intellect. [This occurs] in the dream state.

Transmigration occurs through the wondrous power of the mind alone in assuming the state of the triad beginning with the knower (pramātṛ), and not through a knower consisting of a real body; for if that were the case, there would be the consequence of objects experienced in dreams appearing in the waking state. Therefore, it is the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the mind itself, which possesses great power, that appears in the form of the triad within a dream.
The "shining forth" (*vilasana*) of that very mind—even externally in the form of the senses such as hearing—is its shining forth in the form of objects;

thus, for those whose darkness of illusion has been dispelled by the piercing glance of the Guru, it is universally accepted that the world is not established anywhere, whether internally or externally, as anything other than the reflection [of consciousness], such as atoms or the like. This applies to the dream-like nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Since the state of waking is characterized by the agency of a subject possessing a real body, and because one does not observe the occurrence of such [real] conditions when dreaming—despite the logical necessity for their presence—it is agreed even by common people that "dream is a play of the mind. Therefore, from that perspective, it is undisputed that in the dream state, the mind alone possesses the status of the subject; thus it has been stated.
He reveals that very worldly consensus with the words: "For it is a dream," etc. (9).
p.
68) His own power, consisting of reflective awareness (*avamarśa*), has within its own womb swallowed the body and other forms by that very mind.
The Sun himself does not shine at all within the fivefold sheath, being veiled by a mass of his own rays.

Now, [one should contemplate] the wonder of the concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*) of the internal manifold consisting of the body and so forth— which takes the form of the external manifold of earth and so on— by means of the power of the mind (*manaḥ-śakti*), which is a synonym for reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) residing within the Self that is the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*).
He brings it forth—“of its own,” and so on. The power consisting of reflective awareness (*avamarśa*), whose nature is *vimarśa*, belongs to itself alone;

that is, it belongs only to that which is related to itself. Its very abiding is within its own womb, because it is a property [of consciousness], by means of the mind, which is of the nature of the mental organ (*manas*).

He is "seized" or pervaded by that very primordial form, the body which assumes the stage of the phenomenal world consisting of ether, earth, and so forth. Having reflected that "I am swallowed up by this phenomenal world," he becomes an object of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkriyā*) of trembling due to the emergence of the aesthetic wonder of a contrary perception; however, this is not so in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

"Seized. Immediately after the dawning of knowledge (*vidyā*), when one reflects upon one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), the devouring of oneself by the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) results in nothing but the wonder of self-awareness (*vimarśa-camatkāra*). Thus, it is merely the play of one's own attributes (*svadharma-vilāsa*); how, then, could that constitute an obscuration of oneself?
This is established by means of a simile: "by the mass of its own rays," etc. By the mass of its own rays...
The Āryaman (the Sun) is shrouded and concealed, like the sun by the fivefold sheath (*kañcuka-pañcaka*).
This sheath consists of five limbs: the mind (*manas*), power (*śakti*), the emergent and delimited volition (*saṅkalpa*), form (*rūpa*), and the object of knowledge (*vedya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that he remains within the sphere of pervasion (*vyāpya-kakṣyā*); he does not shine forth, he does not manifest, just as the sun [is obscured].

Just as the reflection of an object is not perceived when covered by a mass of one's own rays, so too this Self is [unperceived] due to the play of its own power. Therefore, the sense is that it is logical to say that its fundamental nature, which consists of consciousness, is concealed and hidden by the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form of its own circle of rays. || 10 ||
The body endowed with the self, the ego, the intellect, and the mind— these three internal instruments are the locus of the cognizer.
If this fivefold form is a mere play of the mind, then this state is directly the realm of illusion and of primordial nature (prakṛti).

Now, demonstrating the configuration of the state of dream— which is conceived as possessing five limbs by virtue of being the object of the pervasion of emission (*visarga*)— he establishes the distinction of the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) from the nature that is about to be described:
"Self," and so forth. "The body endowed with the self" means the body reckoned together with the self.
"Ego, intellect, and mind" refers to those consisting of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*). These are the three internal instruments (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Together, these constitute the five-limbed state of the knower in the form of a dream; this is the meaning of the word "pada."

It has been stated that sovereignty belongs to the cognizing self alone. Since this state consists of the playful manifestation of the power of the self, its nature as the self’s own play is established by implication; thus, in the waking state, the category of *prakṛti* takes the form of the mental world, while the category of *puruṣa* takes the form of liberation (*apavarga*) as will be described. In that [liberation] as well, it is the self—
The body, which is the nature of the successive states, and the triad of internal organs beginning with egoism—this is the five-limbed state (*pada*).
To the question, "In that case, what is the difference between the state of *prakṛti* and the state of dream? he says: "This," and so forth.
This five-fold state is a manifestation of the mind. If [it were] only of the mind, in a real body...

If that which manifests is independent of a cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), then it becomes the state of *māyā*, which is synonymous with dream; however, if it is rooted in a cognizing subject whose nature is that of the waking state—such that one directly remembers, "I am indeed thus"—then it becomes the state of *prakṛti*. This is the intended meaning. || 11 ||
70) In this state of illusion (*māyāpada*), those who know the individual soul (*aṇu*) teach that within the letter *va* there is the manifestation of one's own mind itself as the body, and so forth.
And even beyond that, while recollecting the letter *la*, this five-limbed word becomes indeed four-limbed. || 12 ||

Now, it has been stated that the "state of dream" (*svapnapada*) consists of five limbs by virtue of being the object of the pervasion of the *visarga*. In that context, there are four phonemes beginning with *ya* and ending with *va*;

from the two—namely, the insentient and the sentient will and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—the phoneme [occupying] the locus of the subject of the *visarga*, which corresponds to the insentient will, is...
"It is neither heard nor seen externally; how then can this state (pada) possess five limbs?

To this he says "māyā" and so forth. "Aṇividaḥ" means those who know the mantras. Regarding the "state of māyā" and the "state of dream": the state of dream is the very first place of manifestation for the reflective awareness of the differentiation of māyā (māyābhedavimarśa); thus, it is called the "state of dream."

And the conventional expression "the locus of *māyā*" refers to this state. In that state, the mind itself—assuming the form of time and possessing the nature of a body—is that which possesses the status of being the embodied subject (*dehapramātṛ*). It has been established previously that apart from the mind, there is no body acting as an agent in a dream. Therefore, they declare that the mind alone possesses the nature of the body. Why? Because it performs [all functions].
In this context, "within the *ra-vakāra*" means that the letter *ya* is inside the *va*, that is, in the word immediately following [the syllable containing] *ya*.

Furthermore, "even outside of that" refers to the word preceding the *va*; those who recollect and apply the letter *la* in these positions perceive that when the mind-like element is separated, the mind itself attains the state of being the body. Therefore, by such an application [of the letters], [the result follows].

The intended meaning is that instruction (*upadeśa*) consists precisely in the transmission of the tradition. In the word preceding the letter *va*, which is regarded as external, the letter *la*, representing the mind (*manas*), is to be contemplated. In the word following the letter *va*, which is regarded as internal, there is the placement of the letter *la*, representing the body (*deha*). Now, [one might ask] regarding the verse on the pervasion of the *visarga*:

To the question, "How can the body, which is the nature of the subject of emission (*visarga-pramātṛ*) and resides within the *ātman*, be situated within the womb of the letter *va*?"—it is said here: In the state of dream, the persistence of emission (*visarga*) occurs precisely within the womb of the point (*bindu*). Nevertheless, there is the perception that the point is not pervaded by the emission. For this very reason, [the dream] exists in the region where consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) mutually pervade one another.
One might ask: how can the body, which consists of the subject of emission (*visarga-pramātṛ*) and resides within the *ātman*, be situated within the womb of the letter *va*?

To this, he will state that because it is not a locus of conventional designation (*asaṅketasthāna*), it is "mixed" (*miśra*) and non-dual. In the waking state, however, the subject of emission is situated outside the sphere of the *bindu*; for this very reason, its impurity will be stated.

Since the body is contained within the Self, it can be inferred that the three internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are likewise contained within the Self. Their arrangement as being external to that [Self] is logically consistent with the requirement for the realization of its pervasiveness; thus, there is no fault.
Now, this word is said to consist of five limbs; if so, how does it [combine] with the group of consonants (śavarga), which consists of four limbs?

How can [the letter *va*] be arranged with an equal number [of parts] within an eight-cornered [figure]? Furthermore, if it were to have four limbs (*caturaṅga*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by the *visarga* would not be consistent; to this he says: "consisting of five limbs" (*pañcāṅgaka*), and so forth. When the letter *la* is placed outside the letter *va*, it indeed has only four limbs; however, according to the tradition (*sāmpradāyika*), [it is considered five-limbed] when [the *la*] is inside the letter *va*.
It should be understood that those who possess specialized knowledge agree that it consists of five limbs by means of the secret arrangement of the interior of the letter *la*. || 12 ||
The letter *la* here is the earth, consisting of the body; its own abode is the knowledge of the agent; and the letters *ya* and *ra* consist of wind and fire.
In the pervaded [element], earth and water are modified; and the two digits (lavau) are the instruments for the body abiding within its own self in the womb.

According to the stated rule, regarding the conceit pervaded by the *visarga* in the five-limbed state of dream, he demonstrates the arrangement of earth and the other elements in reverse order among the phonemes that constitute the limbs of the word for "beast" (*paśu*), because [the dream state] is the state of the beast:
"earth," and so forth. Here, in the word for dream, the letter *la* is the *la* situated within the letter *va*.
Having attained another station in the sky through her own power (*svadhā*), the Earth has assumed a bodily form.

Of this body in the form of Earth, which is the subject of emission (*visarga-pramātṛ*), there are the two phonemes *ra* and *la*, consisting of air and fire—that is, having the nature of wind and fire—which are the instruments of action and knowledge, the agency and the knower. These constitute the pair of principles (*tattva-dvaya*) in the stages of *vidyā* and *āpti*, which have the natures of water and inert fire.
Thus, at this point in the sequence of transposition, the positions of air (vāyu), the insentient (jaḍa), and fire (agni) are indicated by the forms of the letters *ya* and *ra*.

The sense is that for the embodied subject whose nature is earth, these two—the instruments of action and knowledge—serve as the means for the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). This is because the body, whose nature is action, possesses the status of a subject (*pramātṛtva*).

It should be understood that its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is likewise primarily action (*kriyā*). When the letter *la* precedes the letter *va*, and the letter *la* follows the letter *va*— that is, when the wind (*vāyu*) and fire (*agni*), represented by the letters *ya* and *ra*, have undergone modification (*vikṛta*) and reached a state of transformation, [this occurs] through the two principles (*tattva*) consisting of wind and space (*ākāśa*) as their primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

The two parts of earth and water [are] *va* and *ka*, earth and water; thus, for the body situated within its own self—that is, for the body of the subject of emission (*visargapramātṛ*) residing within the womb of the syllable *va* which stands in the place of the Self—the instruments [of perception and action] come to be. This is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For there is a rule that the state of emission is delimited by the plane of consciousness (*citpadāvaccheda*) in its own sphere of pervasion.

The non-limitation of consciousness (*cid-anavaccheda*) is understood precisely through the specific configuration of the *visarga* syllable, whose nature consists of space (*ākāśa*) and the other elements.

Neither the destruction of earth and water nor the destruction of water by air and fire—by means of which the *visarga* and the subject (*pramātṛ*) are established—is accomplished. [Specifically,] there is no destruction of water by air, nor of earth by fire.
Annihilation is possible; however, the annihilation of earth by wind or the annihilation of water by fire is not conceivable. || 13 ||

The Great Person (puruṣa) is immersed in the body; the mind is within the ego-function (ahaṃkriyā); and the non-inert portion [of the intellect] is within the intellect (buddhi), even though that intellect is in its inert part.
Thus, within the cognizer, the great cosmic egg (mahābrahmāṇḍa) manifests as the internal knowledge and action residing in the non-inert aspect of that which possesses an inert portion.
Now, demonstrating the pervasion of the Self by means of the very body and so forth situated within its own womb,

he shows the wonder of the external world's emission following the internal world's emission in the form of the body and ego, which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of mind and intellect:

"Immersed," and so forth. The *puman* (the person) is the self (*ātman*) in the form of the letter *va*. It is "immersed" in the "body" (*vapuṣi*), which is in the form of the letter *la*—this is the ellipsis. The "mind" (*citta*) is the mind in the form of the preceding letter *la*. The construction is: "I am immersed in the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of the letter *ya*, within the activity of 'I'. The construction is: "The non-inert part [of the self] is immersed in the belly of the inert portion, within the intellect (*buddhi*)."

The nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) as fire and its dual character as both insentient and sentient have been established. Now, one might ask: "In the preceding aphorism, it was revealed that the swallowing of the mind (*citta*), which has the form of earth, by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)—which has the form of air—and the swallowing of the self (*ātman*), which has the form of water, by the intellect (*buddhi*)—which has the form of fire—have been explained. How then is the swallowing of the self by the body to be understood now?"

It is said: the two instruments, consisting of knowledge and action, are indeed limbs of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, their "devouring" is in effect nothing other than the devouring of the subject; thus, there is no contradiction. In this way, by the process of immersion described above, [the objective aspect] within the subject—which is of the nature of the letter *va*—is absorbed into the non-inert portion of the subject.

When one's own self and its limbs are submerged within the emission (*visarga*)— that is, within the interior of knowledge and action, which contains the mind and intellect; the meaning is that it contains the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose form is mind and intellect— the "Great Egg" (*mahā-aṇḍa*), the cosmic egg of Brahmā, which is exceedingly vast, shines forth, or emerges, from the interior of that reflective awareness.

The sense is that immediately after the unfolding of the internal manifold (*prapañca*), one emits the external manifold. In the state of dream, even according to common worldly understanding, the microcosmic body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) is the cause of the macrocosmic universe (*brahmāṇḍa*). In the waking state, however, it is the common perception of the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*) that the macrocosmic universe is the cause of the microcosmic body.

For the yogin of the Left Path (vāmamārga), however, the established conclusion in the Siddhadarśana is that the microcosmic body (piṇḍāṇḍa) itself is the cause of the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa). In the Yāmala, on the other hand, there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the two, because their establishment occurs simultaneously; thus, there is an inseparable connection (avinābhāva) between the microcosmic body and the macrocosm, which are both of the nature of Śakti. [This is] within the state (pade).
The macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa) is a limb of the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa), while externally the microcosm is a limb of the macrocosm; such is the thorough discernment. || 14 ||
Even the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa), which is its root, appears as if it were not its root;
even the interior of the macrocosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) appears as if it were its exterior— how wondrous!
Then, with a vision deluded by māyā, having perceived that subtle atom, he assumes his five limbs, which possess subtle powers.

Now, he explains that play of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of a contrary perception which arises from the vision of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)— which has emerged from the microcosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) that constitutes the individual soul’s own true nature— by means of the verse beginning with "the microcosmic egg" (*piṇḍāṇḍa*). Even in a dream, for one who identifies with the body, there is a dispute regarding the root of the cosmic egg and the microcosmic egg.
Because it is rooted in the mind (*manas*), this physical body (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) also appears as if it were itself the root.
Furthermore, because the mind resides within this physical body, even that which is internal appears as if it were external—this is wonderful and marvelous.
It is marvelous because that which is situated within oneself is perceived as being all-pervasive. It is subtle (*aṇu*).

The contracted subject (*saṅkucitapramātā*). Such and such a cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) of this kind. With a vision deluded by the wonder of *māyā*—that is, with a vision that has become distorted through the grasping of the marvels of *māyā*.
Having gazed upon it through the reflective awareness of vision (*dṛgvimarśa*). The five locations of the physical egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), beginning with the body. One's own limbs (*svāṅgāni*).
Possessing minute powers, they have very little substance in comparison to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). He impels them; he perceives them. || 15 ||
The withdrawal of air, fire, earth, water, and space as previously conceived constitutes the bonds of the inner atom; this is the aggregate of ignorance.
Passion (rāga) and time-determination (kālaniyati)—these are the coverings (kañcukas) of the nature of Māyā; they constitute the first covering of deep sleep (suṣupti). || 16 ||

Now, he explains that by perceiving the limbs of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which consists of the five great elements, within oneself, one forms the intention to withdraw the limbs of the individual egg (piṇḍāṇḍa)—the contracted self composed of the elements—and these very intentions become the sixfold sheaths (ṣaṭkañcuka) designated by terms such as "kalā" and so forth; these are the internal bonds. idānīṃ paśoḥ pañcamahābhūtātmakabrahmāṇḍāṅgadarśanena saṃkucitabhūtātmakasvasvarūpapiṇḍāṇḍāṅgānāmapakarṣasaṅkalpā eva antarbandhāḥ kalādiśabdavyavahriyamāṇāḥ ṣaṭkañcukā bhavantītyāha -

Regarding the term *saṅkḷpta*: it refers to the contractions of air, fire, earth, water, and space that have been contracted—that is, intended—by the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *la*. These are the contractions of the air, fire, earth, water, and ether that correspond to the places of articulation (*sthāna*) of those respective letters.

For the limited subject (*aṇuka*), there would be internal bonds (*antarbandha*). They are called "internal bonds" because the *saṅkalpas* (volitions) reside within the heart of the bound soul (*paśu*), and because they are the root of bondage characterized by the pervasion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This is well known from the fact that [the soul] is bound by the power of its own *saṅkalpas*. Of these...

He sequentially indicates that the bonds consisting of mental constructs (saṅkalpa), through the sequence of the wind and other elements located at the place of the letter *ya*, take on the form of the sixfold sheath beginning with *kalā*, as is well known in the tradition of the Siddhas— beginning with the words "kalā" and so forth.
The contraction of the wind located at the place of the letter *ya* is the mental construct (*saṅkalpa*), which becomes the sheath named *kalā*.

The volition (*saṅkalpa*) consisting of the contraction of fire, which has its locus in the letter *ra*, becomes the sheath (*kañcuka*) called ignorance (*avidyā*). The volition consisting of the contraction of earth, which has its locus in the letter *la*, becomes the sheath called attachment (*rāga*).
The volition consisting of the contraction of water, which has its locus in the letter *va*, becomes the sheath called time (*kāla*).

The contraction of the space situated in the letter *la* is the *kañcuka* (sheath) called *niyati* (fate). Due to the contraction of the wind (*vāyu*) of universal agency at the level of the undivided subject into the state of the bound soul (*paśu*), there remains only limited agency; thus, *kalā* [is the sheath] of the fire of omniscience, which takes the form of *vidyā*.

Through contraction, there arises the state of ignorance (*avidyātva*) from the reversal of the power of fullness; through the contraction of earth, there arises the state of passion (*rāgatva*) due to the emergence of attachment—a synonym for longing—expressed as "this is mine" and "I desire this"; through the contraction of water, which possesses the power of eternity, there arises the state of time (*kālatva*) from the perception of impermanence; and through the contraction of space, which possesses the power of pervasiveness...
The establishment of the *kalās* and the other coverings is based on their necessity (*niyatitva*), as indicated by the restriction of space in the phrase "right here" (*atraiva*).
Now, it is well known that there are six coverings (*kañcukas*), and among them, *māyā* is heard to be the first; why then is no separate mention made of it here? To this he replies:
"of the nature of *māyā*" (*māyātmanaḥ*). This [state] is that which precedes the dream consisting of the five coverings.

Inert deep sleep (*jaḍasuṣupti*) is the causal form of that [state]; it is indeed *māyā*, because it is the fundamental nature of the differentiated cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). It is a traditional tenet that the letters from *kṣa* down to *ka* constitute the first "sheath" (*kañcuka*) of that deep sleep whose essence is *māyā*, and that these letters consist of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) ranging from Śiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*). And those letters...
Because, according to the tradition, the letter *la* is of two forms and is accepted as being of a single phoneme together with the letters *ṣa* and *kṣa*,

there is the presence of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) within the phonemes when the internal group (*antaḥsthā-varga*), which is of the nature of the principle of Māyā, is placed at the root of the [other] groups of consonants.

It is in harmony with the Sun. The section on vowels (*svara-khaṇḍa*) is indeed the root of the pervasive section (*vyāpaka-khaṇḍa*), because it is the seed of the dream of differentiation in the form of the *ya*-group, and because it is the state of rest in the dream of non-differentiation in the form of the *śa*-group.
With respect to origination, knowledge (*jñāna*) is primary; with respect to manifestation, action (*kriyā*) is primary.

The distinction is this: between the states of dreaming and waking—which consist of the predominance of knowledge and action, respectively—the deep sleep state, which is the cause of all and consists of the group of vowels (*svaravarga*), is situated therein; thus, within the vowel-group, the letter *ya*, which takes the form of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of dreaming, is the locus of the *māyā-tattva*. || 16 ||
The power of agency is the wind; omniscience is the fire; the earth is fullness; non-dissolution is the water; and pervasiveness is the ether.
These five powers are expanded as the very nature of Śambhu, yet they become contracted in the case of the bound soul (paśu). || 17 ||

Now, he explains how the elements beginning with air (yakārādi), such as wind and the rest, possess the five powers—beginning with agency—which constitute the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva through their states of being full or incomplete:
"Agency," etc. Wind is the power of Śiva’s universal agency; fire is the power of omniscience; earth...

—The power of fullness (*pūrṇatā-śakti*). Water is the power of non-dissolution and eternity (*nityatva-śakti*). Space, the ether (*viyat-ākāśa*), is pervasiveness, the power of omnipresence (*vyāpakatva-śakti*). All these five powers, when expanded and complete, constitute the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Śambhu; however, when contracted, they constitute the essential nature of the bound soul (*paśu*). Of all [this]...

Since action consists of vibration (*spanda*), and vibration is a property of air, air possesses the power of agency (*kartṛtva*). Since cognition consists of manifestation (*bhāsana*), and manifestation is a property of fire, fire possesses the power of knowledge (*jñatva*).
[This pertains to] fullness (*pūrṇatva*), which is synonymous with perfection (*sampatti*).

Because all objects of enjoyment have the earth as their root—since all objects of enjoyment are rooted in the earth—the earth possesses the power of fullness (*pūrṇatva-śakti*). Because the state of permanence has the uninterrupted process of replenishment as its root, replenishment possesses the power of permanence (*nityatva-śakti*). Because omnipresence has pervasion as its root...
The distinction is that because space is the nature of both [ether and dharma], space possesses the power of pervasiveness (vibhutva). || 17 ||
(77) Prakṛti consists of the five powers of Śiva; furthermore, she is the internal manifestation of the universe for embodied beings.
The differentiation of the external world arises precisely from the power of delusion, even though the world exists within oneself. (18)

He establishes a distinguishing attribute within the general state of both Śiva and Śivā consisting of the five powers, stating: "It may be. The nature or essential character (*prakṛti*) of Śiva may consist of the five powers; for it is well known that Śiva has eight forms (*mūrti*). Among these, since the moon and sun are included within the light of fire, [the form] of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)...

Since the five great elements, having been transformed into the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), are contained within the light of space—which is itself contained within Śiva—within the space of the conscious self (cidātman), it is logically established that the very nature of Śiva consists of the elements beginning with space. He states the attribute that distinguishes Śiva from the individual soul (jīva): "the fashioning of the world within Himself."

Since the worlds such as Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ—which consist of forms resulting from the transformation of the great elements—abide within those very great elements, Śiva, whose self is that [world], projects the world within himself; this much is the nature (prakṛti) of Śiva. Now, as for the embodied being (dehin)—that is, in the alternative view—it is because he consists of the five elements.

Of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the five powers and contains within itself the world in the form of the microcosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*); since the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) arises from the microcosmic egg and the latter is situated therein, it is logical that the world contained within it is also [situated there]. Through the power of delusion (*vimoha-śakti*), there occurs a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of a contrary perception.

By power (*śakti*). In the external sphere of pervasion (*vyāptipada*), that which is the "formation of the world"—the volition for the existence of worlds—is itself the distinction from Śiva; it is the differentiating attribute (*bhedaka-dharma*). When one considers one's own essential nature (*nijasvarūpa*) as the microcosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) to be the root of the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and thus superior to the macrocosmic egg, then [it is realized as] the very nature of oneself.

The meaning is that when both the state of being the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍatva*) and the state of transcending it have been attained, Śiva attains nothing other than *śivatva*—the very nature of Śiva which consists of both the universe and that which transcends the universe. || 18 ||
For there is no possibility of fulfillment for the mind situated within,
because it is certain that the mental object (*caitya*) has been swallowed by that [mind].
In the same way, there is no fulfillment for consciousness either; therefore, this state manifests as a union of both non-fulfillment and fulfillment within two aspects. (19)

Now, in order to demonstrate that dream possesses the nature of mixed paths (*miśrādhvatā*), he shows the intermingling of the conscious and the unconscious therein, beginning with the words "within" (*antaḥ*) and so forth. [This refers to] the mind; and of the object of cognition (*caitya*) situated within; [namely], the object of knowledge (*vedya*) in the form of the body and the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

The "fulfillment-yoga" (*pūrtiyoga*) is the attainment of fulfillment. Indeed, it is so called because it possesses a certainty regarding being "devoured" by that—that is, a certainty (*viniścaya*), which is the firmness of realization (*pratipattidārḍhya*), concerning being devoured (*kabalitatva*), or pervaded (*vyāptatva*), by that twofold *caitya*. It is likewise so for the *cit*, the self (*ātman*) whose locus is the letter *va*.

No; the meaning is that it is just as it is with a *caitya*. As for the fulfillment of the *caitya*, since it is contained within consciousness (*cit*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), let there simply be the pervasion of consciousness. Otherwise, one should not suspect that the ultimate reality is contradicted by the defect of conceptual apprehension, for the non-conceptual ultimate reality is indeed the fundamental substance precisely by virtue of its non-conceptuality.
This is attachment to saṃsāra. For saṃsāra is not ultimately real.
Therefore, entities manifested by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose form is the perception of this or that [object] must not be denied on account of their lack of ultimate reality;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the entirety of saṃsāra must be denied. Enough of this.

This state is called "dream" (svapna), because it is characterized by discourses that obstruct the instruction on the secret [truth], and thus lacks the certainty regarding the determination of the pervasion between consciousness (cit) and the unconscious (acit). It is so called because, within both sides—the two aspects of consciousness and the unconscious—it possesses a conjunction of a manifest lack of fulfillment and a manifest fullness;
that is, it is that in which there is a union, a commingling, of the manifest non-fulfillment and the manifest fulfillment. || 19 ||
The temporal path (adhvan) becomes impure through the diminution of consciousness,
whereas it becomes pure through the diminution of the state of the object of worship (caitya).

Because there is no distinction between increase and decrease in the case of the individual soul (*cic*) and the sacred site (*caitya*), this path is indeed a mixed state of the realm of illusion (*māyika*). || 20 ||
In the *Svapnāśuddhādhvatāpravacana*, the nature of every path (*adhvan*) is explained [in the verse beginning with] "path" (*adhva*).
Due to the diminution of consciousness (*cit*), the object of consciousness (*caitya*) is pervaded; thus, when consciousness itself is diminished, it becomes that which is pervaded.

By virtue of that, the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) comes into being. That state wherein there is a decline due to being pervaded is designated as the "impure path. This means that the waking state characterized by duality (*bhedajāgrad*), the state of insentience (*jaḍa*), and deep sleep (*suṣupti*) constitute the impure path. And therein, through the singular sovereignty over the pervasion of the objective field (*caityavyāpti*), [the state is established].
Because consciousness (*cit*) is all-pervasive. This [state] becomes pure through the removal of the pedestal (*caitya*) from the path (*adhvan*); thus it is designated as "pure.
