The fourth state (*turyapada*) is the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), because consciousness pervades the pedestal by virtue of its sovereign oneness. This is the state of *māyā*, the state of dream, because there is no distinction between the increase or decrease of consciousness and the pedestal.
Accumulation (*upacaya*) is pervasiveness; depletion (*apacaya*) is pervadedness. The non-distinction between these two is the state of generality (*sāmānyabhāva*).
Because consciousness (*cit*) and its objects (*caitya*) each possess the generality of being both the pervader and the pervaded, they become intermingled;
thus, it is designated as the "intermingled path" (*miśrādhvan*). Since the ultimate reality of the universe consists of pure consciousness, the very perception of its pervasion [is that reality].

Purity (*śuddhi*): one who possesses that is pure (*śuddha*). Since the pervasion of consciousness (*caitanyavyāpti*) consists merely of a wondrous manifestation and thus acts as a veil over the true nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), it is synonymous with impurity (*mala*). Therefore, the perception of this pervasion of consciousness is impurity; one who possesses that is to be known as impure (*aśuddha*). This applies specifically to the states (*daśā*) of waking and so forth for both Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, in the context of "wandering" (sañcaraṇa), the conventional usage [of the term] refers to the state of repeated recurrence. || 20 ||
The Self, indeed, has the form of the syllable *va*; the syllable *ru* is the body.
Truly, for this living being, transmigratory existence consists of the body and the self.
And its real body is indeed in deep sleep; here in the dream state, it is the mind alone that assumes the nature of a body.
Thus ends the third section, the Investigation of Dreams, in the Investigation of the Wheel of the Mother-Syllables (Mātṛkācakra).
Concluding the section, he explains with specific detail that in a dream the mind alone constitutes the body, because this is a point of contention:

"The Self," etc. That which is the letter *u* within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti-pada*), which consists of the letters *a* and so forth and serves as the locus for the Self—that is this very form of the letter *u*.

Thus, in the state of dream, this very Self, in the form of the letter *va*, is subtle and contracted. For this living being (*jantu*) whose nature is the letter *va*, transmigration—the process of wandering—occurs indeed through the body itself, as the body; for without the bondage of the body, it exists in the form of the stainless space of consciousness, like Śiva.

The sense is that it is impossible to conceive of the wondrous play of transmigratory existence [as occurring otherwise]. Therefore, regarding the soul’s transmigration, the body is necessarily imagined by the mind even in a dream;
the true body remains in deep sleep, having closed the collection of external senses and not abandoning its bed. This is the meaning.

If that very dream-experiencer were the presiding agent [of the waking state], then there would be the consequence of the actual occurrence in the waking state of things such as the cutting off of a finger that were experienced in the dream. Although even a real body has its root in the mind, it is nevertheless said to be "unreal" and "created by the mind" from the perspective of worldly perception. For that reason, in this case...

In a dream, it is the mind alone; this is the sense, because of the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). The meaning is that even for an ordinary person, it is commonly accepted that [the mind] "possesses corporeality," that is, it assumes the state of being a body. || 21 ||
The letter *ya* is the powerful eye of Śambhu’s vast right eye during the drying up [of the world];
the letter *ra* is his middle eye, ever-awake in the burning of the worlds.
For embodied beings who perform recitation, this triad bestows the imperishable three-eyed state upon the left eye of Paśupati— that which is skillful at flooding the universe.
Because it sustains the universe that has been submerged in the ocean of deep sleep by lifting it up, this power known as *dhāraṇā* is called the *ya*-group by those who know the mantras. (1)
For the stability of the universe resides in Indra, and likewise in the letter *la* within the mind;
thus, the knowledge of the mantra concerning the letter *la* is traditionally transmitted as being named after Indra.
Having split the syllables *va* and *la* with his exceedingly sharp intellect, [he said: "The breaker of Vala is called Valabhid; the Rākṣasa is named Nava-la. (3)

For those of refined intellect who worship Māyā, the group of *ya*-consonants resides within them— [Māyā] who consists of the *ya*-sounds acting as pickles for the act of producing teeth, and who are the fruits of that act, consisting of the nine flavors (*nava-rasa*) that devour the notion of duality.
The secret of the manifestation of Māyā shines forth within oneself after a long time.
By the sage Śivānanda, who abides by the command of his teacher, the third section has been explained in this *Mātṛkācakraviveka*. (5)
Thus ends the third section. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth section.
Thus, when reflective awareness (vimarśa) has contracted here within the intermediate space,
it assumes a profound contraction upon the external level; then,
they perceive each object as a distinct entity in this manner.
The five elements are the fixed aggregate of the world. || 1 ||

Now, beginning another section, in order to demonstrate the connection between the preceding and succeeding aggregates (*skandha*), he introduces the object of the subsequent aggregate following a restatement of the object of the preceding aggregate, beginning with "Thus" (*iti*) and so forth.
"Thus" means in the manner previously described. "Within" (*antar*) means within the sphere of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Here" (*iha*) means in the state of dreaming.

When reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is slightly contracted, that is, within the sphere of the external senses (*bāhyendriya-kakṣyā*) in the state of waking (*jāgrat*), it undergoes an intense and extreme contraction. The "elements" (*bhūtāni*) refer to the fixed aggregate of the world; since the world consists of the transformation of the elements, the elements necessarily constitute the aggregate of the world. [This applies] to each one individually.

They conceive and attain a fivefold state. This occurs in the waking state, which is the locus of extreme contraction of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because even the elements undergo an extreme contraction by assuming a fivefold nature; that is, each element, such as earth and the rest, possesses the fivefold form of earth and so forth. This is the state of the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*) who is like water.
There is an extreme contraction [of consciousness] into the nature of the five elements in the form of the *puruṣa*, *prakṛti*, and so forth;

and there is an extreme contraction of the earth— which is the locus of the sense organs of the bound subject (*paśupramātṛ*)— into the nature of the five elements in the form of the ear, skin, and so forth.

The extreme contraction of the fire-element, which constitutes the state of the sense organs of action belonging to the limited subject (paśu-pramātṛ), occurs through its manifestation as the five elements in the form of speech, hands, and so forth. The extreme contraction of the wind-element, which constitutes the state of the objects of knowledge and the perceivable for the limited subject, occurs through its manifestation as the five elements in the form of sound, touch, and so forth. [This applies] to the limited subject.

The space that has the nature of being an object of experience undergoes contraction by assuming the form of the five elements, beginning with ether and air. Herein this meaning is understood: the manifestation of each of the elements as having the nature of all five elements is their inherent nature (*svabhāva*); because it is not an object of contraction even in deep sleep and dreaming, it does not fail to manifest.

"But it unfolds in the state of extreme contraction during the waking state. By this, it should be understood that there is a rule of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) for all beings with respect to all other beings. || 1 ||

When that group of five letters, unprecedented and belonging to the first class, attains the state of being a semi-vowel (*antaḥstha*) within the contracted [vocalic sphere], it becomes slightly diminished.
It possesses an intense nature of heat, contracted within the body of the *ka*-group and other [consonant] groups, and maintains an incipient fulfillment.
Now, in the context of the waking state, in order to demonstrate the increasing contraction of the consonants from *ka* to *ma*,
he explains the process of manifestation (*pratipādiprakriyā*) of the five vowels beginning with *a*, which constitute the causal form of all phonemes:

Regarding the passage beginning with *yadvarṇa* and so forth: "The first group" (*ādivarga*) refers to the group of vowels (*svaravarga*), because it is the first among the groups. That which exists therein is "belonging to the first group" (*ādivargya*). "Preceded by nothing" (*apūrvaka*) means that group of five letters for which the letter *a* is not preceding; this group of five letters consists of the forms *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*.

Thus, this pentad of phonemes, being slightly contracted—being slightly contracted by virtue of being the object of the articulatory effort known as *īṣatspṛṣṭatā*—attains the state of being semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), taking the forms of *ya* and so forth: the slight contraction of *i* becomes *ya*;
[the slight contraction] of *ṛ* becomes *ra*; [the slight contraction] of *ḷ* becomes *la*; and [the slight contraction] of *u* becomes...

The letter *va* is contraction (*saṅkoca*). Because the mind itself, which is the locus of the letter *la*, consists of the body—a synonym for the subject of emission (*visargapramātṛ*)—there is no contraction of the letter *a*.
Thus, the group of semivowels (*antaḥstha-varga*) is simply another form of the pentad of letters beginning with *a*. That very [pentad]...

The five-fold group of phonemes (varṇapañcaka) is extremely contracted; being contracted by way of being the objects of touch, it consists of the five groups beginning with *ka*—namely, the nature of the five groups starting with the *ka*-group. The contraction of the vowel *a* is the *ka*-group; the contraction of the vowel *i* is the *ca*-group; the contraction of the vowel *ṛ* is the *ṭa*-group.

The *tavarga* is the contraction of the phoneme *ḷ*; the *pavarga* is the contraction of the phoneme *u*. Now, that same pentad of phonemes, by virtue of being the object of a slightly opened articulatory effort (*īṣadvivṛttiprayatna*) that has sprouted toward fullness, possesses a sprouted completeness and consists of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
(They maintain—[the subject] partakes in.)

The meaning is that the sibilants (*ūṣman*) consist of the state of slight fullness of the five letters beginning with *a*, which have been contracted into the form of the five consonants of the *pa*-group. The letter *śa* is the slight fullness of the *ca*-group; the letter *ṣa* is the slight fullness of the *ṭa*-group;
the letter *sa* is the slight fullness of the *ta*-group; and the letter *ha* is the slight fullness of the *ka*-group.

Thus, the distinction is that all phonemes (varṇas), which are the effects of that [source], are merely the ten specific states of the five phonemes beginning with 'a', which constitute the causal form. || 2 ||

In the collection of phonemes whose nature as the earth and other elements has been established by means of their positions, the labial class (*pavarga*) becomes the locus of the Mothers (*mātṛpada*).
Following that, the self, the mind, the intellect, and the ego-sense [arise];
and prior to the mind, primordial nature (prakṛti) also [emerges] by way of this descending sequence. (3)

Now, indicating by way of the aforementioned objects of knowledge (*prameya*) the discernment of how the aggregate of touch (*sparśakadambaka*) takes on the forms of earth and the other elements according to its location, he explains the five principles (*tattva*) to be expressed by the five letters of the *pa*-group within that locus of the knower (*pramātṛpada*).

Regarding the word *sthāna*: by means of the *sthāna*, that is, the throat, palate, and so forth; in the nature of earth and the other elements established through the previously mentioned procedure and by considering their positions as low or high; in the multitude of phonemes (*varṇotkara*), that is, in the collection of consonant-phonemes (*sparśavarṇa*); the labial group (*pavarga*) becomes the state of the subject (*mātṛpada*).

Although the status of being the subject (*pramātṛpada*) belongs exclusively to the *ka*-group due to its pervasiveness, nevertheless, the subjecthood of the *ca*-group is derivative, and the objecthood of consciousness (*cit*) is likewise [derivative]; thus, the designation of the *pa*-group as the "subject-position" (*pramātṛpada*) according to the previous teaching is beyond reproach.
By way of descent (*avaroha*), that is, in reverse order; the meaning is from the letter *ma* up to the letter *pa*.

The letters of the *pa*-group—namely *ātman*, *manas*, *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *prakṛti*—possess the nature of the five principles (*tattva*) in reverse order. By virtue of manifesting those [principles], they possess their nature figuratively. The letter *ma* is *ātman*.

The meaning is that the letter *pu* is the principle of the Puruṣa (*puruṣatattva*). The letter *bha* is the principle of the mind (*manastattva*). The letter *ba* is the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).
The letter *pha* is the principle of the ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*). It should be understood that the letter *pa* is the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*).
This is so because the five letters beginning with *pa* correspond respectively to the elements starting from earth and ending with space (*ākāśa*).

The conventional usage of *prakṛti* and so forth is as follows: the earth-element is *prakṛti*; the water-element is *ahaṅkāra*; the fire-element is *buddhi*; the air-element is *manas*; and the ether-element is *puruṣa*. This is the discernment (*viveka*).
In this same manner, for each of the other four groups as well, starting from the first letter, there is a correspondence with the earth-element and the others.
It should be understood that the nature of each respective principle (tattva) which is about to be described exists precisely [therein].

Now, one might object: "Is there not a traditional teaching that the principle of Nature (prakṛti-tattva) follows immediately after the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva)? How then is there no contradiction here regarding the sequence?
To this he says: "prior to the mind" (prākcetasaḥ). That is, Nature comes first, prior to the mind (cetas), which is to say, prior to the intellect (manas).

The Sequence of the Emergence of the Principles (Tattvodayakrama): Following the emergence of the two substrata—Puruṣa and Prakṛti—which take the forms of space and earth, there arises the emergence of their attributes, namely mind, intellect, and ego. Nevertheless, because those attributes emerge precisely within the interval between the two substrata, they are enumerated as being situated in the middle with respect to their emergence.

The sense is that, because there is no interval between two properties (*dharma*) belonging to two different substrates (*dharmin*), and because there is no infinite regress, the two properties are considered to be "in the middle" of the two substrates. Furthermore, although the mind (*manas*) is situated in the middle, it remains in close proximity [to the soul] because it is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*); whereas the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), being a property of primordial nature (*prakṛtidharma*), [remains near its own substrate].

It should be understood that the state of the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses the characteristics of both [mind and ego], is situated between the mind (*manas*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and exists in close proximity to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Regarding the pervasion of emission (*visarga-vyāpti*), the sequence is: primordial nature, ego, intellect, mind, and person (*puruṣa*);
whereas regarding the pervasion of the point (*bindu-vyāpti*), the sequence is: person, mind, intellect, ego, and primordial nature. This is the order here.
Because the pervasion of the *visarga* occurs first, the sequence beginning with the *prakṛti* must be accepted. || 3 ||
Indeed, the group beginning with the ear consists of the *tavarga*, while this pentad beginning with speech consists of the form of the *ṭavarga* in reverse order.
Sound and the rest, as well as the letters of the *ka* and *ca* groups, are the playful manifestations of air, fire, water, and earth. (4)
Having explained the principles (tattvas) denoted by the letters of the *pavarga* class, he now elucidates the principles denoted by the letters of the *tavarga* class and others,
beginning with the words "the ear and so forth" (*śrotrādikam*). "The ear and so forth" refers to the form consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.

The pentad of principles (*tattvapañcaka*). This means it consists of the five letters beginning with *na* and ending with *ta*, which are formed from the *ta*-group in reverse order. Here too, the principle of space (*ākāśa*) is the element represented by the letter *na*, while the skin is represented by the letter *dha*.

The letter *va* represents the portion of air (*vāyu*). That which is represented by the letter *da* is the eye, the portion of fire (*tejas*). That which is represented by the letter *tha* is the tongue, the portion of water (*jala*). It should be understood that that which is represented by the letter *ta* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the portion of earth (*pṛthivī*). And this pentad beginning with speech is directly perceptible.

The fivefold group of principles consisting of speech, feet, hands, genitals, and anus is [formed] from the reverse order; this connection applies here as well. It takes the form of the *ṭa*-group in reverse sequence. The letter *ṇa* is the portion of space (*ākāśa*), representing speech. The letter *ḍha* is the portion of air (*vāyu*), representing the feet. The letter *ḍa* is the portion of fire (*tejas*), representing the hands. The letter *ṭha* is the portion of water (*jala*), representing the genitals. The letter *ṭa*...

The earth-element is the anus (*pāyu*). Furthermore, there is the pentad of principles consisting of sound and so forth—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—as well as the pentad of principles beginning with space, which consists of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
These correspond respectively to the *ca*-group and the *ka*-group of consonants. Here too, [the same applies].

The sequence of *viloma-āditya* continues: the letter *ña* is the portion of space, sound; the letter *jha* is the portion of air, touch; the letter *ja* is the portion of fire, form; the letter *cha* is the portion of water, taste;
the letter *ca* is the portion of earth, smell; the letter *ṅa* is space; the letter *gha* is air; the letter *ga* is fire.

The letter *kha* is water; the letter *ka* is earth—this is the distinction. These are the principles (*tattva*) of the four groups beginning with the *ta*-group: the manifestations of air, fire, water, and earth.
Since air is the presiding deity of the *ta*-group, it should be understood that the principles expounded by the *ta*-group are the manifestations of air.

Because Fire is the presiding deity of the *ṭa*-group of consonants, the principles (*tattvas*) signified by the *ṭa*-group are the manifestations (*vilāsas*) of Fire. Because Water is the presiding deity of the *ca*-group of consonants, the principles signified by the *ca*-group are the manifestations of Water. Because Earth is the presiding deity of the *ka*-group of consonants, the principles signified by the *ka*-group are the manifestations of Earth; such is the distinction. (4)
The primordial nature (prakṛti), whose essence is the body, is indeed the internal form of the earth; the subtle form of water would be the principle of egoity (ahaṅkriyā).
From fire comes intellect, from wind comes the mind, and the inner self is indeed the creation born of primordial nature— the seed for the creation of the earth.

Now, he demonstrates that for the gross cosmic egg (pṛthivyaṇḍa), which consists of the principles beginning with the *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *ta* groups, the cause exists in a subtle form as the phonemes of the *pa* group, ending with the *prakṛti*: "Dehātmikā" [etc.].
"Dehātmikā" means having the body as its form. *Prakṛti* is conventionally designated as the very conceit of being the body (*dehābhimāna*). That...

Nature (prakṛti) is the inner form— the internal, subtle essence— of the earth (urvī), that is, of the pṛthivī which has the form of the letter *ka*. Indeed, the ego-function (*ahaṅkāra*) must be the inner form of the water which has the form of the letter *ca*.
The intellect (*buddhi*) is the inner self of Fire, whose form is the *tavarga* [dentals]; the mind (*manas*) is the inner self of Wind, whose form is the *tavarga*.
Thus, the creation born of *prakṛti* is *saṃsāra*. There are four groups of letters beginning with the *pavarga*;
this is the *saṃsāra* of the *prakṛti* of form. Earth is the essence of the four groups of consonants beginning with the *kavarga*, which constitutes the creation of earth.

Of *saṃsāra*—the seed, that is, the cause. The gross state of the subtle *prakṛti-saṃsāra* itself is the earth-*saṃsāra*. Thus, the *prakṛti-saṃsāra*, which is synonymous with the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), is the effect; and while it naturally culminates in *prakṛti*, its root extends down to the earth. As for that which culminates in *prakṛti*:

The intended meaning is "the play of illusion" (māyāvilāsa). For this very reason, the great yantra is visualized as having the solar orb for its form, consisting of the eight squares ending with *prakṛti*, and as having the circle of rays for its form, consisting of the two sets of ten spokes ending with the earth (*pṛthivī*).
88) Between the body and the self—that is, between *prakṛti* and *puru�षа*—the cognizer is the body here; the self is its abode and also its limb.
If the body is the state of the Mother just as the Self is, then its being dissolved therein is the inseparable nature of Śiva and Śivā.

Now he begins the section on the primordial egg (*prakṛtyaṇḍa*), starting with the words "of the body and the self," and so forth. Between the body and the self—that is, between the two synonymous terms "body" and "self"—which correspond to *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, [the following is said].
In this context of the emission (*visarga*), the body is the subject (*pramātā*). Of that body, even its "abode" (*nilaya*)—that is, its support—is [discussed]. The word "even" (*api*)...

By the word "aṅgin" (the possessor of limbs), the possibility of being the principal is understood. For the body—which is a transformation of the principle of reflective awareness (vimarśatattva)—no existence whatsoever is possible without the Self (ātman), according to the rule that a quality (dharma) must necessarily reside in its substratum (dharmī). Thus, the Self is the "aṅga" (limb/part) of that body; it is the limb of that body.

Its being an "aṅga" (limb/member) consists in its being contained within that. When the body of the subject (*visarga-pramātṛ*)—which is a synonym for *prakṛti*—is pervaded, the Self, being contained within it, assumes the state of being its limb. Just as the Self ascends to and occupies the station of the subject (*pramātṛ-sthāna*), so too [the Self] is absorbed therein at the stage of the pervasion of the *bindu*.

In that Self, the body—having become merged and attained a single flavor—exists, maintaining its being; it does not, however, undergo absolute destruction. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-recurrence of the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Since reflective awareness is seen to arise again and again, even while being pervaded by Light (*prakāśa*), [the body persists].

It must be understood that the absolute cessation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not possible. He establishes the non-cessation of both [light and awareness] through their mutual pervasion by stating "non-separation" (*aviraha*). Regarding the term "of the two Śivas" (*śivayoḥ*): she who is Śivā and he who is Śiva are the two Śivas; [it refers to] those two, Śivā and Śiva. Non-separation.

It is mutual inseparability (*anyonyāvinābhāva*). *Svabhāva* means innate. Without light (*prakāśa*), there is no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and without reflective awareness, there is no light either; rather, when light is pervasive, reflective awareness exists in a state of identity with light, and when reflective awareness is pervasive, light exists precisely as having a distinct flavor (*bhinnarasa*).
The division. 6.
Due to its insentience, reflective awareness (vimarśa) manifests as the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti);
it is the intellect (buddhi) by virtue of being both insentient and sentient, whereas it is the mind (manas) because of its lack of insentience.
This triad of qualities (traiguṇya) constitutes the three external organs; it is the cause of the states of deep sleep and waking that remain [after the others have ceased]. || 7 ||

Having thus investigated the essential nature of the two substrates— the body and the self— he now contemplates the essential nature of the attribute, which is non-different from its threefold reflective awareness in the form of ego, intellect, and mind:

"Due to dullness," and so forth. Due to the dullness of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—that is, by assuming the stage of insentience—it is proclaimed as "egoity" (*ahaṅkṛti*); it becomes well-known [as such]. The meaning is that when the stage of insentience is assumed, reflective awareness itself is designated by the term "egoity. That very reflective awareness which occurs in the body as "I" is indeed insentient.

Vimarśa is the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense), because it is a property of that [consciousness] by virtue of being dependent upon the inert body. This very same inert *vimarśa*, being the *ahaṅkāra* within the internal sphere (*antaḥkakṣyā*), becomes the fivefold form of sound and so forth in the external sphere (*bahiḥkakṣyā*) as a property of the body; thus, it pertains to the Earth (*pṛthivī*), which is the constituent of the four elements and the possessor of those constituents.
Dharma. Now, he states that it is precisely *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) which, when assuming the stages of being both insentient and sentient, is designated as "intellect" (*buddhi*):

"Intellect, by virtue of being both insentient and sentient. The sense organ is the instrument of action; yet, because it itself possesses grossness, it is insentient due to its nature as an object of action, and because it vibrates by its own nature, it is sentient. Therefore—
Vimarśa (reflective awareness), in its form as the means of action, is called *buddhi* (intellect) within the internal sphere;
in the external sphere, it is called the pentad beginning with speech (*vāk*).
Furthermore, that very *vimarśa*, by assuming the state of non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*), is called *manas* (mind).
Reflection (*vimarśa*) abandons insentience by means of being the instrument of knowledge.

Indeed, the instruments of knowledge—such as the mind, the eyes, and so forth, which are divided into internal and external domains—are essentially insentient entities, distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), speech (*vāk*), and other such subtle forms. Thus...

He states that the triad of internal organs, beginning with ego (ahaṃkāra) and consisting of the nature of reflection (*vimarśa*), is indeed the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) by saying "the state of the three qualities" (*traiguṇyam*). This triad of external organs is the "threefoldness of the internal organs," which is the aggregate of the three qualities such as *sattva* and so forth. Ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the quality of *rajas*, because its nature is that of production (*utpatti*). Intellect (*buddhi*)...

Sattva [is predominant] because its nature is maintenance (*sthiti*). For the mind, the quality of *tamas* [is predominant] because its nature is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Indeed, withdrawal—which consists in the resting of the light within the singular form of consciousness—is called "darkness" (*tamas*) by worldly people. Thus, this mind possesses the quality of darkness only from a worldly perspective. Alternatively, [it may be so] regarding the aspect of withdrawal of activity (*kriyā*).

The worldly view is that *ahaṅkāra* is of the nature of action (*tamas*), the mind (*manas*) is of the nature of knowledge (*rajas*), the state of the world's manifestation is non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*), and its dissolution is inertness (*jaḍatva*). The established doctrine of Yoga, however, holds that the state of the world's manifestation is inertness, while its dissolution is non-inertness. Therefore, it should be understood according to one's intended purpose.
One must effect the conjunction of the inert and non-inert ego (ahaṅkāra) and mind (manas), which possess the qualities of tamas and rajas respectively.
Now, he states that these three internal organs within the body are the seeds for the three states beginning with deep sleep—using the term *sauṣupta*:
deep sleep itself is *sauṣupta*; the state remaining after both deep sleep and waking is dream; and the ego is...

The distinction is as follows: because of its insentience, the intellect (buddhi) is the cause of deep sleep; because it possesses both insentience and sentience, the intellect is the cause of the waking state; and because of its pure sentience, the mind (manas) is the cause of the dream state.

The embodied soul, whose nature consists of the three qualities (*guṇatrayamaya-prakṛti*), wanders incessantly through the states of existence, such as deep sleep and the rest, according to fixed necessity.
Even in those [perceptions], because they are preceded by the sense of "I," one perceives the elevation of the triple-fold (tripuṭī) as the primary constituent of the act of knowing.
Now, he describes how the embodied soul wanders through the three states, such as deep sleep, due to its connection with *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*. He says:
"The embodied one," etc. The embodied one is the cognizer who identifies with the body; his nature consists of the three *guṇas*.

He is described as one whose nature (*svabhāva*)—which is synonymous with the body—is *prakṛti* (primordial matter) in the form of a conjunction of the three *guṇas*. By this, the definition of *prakṛti* is stated: it is precisely the conjunction of the three *guṇas*.
The individual soul (*jīva*), having such a *prakṛti*, [exists] in states such as deep sleep, namely in the conditions of deep sleep, waking, and dreaming.

By necessity, that is, through non-deviation, it wanders again and again; even in those states, because egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) precedes them, due to the predominance of egoity which is a property of the body. Within the "threefold fold" (*tripuṭī*) consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—the casket containing the entire mass of saṃsāra—it attains its birth.

The pervasion of the object of knowledge (*prameya-vyāpti*). "The primary aspect of action" means that in this act, the primary aspect is action. "He perceives" means he reflects. When the body is the knower (*pramātṛ*), because its attribute—reflection—is insentient, there can be no investigation of the pervasion of the object of knowledge, which belongs to the side of the insentient.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 8 ||
The triad consisting of the object of cognition and the rest is constantly joined; it is the mind,
whose nature is the deluded ego-sense, that manifests the object of cognition and the other [factors].
Furthermore, it manifests as the mother and so forth by virtue of its own inherent nature;
and in the intermediate state, it should be understood that the intellect and the mind are one and the same.
Now, since the mind alone is the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) for the entire internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and since the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and other stages are merely levels of the mind—
because the mind is the primary form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— the author explains that the majesty of reflective awareness is the majesty of the mind.

"Me-y-ādi" means "the triad beginning with the object. The triad (*tripuṭī*) is the collection of the three components—object, means of knowledge, and knower. It is "constantly joined," meaning its nature is one of mutual inseparability. That triad is [perceived] by the mind (*manaḥ*), which is the root-form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), when it has become "stupefied"—that is, having assumed the stage of delusion (*auḍhya*), a synonym for insentience (*jāḍya*).

The "I-making self" (ahaṅkriyātman) is that which has the nature of ego (ahaṅkāra). It manifests the objects of cognition and so forth; that is to say, it manifests the objects of knowledge (prameya) and the rest in whatever manner they exist. The meaning is that it demonstrates the pervasion of the objects of cognition. The meaning is that the synthesis (anusandhāna) belonging to the mind alone is superimposed upon the ego. Now, that very mind—

"From its own non-inert nature"—the meaning is: having assumed its own non-inert nature as its inherent essence. "That triad" is understood from the previous context. "It causes the knower and so forth to appear"—that is, it causes the subject (*mātṛ*) and the rest to appear in such a way.
The meaning is that it demonstrates the pervasion of the conscious subject (*cit-pramātṛ*). The mind itself is in the intermediate state.

"In the state common to the insentient and the sentient" means by way of embracing both the insentient and the sentient states. Furthermore, it should be understood that "intellect" (buddhi) refers to that which demonstrates the equal pervasion between the object of knowledge and the knower, and that this intellect is indeed the mind (manas). || 9 ||
Therefore, from the primordial nature whose form is the letter *pa*, the Self of the knower, whose form is the letter *ma*, remains merged within as something distinct.

The state of abiding in the midst of that [unmanifested nature] constitutes the "I-maker," the intellect, and the heart; this is the station of the subject, wherein the entire universe is attached to the senses. || 10 ||

Taking the aforementioned object of knowledge as the cause and thereby strengthening the arrangement of the principles (tattvas) beginning with the group of labials (pavarga), he demonstrates it [with the words] "Therefore" (tasmāt).
"Therefore" means from the aforementioned cause in the form of the object of knowledge; [it refers to] that which has the form of the letter *pa*.

Of the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) which is to be conveyed by the letter *pa*; "having the form of *pa*" means having the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *pa*—this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Of the knower (*pramātṛ*), who consists of the *prakṛti* that is a synonym for the body; "only within" means precisely in the state of being pervaded.
Having the form of *ma*, having the essential nature of *ma*—here too it is a metaphorical designation. The Self (*ātman*) is the *puruṣa* (Spirit); "merged" means pervaded.
This is the meaning. *Tanmadhyataḥ* means in the middle portion between those two, namely *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

*Ahaṅkṛtidhīhṛdām* refers to the arrangement (*sthitiḥ*) or placement (*sanniveśaḥ*) of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*). Although the letter *M*, representing the Self (*ātman*), is placed in the category of the pervasive subject (*pramātṛpada*), nevertheless—

Because it is situated between the *pavarga* and the *vyāpakavarga*, its connection to the procedures of both sides should be understood. Since the group of *sparśa* consonants constitutes the locus of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the letter *m*—representing the knower (*pramātṛ*)—is enumerated according to that illumination. Nevertheless...
One must indeed accept, from a standpoint of neutrality, the mere relationship between the means of knowledge, the categories, and their functions;

therefore, it is faultless that the pervasion of *prakṛti* extends as far as the *puruṣa*. However, in the arrangement of the square wheel, the pervasion of the *ahaṅkāra* and *prakṛti* extends only to the mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*), which take the forms of the self (*ātman*) and the person (*puruṣa*). By these two—

And this is the distinction: that there is a pervasion by both of these. Now, within this very context of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he demonstrates the wonder of the unfolding of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) for the mind and intellect, as if in the state of dreaming—beginning with the words "this" and so forth.
This state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*) is of the form of another primordial nature; it is the universe attached to the senses.
The universe becomes connected with the mind, intellect, form, cognition, and the organs of action; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 10 ||
And this locus of the mother, which is dependent upon the sense faculties, as well as that which is its support, is the mind itself; it would be that very faculty.
Indeed, the power of discernment belonging to that family of the sovereign senses is the consciousness itself; everything mixed with the object of thought is truly its manifestation. || 11 ||

Now, he demonstrates that all this play of the internal and external world has its root solely in the mind: "And this" (*etacca*). This refers to the state of the subject (*mātṛpada*), which is the aforementioned form of the cognizer (*pramātṛpada*).

And it is "supported by the senses" (*indriya-saṃśrita*) because it consists of the manifestation of the senses in the form of the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*); thus, it is supported by them.

That which is supported by both mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*), and the support of those two—namely, the support and the locus of mind and intellect—is stated to be nothing other than its own inherent locus. Therefore, upon careful consideration, that sense organ which possesses these two forms would also be the mind alone; it is merely a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the mind itself.
Because it has been stated that [the mind] is the intellect (*buddhi*); it is the leader—that is, the activator—of the group of senses, the network of internal and external instruments.

That is the mind (*manas*). It is the power of deliberation (*vimarśa-śakti*), characterized by the flurry of the unfolding and closing of the eyes, and the activity of ejecting and re-swallowing the manifold universe.

It is the power of reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*). It is the mind itself. And it is everything—mixed with consciousness and its objects—in the form of the knower, the known, and the means of knowledge. Its manifestation is indeed the manifestation of that mind.
By means of this, there is the well-known fact that "this splendor of the network of senses shines forth intensely in the waking state. (11)
In a dream, as well as in the waking state and the state of the mother’s womb, the object of knowledge appears to the mind of the self of will within the belly.
In the former case, it is the mind alone that possesses corporeality as perceived; in the latter term, however, it is the body itself.

Thus, he awakens [the student] to the fact that the universe shines within the womb of the mind alone—which is of the nature of will—both in the state of dream and in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*):
"And in the dream... and so forth. This means: both in the dream and in the waking state, which is the locus of the subject (*mātṛpada*).

The word *mātṛpada* refers to that which is non-transformative (*avaikārika*), meaning it is the nature of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) characterized by *prakṛti*, which is to be understood through the labial class of consonants (*pavarga*).

Within that, the object of knowledge (*vedya*), consisting of the internal and external manifold (*prapañca*), shines forth— that is, it manifests— as a very embryo within the womb of the mind whose essence is will (*icchātman*).
The meaning is that the dream-state is the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) of the innate nature (*prakṛti*), while the waking state is the cycle of existence of desire.

In the case of knowledge, the sense of the phrase is that the waking state is the cycle of existence of the organs of cognition and the organs of action—that is, the cycles of cognition and action. Now, one might object: since the dream state is of the nature of cognition, it is the cycle of existence of the mind (*manas*), whereas the waking state is the cycle of existence of action.

It was previously taught that the desire for deep sleep, which is of the nature of rest, constitutes the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). One should not wonder how there can now be a teaching of a different form; for when that very rest turns outward, it is the cycle of existence consisting of desire (*icchā-saṃsāra*), which is indeed the dream state; it is the cycle of existence consisting of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃsāra*), which is indeed the waking state; and it is the cycle of existence consisting of action (*kriyā-saṃsāra*).
There is repose in the insentient and repose in the sentient; thus, in deep sleep and dreaming, there is the conceit of repose in the insentient and the sentient.
For one who is awake, the state of the cycle of knowledge and action arises from the established functioning of the organs of knowledge and action.
Alternatively, the cycle of nature becomes the cycle of knowledge, as does the cycle of the earthly.

The distinction is as follows: the state of the *saṃsāra* of action is indeed the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) consisting of both the insentient and the sentient; the state of the *saṃsāra* of the conceit of desire for both the insentient and the sentient is the dream, which is the *saṃsāra* of knowledge; and the waking state is the *saṃsāra* of action. Therefore, in this context, because one who rests in the dream-state possesses the conceit of the *saṃsāra* of non-insentient desire, it is a mental *saṃsāra*, just like a dream.
It is thus beyond reproach that the natural cycle of existence (*prakṛti-saṃsāra*) has also been described as the cycle of existence through desire (*icchā-saṃsāra*).

Since the dream state and the natural cycle of existence are identical in being cycles of existence through desire, [the author] reveals the previously established point of distinction with the words "in the former case": "In the former case," i.e., in the dream state, it is the mind itself that assumes the state of a body.
*Mātṛ-pramātṛ* (Mother-Measurer). However, regarding the subsequent state of *prakṛti-saṃsāra*, it is held that the body itself, as being perceptible and mental, is the measurer (*pramātṛ*).
The meaning is that this very [body] is the case for both of these states of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). || 12 ||
The mind, having internalized the entire universe, emits it externally as a state of aesthetic wonder, through the manifestation of the group of senses beginning with hearing.
Therein also, the group of the intellect and the senses, as well as the wind, earth,
objects of knowledge, and even the waters, are stirred within by the vital airs.
Now he begins the exposition of the process of the worldly cycle (*saṃsāra*) of the earthly realm, starting with the words "If" (*cet*), and so forth.

The "locus of wonder" (*camatkṛtipada*) is the site of all marvels. The "mind" (*cetas*), which is the very essence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is the agent. "Dissolved within itself" (*svalīna*) means internalized within its own nature. This occurs within the cycle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Just as the world of dreams is accepted even by worldly people as being a mere play of the mind, it is "situated in the mind" (*manoniṣṭhatva*), meaning its dissolution is in the mind; the sense is that the mind shines forth within its own essential nature. It emits the universe externally, and this emission of the universe is [the state of] *bhairava*.
The mind (*manas*) is a particular wonder. To the question, "In what form does it project itself outward?", he says:
"Because of its becoming the group of organs whose mouth is the ear.
This means because it assumes the nature of the entire group of sensory and motor organs, beginning with the ears and ending with speech.

The meaning is: by way of not being grasped as belonging to the levels of the ear and so forth. From the ear and so forth alone there is the emergence of the universe in the form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-rūpa*); from speech and so forth alone [there is the emergence] of the universe in the form of action (*kārya-rūpa*).
Because the universe necessarily shines within the illumination of the senses, the senses possess the status of being its cause; thus it is.
The internal nature of the various sense-faculties (*indriya-rūpāntaratva*) of the universe culminates precisely in the manifestation of the sense-faculties.

Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the unfolding of the manifestation of the sense-faculties is their radiance (*sphuraṇa*), whereas in the absence of such unfolding, there is no radiance.
The universe is the manifestation of the senses [emanating] from Him, and not atoms and other such entities as accepted by the Kāṇādas who are deluded by *māyā*; enough of this digression.
Thus, regarding the subject of the bound soul (*paśu*), the universe has emerged as the manifestation of the senses from the ultimate reality.

He describes the process of erroneous cognition with the words "tatrāpi" (there too). "There" (*tatra*) refers to the external stage (*bahiḥkakṣyā*). The word "api" (also) indicates the inclusion of the internal stage (*antaḥkakṣyā*).
Just as there is an erroneous cognition in the bound soul (*paśu*) regarding the evolution of primordial nature (*prakṛti-saṃsara*) in the internal stage, so it is in the external stage.
The meaning is: even within the worldly egg (pārthivāṇḍa). The "group of senses" refers to the collection of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya).

Even though it is "blowing" (pavamāna)—meaning it occupies the position of air within the all-pervading consciousness that is the ultimate reality—it has attained the position of earth due to its state of contraction. This occurs even through the objects of knowledge (jñeya), which are of the nature of knowables, and through the waters of experience (vedya).

Even by means of the water-places (*jalasthānaka*) within the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). Here, [this occurs] through the contrary winds (*viparītamarut*), having reached the air-places (*vāyusthāna*) by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Internally aroused" (*antarudīritaḥ*) means cast into one's own interior; the meaning is "pervaded. The meaning is that there is a pervasion of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), which consist of the *tavarga* group, by the objects such as sound, which consist of the *cavarga* group. || 13 ||
The organs of action possess hardness and the ultimate limit; they have the form of fire and are supported by the earth situated in the space [of the heart].
One should understand that the elements of this multitude of beings are here oriented toward grasping the sword of the earth-nature when there is a reversal [of their natural state]. 14.
Now he states the reversal of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) and those objects of knowledge that consist of effects, beginning with the words "action" (*karman*) and so forth.

The organs of action are speech and the others, which are denoted by the *ya*-class of consonants. They are described as "possessing the ultimate limit of hardness," meaning they partake of the supreme boundary of hardness. [This pertains] to action (*kriyā*).

Because the organs of action (*karmendriya*) consist of the stages of contraction and expansion, and because their objects of experience (*vedya*), which take the form of effects, possess an extreme state of contraction, they are exceedingly rigid. They have the form of fire and are composed of fire, in which the dull (*jaḍa*) aspect predominates. However, when pervaded by consciousness (*cidvyāpti*), [they become otherwise].

The organs of action consist primarily of fire, which is the non-inert aspect [of consciousness]. That fire consists of both the inert and the non-inert, as was explained previously. Located in the earth situated within the space [of the heart], they depend upon the earth which has pervaded the state of space characterized by all-pervasiveness. This applies to speech and the other organs.

Even though the term *paśu* (the bound soul) is by its very nature dependent on the body as a synonym for *prakṛti*, nevertheless, because of the contemplation of the pervasion of the earth— which is the primary element perceivable through its effects— it is said to be "dependent on the earth.
And in the terms such as "earth" which denote the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*), it refers to the Great Earth (*mahāpṛthivī*) in its full form, which possesses a metaphorical form.

In this way, when the earth-like primordial nature (prakṛti) is grasped— that is, pervaded— the various manifestations of the multitude of elements here should be understood as being oriented toward the opposite.
The intention here is that the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) of a bound soul (paśu) are capable of knowing only some portion of the objects of knowledge, such as sound and the rest.

They are not capable of producing everything; therefore, those [elements] are pervaded by those [objects]. It is sound and the other [subtle elements] themselves that, having attained grossness in the state of being effects through the form of speech and so forth, become ether and the other [gross elements].
Furthermore, the organs of action are capable of producing only ether and the rest in the form of speech and so forth, but not [everything].
Space and the other [elements] are the effects of the great elements (*mahābhūta*); therefore, they too are pervaded by the great elements as their effects.

Thus, the twofold group of sense organs, being pervaded by the twofold group of objects of cognition, provides the two types of subjects—the nature of the self and the body—with a pervasion by the groups of objects of knowledge and effects. However, in the case of the pervasion by consciousness (*cidvyāpti*),...

The self (*ātman*), pervading the objects of knowledge to be known through its own instruments—the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*)—appropriates them to itself; by appropriating all that is knowable, it becomes omniscient (*sarvajña*). And the body, pervading the effects to be known through its own instruments—the organs of action (*karmendriya*)—appropriates those specific effects to itself.

Because of the process of making everything one's own, one becomes the creator of all; thus should the procedure regarding the relationship between the nature and the transformation of the organs of knowledge and action be understood. || 14 ||
For the establishment of the sun that consists of the means of knowledge occurs from both [sides];
and here, by the power of *māyā*, the first [position] belongs to the category of the object of knowledge (*meyakoṭi*).

Those skilled in the sequence should apply the *kalās* both externally and internally, by means of the correspondence between the words and letters of "the grasped" (*grāhya*) and "the grasper" (*grahītṛ*). || 15 ||

Now, he explains the process of the arrangement of the digits (*kalā*) of the sun of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which abides in a form mixed with the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*),
beginning with the words "māna" and so forth: "Of the sun, whose nature is the means of knowledge and whose form is the instrument of cognition, from the two..."

Establishment (*siddhi*) indeed means the attainment of one's own nature (*svarūpalābha*) through both the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the subject (*pramātṛ*). And here, by the power of *māyā*, the side of the object (*prameyakoṭi*) occupies the first position, while the side of the subject (*pramātṛkoṭi*) occupies the second position.
The meaning is that the pervasion of emission (*visargavyāpti*) alone is the first. Here, [the role] of the sun of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇasūrya*)...
In the conjunction of the *kalās* to be expressed by pairs of phonemes (*varṇa*),

through the coordination of the states of being the grasped and the grasper— that is, by the appropriate coordination of the phonemes belonging to the positions of the grasped immediately followed by the phonemes belonging to the positions of the grasper— [the result arises] externally.

Within the range from the *ka*-group to the *ta*-group, ending with earth (*pṛthivī*); and internally, within the range from the letter *pa* to the letter *bha*, ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). By those who know the sequence—that is, by those who understand the sequence of the letters representing the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—the *kalās* are to be joined.
The joining of the letters of the *ka*-group and *ṭa*-group is according to their respective order, and likewise for the *ca*-group and *ta*-group.
The conjunction of *pa* and *ka*, as well as of *pha* and *bha*, likewise forms two sets of ten spokes;
thus, the solar wheel of rays is square, which is the discus of the orb.
As for that [wheel] which consists of the twelve letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ḍa*, read in direct order (*anuloma*).

Through the combination of the twelve syllables read in reverse order from *bh* to *ḍ*, there is the conceptualization of the twelve solar digits (*sūryakalā*). Within the twenty-four consonants (*sparśākṣara*) which constitute the essential nature of the Sun— the subject who is the cognizer of that object of knowledge— one half belongs to the category of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the other half [belongs to the subject].

Because the pinnacle of the subject (*pramātṛkoṭi*) results in the manifestation of the twelve digits (*kalā*) through the conjunction of both sides, it does not attain agreement with the arrangement of the wheel (*cakra-saṃsthāna*), even though it exists; thus,
it has been disregarded by the great-souled ones who know the vital points (*marman*) of the *mātṛkā*-wheel— enough of this.
By means of discourse that deceives regarding the Great Path. || 15 ||
The Mother consists of the ten senses and the eleven objects of cognition; from their union arises the pair of ten-spoked wheels, whose nature is the ten *kalās*.
Within this square diagram, the two internal digits (kalās) are dissolved here into Prakṛti, the mother of the three qualities (guṇas), and the Puruṣa.

It was indicated by the previous aphorism that the *kalā* should be applied through the correspondence of the external and internal [realms], as well as the objects of perception (*grāhya*), the perceiver (*grahītṛ*), the positions (*pada*), and the phonemes (*varṇa*). While corroborating the method of applying the *kalā* within the arrangement of the wheel (*cakra*),
he teaches it clearly with the intention of avoiding distraction toward other subjects:

"Mother," and so forth. For the Sun consists of the knower (*mātṛ*) and the known (*meya*). The knower is the *tavarga* group of consonants, which externally consists of the ten sense organs as represented by the *ṭavarga*.
The known is likewise the *cavarga* and *kavarga*, consisting of the tenfold [elements] beginning with space (*ākāśa*), such as sound and the rest, as represented by those groups. From their union...

This is because, in their respective order, there is a merging of the five letters of the *ka*-group— which represent the effects of earth and so forth and their corresponding objects of cognition— with the five letters of the *ṭa*-group— which represent the organs of action such as speech—
and likewise with the five letters of the *ca*-group which represent smell and so forth.
Through the union of the five vowels beginning with *ā* (representing the nose and so forth) with the group of five consonants beginning with *ta*, there arises, by combining these two pentads,
a pair of ten-spoked wheels consisting of ten digits (*kalās*). Within this,

in the locus of the subject (*pramātṛpada*) which takes the form of the labial class (*pa-varga*), there are two digits [represented] by the letter *pa*, which denotes *prakṛti*— the seed of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) that is to be produced.
The syllable *ekākalā* arises from the combination of the letter *ba*, which denotes the intellect (*buddhi*) that serves as the seed of the organs of action (*karmendriya*),
with the letter *pha*, which denotes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) that serves as the seed of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vedya*).
Furthermore, the syllable *anyākalā* arises from the combination of the letter *bha*, which denotes the mind (*manas*) that serves as the seed of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*).

In this square mandala, which consists of two parts produced from four syllables, the Person (pums)— the Self in the form of the letter *ma*— is dissolved into Prakṛti, the Mother of the Three Qualities (*traiguṇya*) and the progenitor of the three qualities (*triguṇasavitṛ*).
The dissolution of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*) into Prakṛti, together with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), constitutes the dissolution of the Person.

The sense is that it culminates [there]. Since the wheel of touch and phonemes (*sparśavarṇacakra*) is the wheel of valid cognition (*pramāṇacakra*), the person (*puruṣa*) is situated here in this wheel in the form of mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*) alone, and not in the form of the letter *ma*. Nevertheless, because mind and intellect are merely other forms of the person itself, [the person] is also [present there].

Because the letter *ma* occupies the middle between the wheel of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the wheel of the knower (*pramātṛ*), it is connected to both wheels; thus it is said that the Person (*pumān*) is dissolved therein. || 16 ||
100) Within this wheel, which consists of duality, the state of consciousness and the unconscious does not exist by means of the ego itself; here, it arises from the bindu of emission.
Even the persistence of this [consciousness] belongs to the primary state of union, which is the abode of the enjoyment of the single point (bindu) as is fitting for the City of the Mothers. || 17 ||

This [verse] clarifies the connection between both wheels—the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—of that very reality of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) which was indicated by the letter *ma* in the preceding sūtra.
Beginning with "māna" (the means of knowledge), etc.: here, the wheel consists of duality. Of the wheel of the means of knowledge...

Because it is the ground for the inseparable relationship between the distinction of the grasped and the grasper, it possesses the form of two sets of ten spokes; however, it does not consist of fourteen spokes or eight spokes each, as that would constitute a single wheel. Therefore, within this dual nature, its essential character is one of manifest duality. Here, within the Wheel of Means (*pramāṇacakra*), there exists the state of the cognizer and the cognizable—consciousness and the non-conscious—precisely through the nature of the means of knowledge itself.

"By way of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) alone. This means that because the sense-faculties—which are synonymous with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are established as having the nature of both the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), the status of the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the subject (*mātṛ*) exists precisely in the form of the grasped and the grasper. For this reason, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) should be supplied here according to the requirements of the context. In this [verse]:

In the *pramāṇacakra*: because even the *bindu* of the *visarga* consists of differentiation, the meaning is "of the *visarga*. Of the *puruṣa* represented by the letter *ma*, there is no "attachment" (*anuṣaṅga*). In the *pramāṇacakra*, which consists of twenty-four syllables and takes the form of twelve *kalās*, [this refers to] the locus of the *puruṣa*.

The meaning is that there is no placement of the twenty-fifth letter, *ma*. If one asks, "In that case, does this imply a total absence of connection for that Puruṣa, represented by the letter *ma*, within this wheel?

he replies: "Even though there is a primary correspondence (*mukhya-samanvaya*)," [meaning] even though it possesses a connection as the principal element, in the Wheel of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa-cakra*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even for that which possesses a relationship by virtue of being the object of the pervasion of *prakṛti*, there is no attachment (*anuṣakti*) in that wheel (*cakra*).
Why? He says: "of that which is appropriate for the city of the subject (*mātṛpura*), which is the single place of enjoyment (*ekabhogapada*) for the *bindu*.
For the *bindu*'s single place of enjoyment is the city of the subject in the form of the eight-spoked [wheel]; it is appropriate for that. For two...
In brief, there are two types of subjects (*pramātṛ*): the one who perceives non-duality (*abhedānusandhātṛ*) and the one who perceives duality (*bhedānusandhātṛ*).

Among these, the subject who perceives duality is what is indicated by the letter *ma*. Therefore, the well-known subject is fit only for residence within the city of the subject indicated by the letter *ma*, and not within the city of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In that regard, the arrangement of those two other forms belongs specifically to the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*). However, the conclusion is that the connection of that which is signified by the letter *ma* must indeed exist even within the wheel of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacakra*). 17.

101) Having experienced that which was remembered as a dream, one then encounters in the waking state a bondage that is as if real; yet, by the power of one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), [one realizes its nature].
And being under the sway of that earth, having lost his maternal nature, this letter 'a' with the nasal bindu is like the midday sun. || 18 ||

Concluding the section on the pervasion of emission (*visarga*), [the author] demonstrates, by encompassing this very section which begins with the "swallowing of consciousness" (*cinnigaraṇa*), [the passage] beginning with "In a dream," and so forth: "In a dream, that which is remembered is mentally constructed; subsequently, in the waking state, it becomes as if real."

Due to being firmly established in experience, there is an appearance as if it were the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), yet it is not the ultimate reality itself; for Śiva, whose nature is non-conceptual consciousness, appears eternally unobscured through the internal reflective awareness of the inner dimension (*antaḥkakṣyā-parāmarśa*), whereas that which appears externally is merely a fluctuation of the vibration of active reflective awareness (*pravṛttirūpa-vimarśa-spanda*).

Because of the state of being a subject characterized by wonder (*camatkāra-pramātṛtva*): internally, through the power of self-reflection (*svavimarśa-śakti*), [the Self] becomes bound in its own essential nature and form—which is the very power of non-reflection (*avimarśa-śakti*)—as that which is synonymous with *prakṛti*;
and externally, as the earth (*kṣiti*). Thus, having fallen into bondage in both these two stages, it becomes subject to and dependent upon those two: the body and the great earth.

The sense is that his status as a mother has been taken away by those very two, and his status as a knower (pramātṛ) has been stripped from him so that he has attained the state of being an object of knowledge (prameya). "The bindu of the letter *ma*" means the bindu signified by the letter *ma*, which is the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), meaning the Puruṣa.
"The sun at midday" refers to the fact that the midday sun has arisen; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Just as...

Just as the midday sun, shrouded by a mass of its own rays, does not shine forth, so too this conscious self (cidātman), its fundamental nature concealed by the expansion of its own power of reflective awareness (vimarśaśakti) in the form of the internal and external phenomenal world (prapañca), has become obscured; such is the meaning. || 18 ||
102) This avoidance of the contraction of the four letters beginning with *pa* and ending with *va* is indeed according to the system of the Tantra.
Established in the Fourth state, consisting of the fourfold peace of the faces beginning with Ha, it should be applied sequentially to the external and internal creations. 19.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Investigation of the Waking State, in the *Śrīmātṛkācakraviveka*.

Now, at the conclusion of this section, introducing the subject matter (*prameya*) of the subsequent section— namely, the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*)— the two states consisting of the waking-turiya and the dreaming-turiya, which serve as the "counter-throne" (*pratisiṃhāsana*) for the subject of emission (*visargapramātṛ*) within both the waking-wheel and the dream-wheel to be described hereafter, are each unfolded according to the established method by means of the individual phonemes (*mātṛkā*).

He explains this with the words "yatpādi" and so forth: from the four vowels beginning with *pā* [and the consonants] in reverse order, there arises a set of four groups consisting of the four groups beginning with *pa*, the *ta*-group, and the *ṭa*-group— this being the fourfold group in the form of *vargas*.

The four phonemes consisting of *va*, *la*, *ra*, and *ya* belong to both [the groups]. According to the method of the Tantra—that is, by means of a single action consisting in the accomplishment of two purposes, according to the system and logic of the Tantra—this indeed is the avoidance of contraction; that is, the abandonment of the contraction produced by the articulatory efforts (*prayatna*) of contact (*spṛṣṭa*) and slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).
Indeed, that which resides in the fourth [state] is the collection of phonemes consisting of the four peaceful faces beginning with *Ha*.

The letter *Ha* is of the nature of the contraction and abandonment of the *Pa*-group and the letter *Va*. The letter *Sa* is of the nature of the contraction and abandonment of the *Ta*-group and the letter *La*. [The letter *Sa* is also] of the nature of the contraction and abandonment of the *Ṭa*-group and the letter *Ra*.

The letter *ṣa*. The letter *śa* consists of the contraction and abandonment of the palatal class (*cavarga*) and the letter *ya*. Since the guttural class (*kavarga*) and the letter *la*, which signifies the body, possess the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) as *visarga*, and since that [subject] disappears into the very nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*) within the state of the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāptipada*), there is a dissolution into the letter *ha* alone in both word-pairs; therefore, it is not [otherwise].
The phoneme (varṇa) consisting of the contraction and abandonment of that [state] is to be sought.

Likewise, the four phonemes beginning with *ha* and ending with *śa*, which consist of the contraction and abandonment of the touch (*sparśa*) and the contraction and abandonment of that [touch], exist as two words in sequence.

Regarding the two types of creation—external and internal: this means in the state of non-dual waking which is the counterpart to dualistic waking (both external and internal), and in the state of non-dual dreaming which is the counterpart to dualistic dreaming. It should be understood that these correspond to the half-stage of the pair of ten-spoked wheels and the half-stage of the eight-spoked wheel, respectively. This is how they are to be applied.
This is to be applied [in the same way]. || 19 ||
For every entity, having initially existed in a state of differentiation,
subsequently realizes its non-differentiation once awakened consciousness has arisen;
such is the great power of Śiva, which is primordial nature (prakṛti) and whose essence is that [Śiva] himself.
Therefore, one who possesses discernment ought to offer salutation to the reality of discernment. || 1 ||
He who, intent on duality, casts aside the Māyā established right before him by Śiva during his worship—
does such a person, O follower of Śiva’s discipline, not fail to attain perfection? Is he not utterly deluded?
Therefore, from the face of the horse (or yakṣa), a square image [should be fashioned]. || 2 ||
The *bindu* is indeed the withdrawal of the two *ī*-vowels, the female organ (*yoṣit*), the seed-syllable (*ga*), and the digit of emission (*visarga-kalā*).
Through these two digits, the state of emission is truly withdrawn;
immediately, the world, whose accomplishment of differentiation has been suddenly gathered, [is dissolved].
The mantra, whose form is the syllable *klīṃ*, should be recited incessantly. || 3 ||

One should practice from me this mantra, which has *ya* and *kāra* as its core, is most excellent with a pair of *ka*s, and has its head pervaded by *māyā*. Carrying a rosary made of ruby (*aruṇamaṇi*), he, while enjoying, shall attain that which is well-known by the names of *aṇimā* and the rest, whose nature is that of a servant.
Having attained here on earth, through divine means, the tenfold group of perfections that is to be obtained through the Siddhis.
By the sage Śivānanda, who abides by the command of his teacher, the fourth section has been explained in this *Mātṛkācakraviveka*. (5)
Thus ends the fourth section.
Now begins the fifth section:
The dissolution of the senses into the object of knowledge is indeed Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā); the dissolution of those senses into the body results in the state of Īśvara.
For the Lord, possessing the conceit of a body composed of the universe, is Śiva’s waking state, which is joined to the wheel of the waking consciousness of bound souls (paśu). || 1 ||

Now, beginning the fourth aggregate (skandha) which consists of withdrawal (nivṛtti), and because it commences with the waking state of withdrawal, [the author] first describes the subject known as Īśvara— the presiding deity of the waking state of withdrawal— who constitutes the stage of Śiva’s universal agency.

He indicates this [state] along with the subject of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*) through a specific external condition—beginning with the words "in the senses" (*akṣeṣu*), etc. "In the senses" means in the organs of perception (*indriya*) such as hearing, or in the organs of action (*vāk* etc. such as speech, or in the organs of smell (*ghrāṇa* etc.).

"The dissolution of the objects of knowledge" (*vedyavilaya*) refers to the dissolution—that is, the unification—with those [senses] of the objects of knowledge, namely the elements beginning with earth.
Indeed, Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) is the subject who rests upon Pure Knowledge; thus, the term "Pure Knowledge" is used figuratively [for that subject].

In the state of bondage (pāśava), it refers to those objects of knowledge (vedya) which, through the illumination of the senses, appear externally while possessing their own efficacy, and which are contained within the illumination of the senses.

Thus, through the determination that consists of the identity with the senses— which takes the form of the reflective awareness of the light of the senses and the reflective awareness of the certainty of illumination—

pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which is of the nature of an experience of oneness with the senses, emerges by means of the grace of the Guru upon the one who creates delusion through the fetters; this very pure knowledge [operates] toward objects of cognition in the state of the bound soul (*paśu*), where the notion of "this" is the sole domain.
Upon the exclusion of the animal-like state,

because of the determination of identity with the light of one's own self and the senses, the object of the notion of "I" attains the status of being designated by that [term "I"] through metaphorical usage; such is its distinction.

Having thus explained the state of the pure subject of Śuddhavidyā, characterized by the submergence of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) within the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he now explains the stage of Īśvara that follows it, beginning with the words "In the body," etc. "In the body" refers to the subject; "the dissolution of those senses" refers to their [dissolution].

The dissolution, immersion, and unification into a single essence of the senses— which have internalized the objects of knowledge through practice during the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)— is Sovereignty (īśvaratva). In the state of Pure Knowledge, the objects of knowledge,
having been submerged along with the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa) within the body-self...

The meaning is that "lordship" (īśvaratva) consists in the immersion of the objective world into the bodily portion of the state of the subject. In this context, the universe—which is essentially the first object of knowledge—becomes the object of the notion of "I" (ahantā-pratyaya), which is permeated by the cognition of "this-ness" (idaṃ-pratyaya) regarding the body. This occurs for that [universe] which has been immersed in the state of the body.

Because the universe, like the body, is the object of the firm notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) [in relation to the Lord], the Lord is the impeller of the universe as well as of the body; therefore, it should be understood that the Lord is the agent of all. However, in the stage of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), because of the predominance of the notion of "this" (idaṃpratyaya) over both the notions of "this" and "I," [the relationship is different].

There is no arising of the state of being the agent of all activity. Because the Lord, whose body is the universe, possesses the waking state of Śiva, it is demonstrated that there is a conjunction with the waking state of the bound soul (paśu)—this is expressed by the words "For the Lord...
For the Lord, having formed an identification with the body consisting of the universe, [is present] in the limited body which is the waking state of Śiva.

The meaning is that for the bound soul (paśu) who has formed such conceit, [the state] is fixed and joined within the two ten-spoked wheels of the waking cycle; this is because of the fitness of the union between the waking state of the bound soul and the waking state of Śiva. It has been previously established that even during the three states beginning with deep sleep, the nature of the mutual union between the inert and non-inert levels [of consciousness] remains constant. || 1 ||
That which is immersion into the outermost of the external is, within the inner, [immersion] into the state of consciousness; this is the opposite in the state of the insentient.
Here, the letter Śa is that which is to be known as the Self of the senses; for it is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).
The letter Ṣa is the Lord (Īśvara), whose organs of action and perception are non-different from his body. || 2 ||

Now, for the subject of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*), whose nature is cessation and who practices the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) toward objects of knowledge, differentiation has not been stilled; therefore,
the state of presiding over the plane of non-dual waking (*abheda-jāgrat-pada*) is not admitted for the plane of the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti-pada*).

Explaining the nature of the immersion of each successive external object into each successive internal reality, he demonstrates the division of objects for the subjects who are non-different from Śuddhavidyā and the others within the *śa*-group, beginning with the words "That which is external" (*yadbāhya*), etc.
This refers to the immersion of the successive external levels into the successive internal states. Of that which is the most external level...

The meaning is that the immersion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) into the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the immersion of the means of knowledge into the state of the knower (*pramātṛ*). That [immersion] occurs in the state of consciousness (*cit*) and in the state of the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And it occurs in the state of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and in the state of the pervasion of the object of thought (*caityavyāpti*); this is the reverse of the former. It is the immersion of the innermost interior into the outermost exterior.

The opposite is as follows: it means the immersion of the state of the knower (*pramātṛpada*) into the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇapada*), and the immersion of the state of the means of knowledge into the state of the object of knowledge (*prameyapada*). Here, regarding the fourfold group of knowers called Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti, [this occurs] in the common locus, the letter-group *śa*. "Consisting of the senses" (*akṣātman*) means having the singular nature of the light of the sense organs.

The meaning is that [the letter *śa*] has attained identity with the senses (*indriya*). "The object of knowledge" (*vedya*) refers to the entire collection of objects of cognition (*prameyajāta*). It should be understood that the letter *śa* corresponds to this; the meaning is that the letter *śa* occupies the place of the object of knowledge which has attained identity with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Although the letter *śa*—which consists in the abandonment of the contraction of the *ca*-group and the letter *ya*—occupies the place of the object of knowledge consisting of the mere [gross] elements such as sound, etc., [it is here identified with the subtle object].

Even so, it is appropriate that within the *cit* syllable— the *ahaṅkāra*— the letter *ca*, which appears externally as the conjunction of the *ca*-group and the letter *ya*, should also be understood as an indicator of all objects of knowledge (*prameya*), because the letters *ka* and *la* have merged therein. For that letter *śa*...

The subject of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*).
