It is here explained how the subject, whose essential nature is to be established through the three terms consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, attains its own nature within the letter *śa*, which denotes only the object of knowledge. Indeed, the entire group of *śa*-letters (*śavarga*) consists of four phonemes.

In the state of commonality (*sādhāraṇapada*), each of the four subjects beginning with Śuddhavidyā possesses its own specific nature (*svarūpa*). Nevertheless, for each of these four subjects beginning with Śuddhavidyā, there is only one corresponding phoneme each, beginning with the letter *śa*.

Their nature as individual phonemes is [attributed] metaphorically because they convey the specific distinction that serves as the cause for the establishment of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). For instance,

the state of being perceivable through identity with the sense organ of the subject of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*) is that specific distinction which constitutes the cause for the establishment of their essential nature.
Therefore, it has the nature of the letter *śa*, which signifies the identity with that which is to be known through the sense organs.

For the Lord, the cognizing subject, the specific distinction that serves as the cause for the establishment of his own nature is his status as the organ of action (*karmendriya*), characterized by the identity with the effects to be known as non-different from the body. Therefore, of him—
Such is the nature of the letter *ṣa*, which denotes the organs of action (*karmendriya*). This very point is stated [in the verse]:
"The Lord [is] the six sense-organs, which are non-different from the body" (Kārikā 1.2).
p.
107) For that Sadāśiva is the organ of knowledge; in the unity with the Self, his own Self consists of resting in the void—thus here is Śakti.
This fourth state, enriched with four limbs, possesses a similarity of form resting upon both the external and internal states. (3)
Now, he describes the nature of the subject as Sadāśiva-Śakti through two syllables,
beginning with "jñānendriyam" (the organ of knowledge). For the subject Sadāśiva,
there is the state of being the organ of knowledge (*jñānendriya*)— that which knows the object of knowledge— which has been made non-different from his own self and assimilated into his own being.

The specific [phoneme] is the cause for establishing its own nature; therefore, it possesses the form of the letter *sa*, which denotes such a faculty of cognition (*jñānendriya*). This is what is stated: when there is oneness with the Self—that is, when there is identity (*tādātmya*) with the Self—there is such a faculty of cognition. For that [letter] is indeed *sa*.
The letter *sa* signifies the one who brings forth such faculties of cognition; for its meaning is Sadāśiva.
"Consisting of rest in the void" means consisting of repose in the space (*ākāśa*) that is the nature of the equilibrium between the unlimited consciousness and non-consciousness.
"One's own self" refers to the essential nature characterized by both the body and the self. Regarding "ha": this is the phoneme *ha*, here within the *śa*-group.
Śakti is the subject named Śakti.

The specific characteristic that constitutes the proof of Śakti’s own nature is her essence, which consists in the state of equilibrium with the body characterized by repose in the undivided [Absolute]. Therefore, she possesses the form of the syllable *ha*, which expresses such a nature.

Thus, having explained the division of objects by resorting to the phonemes that convey the specific causes for the establishment of the respective natures of Śuddhavidyā and the others within the common locus of the *śa*-group,
[one should proceed] to the exterior of this word-form consisting of the *śa*-group.

He clarifies for the sake of a clear conviction the previously taught identity of form between the two— the internal [state] consisting of the contraction and abandonment of touch, and that which exists within the interior consisting of the contraction and abandonment [of the senses]— with the words beginning with "this" (etad).
[It refers to] the Great Earth, which contains the four great elements and is enriched by the four limbs.

Due to the immersion of the letter *ha* into the conscious state (*citpada*) by its very nature, this fourth state (*turyapada*) is enriched by the four limbs in both respects. This fourth state consists of the non-dual forms of waking and dreaming. Regarding the states of waking and dreaming as expressed by the final consonants (*sparśānta*) and the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) within the external and internal positions, there is a similarity in their assumed forms with respect to the *ca*-group.

When the contraction of the letter *ya* is abandoned, it becomes *śa*; when the contraction of the *ṭa*-group and the letter *ra* is abandoned, it becomes *ṣa*. In this manner, the remainder is to be inferred. || 3 ||
p.
108) And this very word is indeed the indivisible state of the fourfold reality beginning with Śuddhavidyā.
The wise should contemplate the descent into those various states through the process of the vibration of consciousness rising up from the altar and so forth. || 4 ||
It has been stated that for the letters of the *śava* group, *Śuddhavidyā*, and so forth, each individual vowel alone is the common *pada*.
This very point he expresses with the words "this," and so on. This *pada*, which consists of the *śava* group, is indeed undivided (*akhaṇḍita*), that is, entirely inseparable.

The "station" (*pada*) of the four principles beginning with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)— which possess the limbs of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*)— is difficult to establish by means of a single phoneme alone for the knowing subject (*pramātṛ*). Nevertheless, even so,
he provides a brief indication of the reasoning previously established regarding the metaphorical application of the usage of individual phonemes to Śuddhavidyā and the others.

"—from the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and so forth. When the vibration of consciousness (*citi-sphuraṇa*), which has arisen from the object of knowledge and so forth, reaches its culmination in the pervasion of the object (*caitya-vyāpti-avasāne*), and there begins the unfolding of that [consciousness], then this beginning occurs precisely within the object of knowledge and so forth; this is the proof provided by direct experience (*anubhava*). For instance, at the conclusion of the state of the bound soul (*pāśava-avasāne*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*)...

One whose vision of discernment has blossomed through the grace of the Guru immerses the object of knowledge (*vedya*) itself into the light of one’s own self and senses. Through such repeated practice of immersing the object of cognition (*prameya*) into the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), one subsequently ascends to the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
Striving to immerse the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which has made its object of cognition (*prameya*) its own, into the state of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*),

it first immerses the group of organs of action (*karmendriya-varga*), which is the means of knowledge that has made its effect-object (*kārya-prameya*) its own, into that portion of the cognizer consisting of the body. Thus, being the body of the universe, it [immerses them].

Having manifested the power of universal agency through its role as the creator of all things, and having ascended to the level of Īśvaratā (Lordship), it subsequently immerses the means of knowledge— the cognitive faculties whose objects of cognition have been assimilated into itself— into the knowing subject whose nature is the Self. Thus, it is the soul of the universe.

With the power of omniscience fully manifested, having ascended to the level of Sadāśiva, he unifies knowledge through the predominance of action and action through the predominance of knowledge; thereafter,
[he attains] the ground of the equilibrium of knowledge and action, which consists of unconditioned repose and is of the nature of Will (icchā).

"It ascends the activity of power" (*śaktikriyām ārohati*) means, according to the process (*prakriyā*), by way of the upward-shining vibration of consciousness (*cit-sphuraṇa*) starting from the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and so forth;

it refers to the descent into the respective states (*daśā*) such as Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and the rest, through the phonemes corresponding to each respective part, according to the stated rule. This should be contemplated by the wise (*vibudhaiḥ*, i.e., scholars). According to the stated rule, whatever [object] such as the knowable (*vedya*) and so forth [arises] within the flow of consciousness (*cit-pravahaṇe*)—
The meaning is that, with respect to their respective portions (*bhāga*), Śuddhavidyā and the others attain their own essential nature;
the sense is that the state of being a particular subject (*pramātṛpada*) for each respective veil, which consists of those various objective states (*bhāva*), is merely adventitious (*aupacārika*).
That Sadāśiva is indeed composed of the *bindu* and consists of the *tavarga*;
he is fit for the internal *dhāma* which constitutes the limb of Īśvara.
Knowledge and action do not belong to Suśiva, but to Sadāśiva and Īśa.
With their limbs and feet positioned in sequence, both internally and externally. || 5 ||

Now, although the letter *sa*—which represents the external sense organs (*jñānendriya*), consists of the contraction and abandonment of the *ta*-group, and belongs to the *Sadāśiva-kalā*—is present externally, it is inappropriate for it to hold primacy there; therefore, it is subordinate to *Īśvara*.
Conversely, the letter *ṣa*—which consists of the abandonment of the *ra* and *akṣara* (vowels) within the internal state and belongs to the *Īśvara-kalā*—is subordinate to *Sadāśiva*.

He explains [this] with the words "Sadāśiva," and so forth. "Consisting of the Bindu" means that its contraction has been abandoned. [This refers to] the *tavarga* (the dental class). That indeed is the letter *sa*.
This letter *sa* is of the nature of Sadāśiva; it is fit for the state of the internal abode (*antaradhāma*).

This form characterized by the letter *sa* is the nature of Sadāśiva, corresponding to the stage of knowledge regarding the characteristics of dreams. Therein, in the external plane—which is dominated by action—it is the limb of Īśvara; indeed, it is the very limb of Īśvara. In the plane of action, there is the subordination of the aspect of knowledge. He states the justification for this here: "Sadāśiva and Īśa."

The knowledge and action of Śiva. Now, one might object: "Let Sadāśiva be the manifestation of Śiva’s power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and Īśvara be the manifestation of his power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); what is the relevance of this to the present context? To this he says: "These two..."

Sadāśiva and Īśvara: respectively, they occupy the positions of the principal (aṅgin) within and without. For Sadāśiva, the position of the principal is fixed within the enclosure (kakṣyā), because his essential nature is knowledge; and since knowledge is predominant within the internal state, the external enclosure is the position of the auxiliary (aṅga). For Īśvara, the external enclosure is the position of the principal.

Because it is the very nature of action, and because action holds primacy in the external state (*bāhyapada*), its internal stage is the limb-state (*aṅgapada*). Therefore, the discrimination is this: since the letter *ṣa* consists of the contraction and abandonment of the letter *ra*, it is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the power of the Lord (*īśvarakalā*) therein. || 5 ||
The power *Ha* consists of the point (*bindu*) that transcends the proliferation of desire;
she is indeed the state of equality between knowledge and action, possessing a dual nature.
As the point (bindu) unfolds into the state of emanation, their progressive manifestation as a continuous flow of creation should be contemplated until its completion.
It has been stated that the *kalā* of Sadāśiva has internal predominance (*antah-prādhānya*), while the *kalā* of Īśvara has external predominance (*bahiḥ-prādhānya*).

Now, he demonstrates that the *kalā* of Śakti, which consists of will (*icchā-ātmikā*), possesses both external and internal predominance by virtue of being the root of both in a state of equilibrium:

"icchā" and so forth. "Pa-pañcaka" means consisting of the bindu (the nasal dot). This refers to the state of being a bindu belonging to the letter *va*, which is part of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) that consists of five letters. This designation is one where the quality (*guṇa*) is primary; the meaning is the abandonment of contraction. "Tanmayī" means having that as its essential nature. "Ha-śakti" is the state of power (*śakti-daśā*) expressed by the letter *ha*. "Icchā" means having the nature of will (*icchā-svabhāvā*). That [is she].
The power of will (*icchā-śakti*). The "common ground" (*samapada*) of knowledge and action is the root-ground (*mūlapada*) shared by both knowledge and action.
Since neither cognition nor action proceeds without will, will alone is the inner, immutable form (*kūṭastha-rūpa*) of both knowledge and action; for this very reason, it is of the nature of both.

The Self is the fundamental nature of both knowledge and action; therefore, the sense is that it possesses primacy alone—both internally in the sphere of knowledge and externally in the sphere of action—and not merely the status of a subordinate factor.

Now, when the unfolding of the *bindu* has commenced in the state of emission (*visarga*) according to the sequence beginning with *vidyā*, this unfolding of the *bindu* proceeds gradually; as long as it pervades the entire plane (*pada*),
because the scent of emission persists, there is indeed only a fusion of *bindu* and *visarga*.

He explains that the point (bindu) possesses sovereignty over the one: "In the point," and so forth. When the point gradually unfolds within the state of emanation (sarga-pada), until its completion—that is, up to the accomplishment of the pervasion of the point throughout all states—there occurs a fusion of those two, the point and the emission (visarga). In a state consisting of the threefold form (tripuṭī-rūpa), there is at times the unfolding of the point.
In some cases, there is a "vibration of emission" (*visargasphurattā*), which constitutes a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (fusion); this is to be contemplated and inferred. The meaning is as follows:

for the subject of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*), the emergence of consciousness (*cid-unmeṣa*) occurs precisely within the objective portion (*vedyāṃśa*) through the immersion of objects into the light of the senses, [and thus] the senses reside in the state of the subject (*pramātṛ-pada*).

Due to the absence of proficiency gained through the practice of immersion, there is no subsiding of the distinction between the senses and the subsequent stages; thus, the vibration of the *visarga* constitutes the union of the *bindu* and the *visarga*.
In the state of Īśvara, because *śuddhavidyā* follows as the subsequent stage, the emergence of consciousness (*cid-unmeṣa*) toward objects of knowledge is indeed established.
The distinction, however, is this: the submergence of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), whose respective objects have been assimilated by it, into the state of the subject consisting of the body;

and the submergence of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), whose respective objects have been assimilated by it, into that portion of the state of the subject which consists of the Self. It is precisely through their predominance [in the former case] that there is a lack of proficiency, which constitutes their non-predominance [in the latter].
Therefore, since there is a manifestation of differentiation when that [consciousness] and others constitute the subsequent term, the union with the *visarga*—

the unfolding of non-difference from consciousness extending from the state of Sadāśiva up to the state of Īśvara— is indeed established. The distinction, however, lies in the fact that the instruments of knowledge, whose objects of cognition have been assimilated into one's own self, are permeated by the universe.

Immersion in the state of one's own self as the subject (*svātmapramātṛpada*) means becoming one with the principle of the power of will (*icchāśaktitattva*), which consists of resting in undisturbed consciousness even within that state; this is called "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*) because, due to the lingering scent of duality in that portion, there is still the touch of emission (*visarga*). However, in the state of power (*śaktidaśā*)...
The intended meaning is that because it is of the nature of rest (*viśrama*), the empire of non-duality prevails precisely within that which is undivided.

Regarding that [state], at the level of the unfolding of the *bindu* (*bindūnmeṣapada*), the discernment of the gradations in the persistence of emission (*visarga*) is the cause for the clear knowledge of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *śuddhavidyā*; thus, there is an injunction for its performance.
In the preceding group, the subsequent [consonant] is certainly not fixed; in the subsequent group, however, the preceding one is indeed fixed, as in the set beginning with *śa* and *ṣa*.
Or rather, even when consciousness arises in one place, its manifestation occurs elsewhere; thus, this [distinction] is for me exactly like a single drop.

In the groups beginning with Śuddhavidyā, the internal sub-periods (*antarantardaśā*) are not contained within the external periods (*bahirbahirdaśā*); however, in the internal sub-periods, the external periods are contained. He explains this with the words "in the preceding [passage]" (*pūrvatra*), and so forth. "In the group beginning with *śa* and *ṣa*" refers to the group beginning with Śuddhavidyā, which is expressed by the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, and so on. "In the preceding" [refers to the aforementioned context].
"In the prior state" refers to the stage of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and so forth; "the supreme" refers to the supreme stage. Indeed, it is not fixed; that is, it is not restricted.
The meaning is that in the stage of Pure Knowledge, the stage of Īśvara is not fixed; in the stage of Īśvara, the stage of Sadāśiva is not fixed;
and likewise, in the stage of Sadāśiva, the stage of Śakti is not fixed. "But in the other," however, means in the stages of Īśvara and so forth.

The former [state]—the stage of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) and so forth—is necessarily present; it must indeed exist by necessity. The application is as follows: the stage of Pure Knowledge is inherently included within the stage of Īśvara; the stage of Īśvara is included within the stage of Sadāśiva;
and the stage of Sadāśiva is included within the stage of Śakti.

Now, he introduces another position: that when consciousness arises through the process of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the entire multitude of categories beginning with the object—which establish the object and so forth—is simultaneously contracted and abandoned through the unimpeded expansion of the rays of consciousness. This is stated in the verse beginning with "ekatra. "Ekatra" (in one place).

In the objective portion (*vedyabhāga*), when consciousness (*saṃvit*) arises; and "elsewhere" as well, in every instance such as the categories of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—[it is said] "the manifestation (*bhāsa*) of that consciousness. [The ellipsis is:

"manifestations flow forth. This group beginning with *śa* and *ṣa* refers to the four letters starting with *śa* and *ṣa*; or else, according to another interpretation, "simultaneously" (*samam eva*), meaning at one and the same time, [is] the *bindu*.
By the word *bindu*, the state of having abandoned contraction (*saṅkoca*) is indicated; the ellipsis is "one becomes one who has abandoned contraction.

This is the meaning: at the emergence of the *bindu* following the introduction of the stage of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the sequence of the stages beginning with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is not fixed in terms of its dependence on temporal delay. In some cases, for a subject possessing superior fortune, due to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)...
Due to its intensity, the manifestation of the ten stages beginning with Śuddhavidyā occurs simultaneously in an instant without delay;
however, in some cases, it occurs gradually depending on the sequence—these two positions should be considered here. || 7 ||
p.
113) Here, the many [deities] of the waking Śiva, who possesses the awakening of bound souls (paśu), are situated within the intermediate ten-spoked [mandala] at the corners.
This [reality], though manifesting through the emergence of differentiation, attains integration within the limit of non-duality; such is the secret of every stage. 8.

Now, having raised the doubt as to how it is appropriate for the Lord— who presides over the four letters beginning with *śa*— to be situated within the "wheel of the waking state of bound souls" (*paśujāgaracakra*), which consists of a pair of ten-spoked wheels and contains a great many letter-arrangements, he establishes that point.

"Jāgrad" and so forth. Of Śiva: "jāgrad" means the waking state. "Yoginī" is one joined with the waking state of the bound soul (*paśu*), meaning she is closely connected to it. For that reason, [she occupies] the ten-spoked [wheel], which pervades the locus where the ten sense organs are situated; it is "aiśa," presided over by Īśvara.

In the state of the ten-spoked wheel presided over by Īśvara, that multiplicity which resides in the corners— manifested through the emergence of differentiation and fully expanded by the unfolding of duality— attains a synthesis within the pinnacle of non-duality; that is, upon the manifestation of the side of non-duality, it reaches the abandonment of multiplicity appropriate to the state of non-duality.

The secret of the word (*pratipadrahasya*) is the secret of knowledge (*jñānarahasya*). This is the meaning: in the field where all differentiation unfolds during the pervasion of emission (*visarga*), there is a five-limbed word consisting of twenty-four syllables, divided into five groups, within the square of the pair of ten-spoked [circles].

Established within the four pentads of corners: when the awakening of the bound soul (*paśu*) and the awakening of Śiva coincide, and the dissolution of duality occurs, the square-foot consisting of the four letters beginning with *pa* transforms into the letter *ha*.
Furthermore, the *ka*-group situated within the five corners of the outer ten-spoked wheel is also absorbed into the letter *ha*.

The *ca*-group located in the remaining five corners transforms into the letter *śa*. In the inner ten-spoked wheel (*antardaśāra*), the *ṭa*-group located in the five corners transforms into the letter *ṣa*.
The *ta*-group located in the remaining five corners transforms into the letter *sa*. The letter *ma*...
One perceives a connection with the labial class (*pavarga*) as it transforms into the form of the letter *ha*;
and within the sphere of the subject (*pramātṛkakṣyā*), one perceives a connection with the triangle (*trikoṇabimba*) which will be described later.
Regarding the stage of the emission (*visargapada*), the process of the manifestation of the point (*bindu*) consists of three wheels (*cakratraya*) in the form of a square and a pair of decagons.

It transforms into the shape of a four-cornered figure. Those who believe that at the stages of the *visarga* and the *bindu*, the phonemes and the corners must be identical in form, they fail to perceive the distinction between the states of difference and non-difference; enough said. || 8 ||
That which arises even in the earthly realm is indeed Śuddhavidyā;
that which arises in the natural realm is, moreover, said to be Īśvaratā within the Egg.
That which is illusory is indeed the state of Sadāśiva;
this realization of the threefold nature is the deepest secret of the gurus regarding Śiva.

Now, by resorting to another position, he postulates that for Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— who have immersed the phenomenal world within their own sensory bodies— the objects extending from the earth (bhū) up to Prakṛti and Māyā are made of pure consciousness (cinmayīkṛta).

"O Earthly One," and so forth. Within the earthly egg (*pārthivāṇḍa*), which consists of the objects of the external senses, there is the arising of consciousness (*cidudaya*), that is, the pervasion by consciousness (*cidvyāpti*).
For that indeed is the arising of the *bindu*, which is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
This is because within Pure Knowledge, the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is rendered uniform in form through the illuminations of the senses.

In the earthly egg (*pārthivāṇḍa*), the labial class (*pavarga*) corresponds to the subject (*pramātṛ*); it is indeed possessed of relation because of its constant necessity for that relation within the triad [of knower, known, and knowledge]. Therefore, when the limitation is abandoned, there is the possibility of the entire *śavarga*, which consists of the four classes of sounds, within the earthly egg. And thus, in this view:

Since Śuddhavidyā is the stage that initiates the pacification of duality for the subject, it is only when there is a multiplicity of triangles that the arrangement [of the phonemes] is possible; thus, the vowels and consonants (visargasparśāḥ), in the state of transforming into the form of the *śa*-group,
perceive the manifestation of the head of duality within the subject— this is according to the primary sense.

The union of the waking state of Śiva with the waking state of the bound soul (paśu) belongs to Īśvara alone; however, for those whose discrimination is not yet matured, this union with Śuddhavidyā occurs only occasionally as a concession. Enough of this discussion. That which is the emergence of consciousness within the material egg (prakṛtāṇḍa) takes the form of the letters beginning with 'Śa'.
The abandonment of contraction is indeed sovereignty (*īśvaratā*). This is because, in this context, the logical justification is accessible through mere intuition (*pratibhāsa-mātra*).

The word "indeed" (*kila*) refers to traditional lore (*aitihya*). Here, the abandonment of the contraction of the labial *pa*-group into the form of the guttural *śa*-group is to be inferred as follows: the abandonment of the contraction of the letter *ma*, which is a labial, results in the guttural letter [ś].

The term *hakāra* is easy to understand. The letter *ha*, which is the primordial (*prakṛti*) letter, is included within the *citpada*. Now, the reasoning for the three letters beginning with *pha*—namely *pha*, *ba*, and *bha*—becoming the three letters beginning with *śa* is stated: *pha*, *ba*, and *bha* correspond to water, fire, and air, and *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* are likewise [associated with these elements]. Therefore...
The nature of the letters beginning with *śa* as the abandonment of contraction starting from *pha* is due to their conveying the same underlying reality (*tattva*).

Thus, the letters beginning with *śa* convey water and the other elements. In the contemplation (*vimarśa*) on the absence of the aforementioned inversion of the elements, the form of the letters beginning with *pha* is clearly stated: the first letter of each group (*varga*) possesses little breath (*alpaprāṇa*).

Earth has a limited function compared to the other elements; therefore, the second letter of the consonant class, which possesses great breath (*mahāprāṇa*), represents it. Water has a greater function than earth; therefore, the third letter of the consonant class, which possesses resonance (*nāda*), represents it. Resonance has a more extensive function than great breath.

Fire has a function that exceeds that of water; therefore, it is the signifier of that [water]. That which possesses resonance (*nāda*) and possesses sound (*ghoṣa*), namely the fourth letter of each consonant class, arises solely from resonance (*nāda*);

[the letter] possessing resonance and possessing sound has a function that exceeds [that of fire], and wind (*vāyu*) has a function that exceeds that of fire; therefore, it is the signifier of that [fire].
The fifth [element], liberation (*apavarga*), has the nature of being a combination of all the aforementioned properties;

therefore, space (*ākāśa*) has a function exceeding that of the four [elements] beginning with earth. Consequently, the fifth phoneme represents space. Thus, by virtue of representing the reality (*tattva*) signified by the letter *pha* and so forth...

And because they consist of the abandonment of contraction (*saṅkoca*), it is understood that the letters beginning with *śa* are of the nature of the transformation into [the letters] beginning with *pha*.

Since the Lord (*īśvara*) is characterized by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) which consists of the universe, the intention is that the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) of primordial matter, when its contraction has been abandoned, is fit for the state of the Lord. As for the emergence of consciousness within that illusory (*māyika*) egg, it is as follows:

The state of Sadāśiva. Because the Egg of Māyā, which is like a dream, is the locus of the self-luminous nature [of consciousness], the Egg of Māyā—characterized by being the Self of the universe and having abandoned all contraction—is the station of Sadāśiva. Regarding the four letters beginning with *śa*, such as *śa* and so forth: the cognition of their threefold form exists within the Egg of Earth and the Egg of Prakṛti.

And within the egg of Māyā, when the threefold nature of the Siddha has attained oneness, that cognition which is the discernment of the threefold distinctions created by their respective positions— that cognition is here, in this discussion of the discernment of the ten states beginning with Śuddhavidyā, the most secret of secrets among the Gurus. || 9 ||
At the arising of the *bindu*, this creation enters [it]; likewise,
at the arising of creation, that [creation] enters it, and he too [enters] within that state.
What would there be? A *ha*-consonant with a *la* in its heart and a *va*-consonant within it;
externally, however, consciousness (*cit*) is divided at the beginning of the creation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (10)

Now, regarding the *śa*-group (*śavarga*), since the letter *la*—which represents the body and consists of the nature of contraction (*saṅkoca*) and abandonment—is not seen [in that group], he explains the logical possibility of its appearance with the words "at the arising of the *bindu*" (*bindūdaye*), and so forth.
"At the arising of the *bindu*" means at the pervasion of the *bindu*. "This *bindu*" refers to this very [point].

First, this emission (visarga) enters the pervader; the meaning is that it becomes one with the Bindu. Previously, the emission—the creator of the universe—issued outward from within the Bindu itself; now, it again enters that very same [Bindu].
Likewise, at the arising of the creation and during the pervasion by the emission, [it enters] that emission. Then, immediately thereafter, even that Bindu [enters the emission].
The meaning is "it enters. For that reason, within the *pada*, in the place of the pervasion of the *bindu*, what happens?

The letter *ka*, which represents the earth and has its interior occupied by the four letters beginning with *pha*—which represent the four elements starting with water—should reside in the heart of the letter *ha*. The meaning is that it becomes situated therein.

Because even the *svapna* (dream) state is an internal stage; therein, he describes the persistence of the letter *la*, which is the subject (*pramātṛ*) of emission (*visarga*), within the womb [of the letter *ha*].

The meaning is that within the *śa*-group—which consists of the relinquishing of internal contraction—and specifically within the interior of the letter *ha*, the disappearance of the letter *la* occurs. When emission enters into the point (*bindu*), it attains a state of being of one essence with it.
He states the distinction regarding the immersion of the *bindu* into the *visarga* with the words "But externally" (*bāhye tu*). "Externally" means in the place where the *visarga* pervades.

"But" (*tu*) [indicates the contrast]. The *cidbindu* (consciousness-bindu), even while standing face-to-face at the "mouth of the *prakṛti*-emission"—that is, at the opening of the *visarga* which takes the form of *prakṛti*—is "divided"; it does not merge into *prakṛti*, but rather appears in a divided form.

Indeed, the letter *ma* does not disappear through that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which takes the form of the letter *pa*, nor does it suffer a loss of its own essential nature due to becoming one with it— since it is indicated as being situated in close proximity to her, there is no liberation from her. Just as the form of the earth, once emitted outward by the point (*bindu*) of emission, is not made into a single essence with that point.
Because the form of the *pa*-group is seen within the *bindu*, the intention is that when there is the pervasion of the *visarga*, there is no loss of the essential nature of the *bindu*.
The word "antaḥ" (within) occurs; because of the unity of the four factors, there is also a cultivated unity between consciousness (*cit*) and the *caitya* at the limit of the instrument.
The external state consists of five limbs when [the power] has emerged from the cavity containing the fire of consciousness within Prakṛti.

Now, although it was previously stated that the internal word ending with the dissolution of the *visarga* into the *bindu* possesses four limbs, while the external word, through the non-dissolution of the *visarga* and *bindu*, possesses five limbs, he brings this object of knowledge (*prameya*) forth once again for the sake of clear comprehension:

Regarding the passage beginning with *antarityādi*: for that reason—namely, because of the cause which is the form of the dissolution of the *visarga* into the *bindu*—the internal state (*antaḥ-pada*) becomes four-limbed (*caturaṅga*). Why? He says: because of the identity of consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*caitya*), and because of the possibility of the power of consciousness to bring about the state of being of a single flavor with the object. Of what nature is this internal state?

Even at the limit of the instruments (*karaṇa*), there occurs a unity for the subject of emission (*visarga-pramātṛ*) through the indication of the all-pervasive state by means of immersion into consciousness (*cin-majjana*).

Thus, even within the three instrumental positions appearing externally, there is realized a unity of consciousness. This is because, through the immersion of the letter *ha* into the *ka*-group—which represents the state of emission—the [three] instruments are indicated as being situated therein.

The meaning is that one should contemplate that the letters *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *ha*— which consist of the contraction and abandonment of the *ca*-group, *ṭa*-group, and *ta*-group— merely dissolve into the letter *ha*. The discernment of the essential nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and the other categories, which occurs through their outward manifestation, takes place only when they have dissolved into *ha*.

It should be understood as follows: consequently, because the syllable *cit*—which is of an undifferentiated nature and possesses a single limb—is not perceived due to the immersion (*nimajjana*) of the letter *ha*, the true nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is not recognized; therefore, it should be understood that for the sake of recognizing that [nature], those very letters which are contained within *ha* must manifest externally. Now, regarding the vibration (*spanda*) of the emission (*visarga*).

When [the power] has emerged from the cavity containing the fire of consciousness (*cidvahnigarbhakuhara*) into *prakṛti*, it must be understood that this occurs "together with the three instruments. Thus, the external state consists of five limbs. This means that because the nature of the *caitya* cannot be established without the word *cit*, it is together with that undiminished word *cit*. || 11 ||
It is the repose within the non-dual will consisting of the syllable *Ha*, which is oriented toward knowledge and action; its nature is the resting both inwardly and outwardly.
This Śiva, whose body consists of the peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara), is indeed the repose of deep sleep, though it still bears a slight trace of the impurity of conceptualization.

Now, having analyzed the nature of the letter *ha*, which is of the form of *śakti*, and having generated [the state of non-duality], he makes known the nature of the *śivatattva*— which is expressed by the *kūṭākṣara* consisting of the letters *la* and *kṣa* that follow this— as follows, beginning with "jñāna": "Resting in the non-dual will, which consists of the letter *ha* oriented toward knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)."
It is directed toward the objects of knowledge and action, which consist of Sadāśiva and Īśvara;
the meaning is that it presides over them. "Consisting of the letter *ha*" refers to the non-dual will (*icchā*); it is the will for non-difference from the nature of the letter *ha*.
Since it is expressed by the letter *ha*, it has entered into the will for non-difference because its nature is that of the letter *ha*.
That very [power] is repose (*viśrānti*), because it consists in the repose of will. This is the meaning:

she is the presiding deity over the instruments of knowledge and action belonging to Sadāśiva and Īśvara, whose nature consists of unlimited knowledge and action; [she is so called] by virtue of being the immovable substratum (*kūṭasthatva*) of knowledge and action.
As the presiding principle over that [will], it is the object of the designation "will," since the very nature of will is defined as the immutability of knowledge and action; thus,
it is proclaimed by the followers of the Āgamas as the *śakti-tattva*, whose nature is will itself, and which is described as having a form untouched by duality.

It is the great rest (*mahāviśrānti*). That very state is the rest whose nature is non-extroversion within the word, not facing toward the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and consisting of the form of rest. It is devoid even of the slightest scent of the category of conceptual thought (*savikalpa*). It is indeed the rest of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), joined with the conceptualization that consists solely of the experience of one's own true nature; it is deep sleep itself, whose body is the nature of the immutable syllable (*kūṭākṣara*).
His own essential nature consists of the *kūṭākṣara* (syllabic seed-mantra) formed by the unification of the letters *la*, *kṣa*, and *ka*. The meaning is that he is that which is expressed by it.

This [Śiva] is the object of immediate perception; he is Śiva, the Śiva-principle. The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the verb. This occurs even while awake, either through the power of fortune consisting in the means such as the *soma* sacrifice, or by its own inherent impulse.
The distinction is this: if that certain repose in deep sleep is inward-turned, it becomes the Śiva-tattva; if it is outward-turned, it becomes the Śakti-tattva. || 12 ||
In this world, one who has awakened from the sleep of doubt regarding "is" or "is not" perceives the universe here as non-different in form from Śiva.
Thus, consisting of knowledge and action, it is distinct from its corresponding forms;
in this way, it is fourfold, being merely the seed that has been infused. || 13 ||

Now, just as Śakti— expressible through the *svara* (vowel) and whose nature is repose in the internalized states of waking and deep sleep— is the cause of the universe, it is fitting that Śiva, whose nature is repose in the inert state of deep sleep, exists as the seed of the reality of the universe; thus,
his abiding is elucidated by being contemplated in the form of the *kūṭākṣara* (the seed-syllable).

"‘It does not exist,’ and so forth. ‘Awakened by the doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist’ means that while one is awake, there arises the doubt, ‘Does it exist or does it not exist? Here, in this state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is characterized by such a scope of doubt, [the state] is indicated; thus the meaning is ‘in deep sleep. In Śiva, whose nature is such deep sleep—in Śiva who is of the nature of non-duality—[it is] ‘also,’ and thus ‘even’."

Thus, the fourfold world, having come together as a differentiated whole, remains supported by mere seed, and is itself supported by mere seed; this is the remainder [of the sense]. This is the meaning: in the internal state, which has the form of a dream, it consists of the cognition of difference; in the external state, which has the form of waking, it consists of the activity of difference; and likewise [in the other states].

In brief, the world is fourfold: it consists of the form of non-dual knowledge within the state of dream, and the form of dualistic activity without in the state of waking. It has been explained that this very [world] exists as a mere seed in the form of the *kūṭākṣara* (the peak syllable) within the Śiva-principle. || 13 ||
They know that gnosis consists of both duality and non-duality, having the form of the letter *la*;
and likewise, they know that action consists of the letter *kṣa*.
The peak is joined, with two excellent points flashing forth in front, its form reaching into one another, equal, and compact.

Now, he explains how the fourfold seed-syllables of the world are combined with the *sparśa*-consonant clusters beginning with *ka* within the four phonemes consisting of *la*, *sa*, *ka*, and *ṣa*— beginning with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth. Knowledge, which consists of both duality and non-duality— that is, whose nature is both difference and non-difference— is of the form of the letters *la* and *sa*.
Within the *bheda-jñāna-pada* (the word for differentiated knowledge), among the labial consonants (*varga*), there is the letter *la* which expresses the *prakṛti* (nature);
since that very letter is the presiding deity of the *tat-pada*, and because the *tat-pada* is the word for knowledge, it possesses the status of the knower of knowledge.
However, for the letter *la* which expresses the *manas* (mind), the status of being a knower is not established due to the defect of the conceit of being pervaded by that [knowledge].

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the letter *va*, which is the root-form of that [object], nor the letter *ya*, which stands for the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), possess the status of a knower (*jñātṛ*). Since the entire class of objects of knowledge, such as smell and so forth, is everywhere a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of earth and the other elements,
there can be no suspicion of an agent of action (*kriyā-pramātṛ*) within the position of the letter *la*, which represents the earth in its primordial form (*prakṛti-ākāra*).

It is appropriate; therefore, the status of the letter *la* as the knower (*jñātṛtva*) is certain. In the word-group of the *śa*-class, the state of non-dual knowledge belonging to the letter *sa*, whose nature is Sadāśiva, is beyond dispute. Such [knowledge] consists of both duality and non-duality. And [the letter] *ka* has the form of *ka-ṣa*, that is, the form of *ka* and *ṣa*. In the stage of the process of differentiation, within the place of the contact consonants (*sparśasthala*), there is the *ṭa*-class.
Due to the defect of the conceit that the *ka*-group is pervaded [by the Self], there is no agency [belonging to it].

Rather, in the context of non-dual action (*abhedakriyā*), agency clearly belongs to the letter *śa*—which is the letter *k* presiding over the *ka*-group—and to the letter *ṣa*, which is the nature of Īśvara, within the *ṭa*-group. This tetrad is thus conjoined through the knowledge of non-duality.

The letter *sa* is the knowledge of non-duality (*abhedajñāna*) through the letter *la*. Through the activity of differentiation (*bhedakriyā*), the activity of non-differentiation is the letter *ṣa*, because of the nature of the mutual interpenetration of difference and non-difference. And in this interpenetration, the meaning is that it occurs by the power of the valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the two poles of existence that flash forth before one. This refers to the two pairs of letters that are thus interpenetrated.
To the question, "What is the form when the two extremes of existence appear before one? he says: "The form *la*.
When the letter *la*, which consists of the fusion of the letters *la* and *sa*, appears before [the other], the phoneme would be *la*.
This means that in consciousness, knowledge becomes of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). [This occurs] when the letter *sa* [is transformed] into the letter *la*.
Due to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), the letter *la*—whose nature is elevated by its conjunction with the letter *sa*—is heard as *la*.

When there is a fusion of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*, if the letter *ka*, which possesses a dual form, were to manifest before [the *ṣa*] in the action, the action would not attain equilibrium; thus it would become the letter *kṣa*. This *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) is mutually interpenetrated according to the sequence.

They are mutually pervaded. First, the letter *sa* is pervaded by the letter *la*; this configuration is the seed of the differentiated world (*bhedasaṃsāra*). Next, the letter *la* is [pervaded] by the letter *sa*;
this configuration is the seed of the non-differentiated world (*abhedasaṃsāra*). And in the section on action (*kriyāpada*), first—
By the letter *ka*, the letter *ṣa* is pervaded; immediately thereafter, by the letter *ṣa*, the letter *ka* is pervaded.
This state of being the seed of both difference and non-difference is produced by their structural arrangement, as previously described.
Furthermore, because of its equal pervasion in the middle position, it is "motionless" (*niṣpanda*); it is the seed through the mutual blending of both difference and non-difference.

The process of the formation of the *kūṭa* (peak-syllable), which is perceived through its configuration that serves as the seed of differentiated transmigratory existence, should be investigated from the mouth of the Guru by those possessing the intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) transmitted through the lineage.
The *kūṭa*, which is a mass of the Śiva-principle, consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara*), because the Śiva-principle that is manifested is one.

It should be understood that, just as there is no loss of the nature of ultimate rest for the universal class (*jāti*) manifested by the possession of a dewlap and so forth, so too there is no loss of the nature of ultimate rest for the Śiva-principle manifested by the gross form and the peak-syllable (*kūṭākṣara*). || 14 ||

(122) Paśu and Śiva, consisting of the syllables *m* and the *kūṭa*, are the limits of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, corresponding respectively to the qualities (*guṇa*), the corners (*koṇa*), and the point (*bindu*) in the [mandala].

Indeed, the two *sarga-bindu* [visarga] signs are situated within the belly of the rays, which arise from the lineage of the four squares beginning with *o* and *va*, and which possess the ears of the serpent. 15.

Now, he explains the arrangement of the locus of the subject—which consists of ten syllables beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa*—within the circles of the eight-spoked wheel, the triangle, and the point, starting with the words "consisting of knowledge" (*jñānātma*).
[The verse begins: "Consisting of knowledge," etc. [This refers to] the waking state consisting of knowledge, which is the limit between waking and deep sleep.
And they are the limits of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). They exist as the two locations; the meaning is that they abide in the positions of the limits.

Dream (*svapna*)—which is the awakening of knowledge (*jñānajāgara*) to be explained as being situated within—is active at its limit, at the end of the letter *ya*, because of the first stage’s orientation toward the waking state.

Because it proceeds [in this manner], beginning with the letter *va* and culminating in the letter *ya*, the letter *ma*—due to its position immediately following that—constitutes the state of the dream-limit, which is the deep sleep of consciousness (*jñāna-suṣupti*).
This consists of two stages: the non-differentiated waking and dreaming states as expressed by the group of letters beginning with *śa*.

At the limit of that [state], in the portion following the letter *ha*, is the letter *kṣa*. Since the deep sleep of knowledge (*jñānasuṣupti*), which is of the nature of cessation (*nivṛtti*), proceeds toward the state of [ordinary] sleep, it begins with the letter *śa* and reaches completion in *ha*;
because the letter *kṣa* follows immediately after that, it constitutes the locus of the limit of the deep sleep of knowledge.

Thus, the bound soul (paśu) and Śiva are characterized by the waking state of knowledge and the state of deep sleep of knowledge respectively, and consist of the phoneme-cluster *m* (makārakūṭa), having the nature of the syllable *m*. They are joined within the qualities (*guṇa*), the angles (*koṇa*), and the point (*bindu*)—that is, within the triangle and the circle of the point. This is because the point is within the triangle, and the triangle is within the point.

Because the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva possess the nature of mutual pervasion, there is a union (*śleṣa*). Since difference consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), the individual soul—the subject of cognition characterized by difference—is triangular in form. Non-difference, however, is of a single nature; thus, Śiva—the subject of non-dual cognition—is, by way of being characterized by freedom from qualities, of the nature of a dot (*bindu*) without corners.
An objection may be raised: "Is it not the case that the state of being a subject of dualistic perception belongs to *prakṛti* alone—that is, to the earth itself?

For it was previously established therein that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*) within the context of duality. How then can the state of being a subject of dualistic perception be attributed here to the soul, and how is it that the ascent to the throne of non-duality is also spoken of right here? To this, it is replied:

Since the nature of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is characterized by the capacity for synthetic unification (*anusandhātṛtva*), it is established as primarily residing in the locus of consciousness (*citpadam*) alone. Its application to the locus of the object of cognition (*caityapadam*) is a figurative usage based on pervasion.

Thus, the distinction is that at the time of the fruit, the state of being a knower of the object resides only in the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas in the context of conventional discourse, it belongs to the object of cognition itself.

Therefore, from the triangle and the bindu, Jīva and Śiva are conjoined. The letters beginning with *va* and those beginning with *śa*—which reside within the rays of the eight-cornered [figure] arising from the connection of the two sets of four squares starting with *vaśā*—are the letters beginning with *va* and *śa*. By "the two sets of four squares starting with *vaśā*" is meant the pair of quadrangles beginning with *vaśā*.
The first square consists of four letters beginning with *va* and ending with *ya*;
the other square consists of four letters beginning with *śa* and ending with *ha*. The connection (*anvaya*) between these two squares is the *śleṣa* (punning conjunction);
that which arises or is produced from this is the eight-cornered *nāgāśrama* (the serpent’s hermitage), which itself constitutes the rays.
The wheel of rays (*raśmicakra*): the square wheel of rays produced from the letters beginning with *śa* belonging to Śiva, whose essence is the letter *kṣa*;

and the square wheel of rays produced from the letters beginning with *va* belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*), whose essence is the letter *ma*. Within these two wheels, situated in the center as their presiding deities, are the *sarga* (visarga) and the *bindu*.

Indeed! They are of the nature of the *visarga* and the *bindu*. Indeed! The distinction is that the individual soul (*jīva*), whose essence is the triangle, has the nature of the *visarga*, while Śiva, whose essence is the *bindu*-wheel, has the nature of the *bindu*. || 15 ||
(124) The two bindus and the emission (sarga), which reside between the deep sleep and the awakening consisting of knowledge and action, are capable and contain both wings.
The two pervaders, which constitute the limbs of those two, are associated with the states of waking and deep sleep respectively. || 16 ||

Now, he explains the appropriateness of the placement of the letters *kṣa* and *ma*—representing Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*)—respectively in the intermediate state between the sleep of knowledge and action, and in the intermediate state between the waking states of knowledge and action, starting with the words "knowledge and action" (*jñānakriyā*).
They are situated in the middle between the sleep and awakening whose nature consists of knowledge and action; [the letter *ma*] is of the nature of knowledge.

The non-dual state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) consists of waking and dreaming; it is denoted by the sibilants (*ś-va-ra-ga*) and is of the nature of action (*kriyātmikā*). The dual state of deep sleep is denoted by the portion of the *bindu* among the vowels. Between these two states of deep sleep lies the abode of Śiva, whose essence is the letter *kṣa*;
this is the awakening consisting of knowledge (*jñānātmaka*), the waking state denoted by the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), which is the dual state of dreaming (*bhedasvapna*).

Awakening consists of action and is to be understood through touch; this is the state of waking. In the interval between these two lies the placement of the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is the letter *M*. The differentiation of knowledge is also an indicator of non-dual deep sleep (*abhedasuṣupti*). When, in the middle of the interior of that non-dual deep sleep—which constitutes the latter limit of the prior limit consisting of non-dual waking and dreaming—[the soul is situated].

It should be understood that the placement of Śiva consists of the prior limit— which is characterized by non-differentiation, deep sleep, and the awakening of knowledge— while the placement of the individual soul (jīva) occurs within the intermediate space between that prior limit and the subsequent limit, which is of the nature of the awakening of activity.
Thus, Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) consist respectively of the phonemes *kṣa* and *ma*, whose positions and configurations have been described in this way.
The bindu and visarga, situated on both wings, reside upon the two wings characterized by knowledge and action and by deep sleep; they pervade them and are the presiding deities of both.
The letter *kṣa* is the *vaindava*.

The letter *m*, which is the emission (*visarga*), is its presiding deity; it pervades both wings characterized by the waking state of knowledge accompanied by differentiated deep sleep and the waking state of pure action. Thus...

They pervade both wings consisting of deep sleep and both wings consisting of waking accompanied by the deep sleep of the *bindu*. For this very reason, they constitute its limbs (*aṅgin*). This is indicated by their presiding over the two kinds of deep sleep—namely, that of the nature of cessation (*nivṛtti*) and that of the nature of activity (*pravṛtti*) accompanied by the differentiated deep sleep—as well as the two kinds of waking.

Through their central arrangement, waking and dreaming—which are the primary forms of cessation and engagement—are non-different from the state of deep sleep; in the state of "conjunction" (*samavāya*), there is a conjunction or mixture of waking and deep sleep. Indeed, this conjunction belongs to the entire pair of waking and deep sleep, characterized by the internal and the sibilants (*uṣman*), and not to them individually.
In the case of the *antaḥstha* (semivowels), there is a conjunction of waking and deep sleep, because their object is slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*).

In the case of the *ūṣman* (sibilants), there is likewise a conjunction of waking and deep sleep, because through their connection with that [contact], their object is slight openness (*īṣadvivṛtatā*).
Therefore, the ten vowels, which constitute the pervasive class, are the pervaders of both the states of the vowels (*svara*) and the consonants (*sparśa*).

For this very reason, it bears the designation "the class of the pervaders. In that regard, the placement of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva)—who pervade both sides within the middle term and are appropriate for the middle term—is established with logical justification; such is the discernment. || 16 ||
She is Tripureśvarī, whose abode is in the center of the Śrīcakra, whose two meanings reside in the ultimate state where contraction and expansion meet.
The state of emission is threefold, while the state of the bindu is the singlefold fourth; thus she is endowed with four arms. 17.

Now, the essential nature of Tripureśvarī— who resides in the central wheel (*madhyacakra*) as the presiding deity of all wheels— is precisely the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the vowels *a* and *kṣa*, which consist of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva, and which pervade the ten-spoked, double [ten-spoked], and fourteen-spoked wheels that are the essence of the eight-spoked wheel.
He explains [this] with the words "contraction" (*saṅkoca*) and so forth: "having both meanings as its ultimate limit, consisting of contraction and expansion.
This refers to that which has as its ultimate limit (*parasīma*) both the state of contraction (*saṅkocabhāva*) and the state of expansion (*pūrṇabhāva*).
The supreme abode consists of the pair of spokes representing the waking state and the form of fourteen spokes representing the state of deep sleep; it is the center of both halves of those two.
It is the central dwelling of the Śrīcakra, which is composed of the three cities characterized by the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*).
She whose abode— that is, her place of residence— is the city of the subject (*pramātṛpura*), which consists of dreams and has the form of an eight-spoked wheel,
is Tripureśvarī. By this [it is shown that] because the letters *ma* and *kṣa* preside over the eight-spoked wheel, Tripureśvarī is indeed the state of equilibrium between both.
Thus he was awakened to the true nature [of reality].

Now, regarding the fourfold state of Tripureśvarī—who embodies the essential nature of the entire wheel (cakra) characterized by the four states of deep sleep, dreaming, waking, and the fourth (turya)—he explains its division as her four limbs, beginning with the word "tridhā" (threefold). Tridhā...

The state of emission (*visarga*) is threefold, and the state of differentiation (*bheda*) consists of the differentiation of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the differentiation of dream (*svapna*), and the form of waking (*jāgara*).

The single state of the *bindu* is the form of the fourth (*turya*). Although here a threefold nature is possible by way of non-differentiated waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, nevertheless, regarding that threefold nature...

Manifestation occurs due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being the counter-correlative of difference, but not in an ultimate sense; thus, the fourth state (*turya*), which is the state of non-difference, is indeed of a single uniform nature. By means of the "four arms," which serve as an illustration for the four previously mentioned states, she is "endowed" (*āḍhyā*)—that is, fully possessed—of them.
This conventional symbolism of the four arms of Tripureśvarī is merely an indicator of her being the constituent of the four states (daśās), and not her ultimate reality;
thus it is to be known by the fortunate one whose every doubt has been destroyed by the grace of the true Guru.
"This is a great secret"—such is the traditional oral teaching. || 17 ||
126) In the states of deep sleep and waking, as well as in the external waking state consisting of water, earth, and air, [the Self acts] by means of its own power as the partless essence.

With three arms, he holds a bow made of sugarcane, a flowery arrow, and a noose, which are his own attributes consisting of the letters *ā*, *t*, *e*, *ca*, *va*, *ga*, *ya*, *ma*, *ya*, *sa*, and *va*. || 18 ||

Then, in this very manner, he clearly explains the convention of the four arms along with the convention of the four weapons, beginning with the words "sauṣupta" and so forth: *sauṣupta* is deep sleep (*suṣupti*); *jāgrat* is waking (*jāgara*); and *svapna* is the waking of the state beyond the external (*abahiḥ-padajāgara*).
In deep sleep, waking, and dreaming—consisting of water, earth, and air, that is, in the forms of water, earth, and wind:

deep sleep is of the nature of water because of its insentience; waking is of the nature of earth because of its hardness due to the state of contraction; and dreaming is of the nature of wind because it is a play of the mind, which is synonymous with wind.
In these ten stages in succession: by the power of *a*, *ka*, *la*, and *ā*—that is, by the power whose nature consists of the letters *a*, *ka*, *ra*, and *la*.

The underlying sense is that it is of the nature of the *caitya* (the sacred seat), which is the form of the Earth (*pṛthvī*), because the Earth itself, being of an extremely solid nature, is the supreme *caitya*. By what kind of power? By such a power.

In the states of deep sleep, waking, and dreaming, the consciousness is sequentially grasped by its own qualities— consisting of the letter *i*, the *ca*-group of consonants, and the letter *ya*— which are held like a bow of sugarcane, arrows, and a noose; these qualities belong to the earth, which presides over the five elements.

Indeed, the pentad beginning with sound (śabda) is of the nature of *dharma*, because it is invariably dependent upon that [substratum]. It is by means of these very elements—sound and the rest—which possess varying degrees of intensity attained during the three states beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), that they are designated as "deep sleep" (*suṣupta*), "sugarcane" (*ikṣu*), and "bow" (*cāpa*). This is because they consist of water and are sweet.

And because they conceal the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*): in the waking state, when duality is fully developed, they are designated as "flower-arrows" because their function consists solely in subjugation through their five manifest forms; in the dream state, during the stage of slight swelling [of consciousness].

Because it has the nature of wind (*vāyu*), like a whirlwind, it is designated as the "noose" (*pāśa*) due to its activity of whirling, which generates the delusion of difference and non-difference. In this way, the objects of sound and so forth, which are expressed by the phonemes *i*, the *ca*-group, and *ya*, are themselves designated as the sugarcane bow, the flower-arrows, and the noose; by such means, [the senses] are restrained.

By that power of Earth (pṛthivī-śakti), which is bound and veiled yet consists of the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva-svarūpiṇī-citi), she possesses three arms—that is, she is endowed with a triad of arms. Thus, through this very power whose nature is consciousness (caitanyātmikā), the Sovereign of Tripura (Tripureśvarī), who presides over the three states beginning with deep sleep, possesses three arms. That which rests upon them is precisely the pentad of sound and the other objects of the senses.
Being that which possesses specific forms established in their respective states, it is the triad of weapons beginning with the sugarcane bow;
such is the great instruction. || 18 ||
In the fourth abode of fire, he who has offered oblations with the *sṛṇi* (goad),
whose single arm is the remedy for the disease of the extreme dullness of the most base beings— those who are like funeral mounds (*caitya*) driven away by the *sṛṇi*— [is victorious].
Thus, she who is meditated upon as four-armed, whose fourth limb consists of ten parts, whose body is the earth, and who is beyond the fourth state in the central position, is victorious. (19)

Having thus explained the three binding arms along with their three weapons, he now explains the fourth arm, the liberator, together with its weapon, beginning with the words "In the fourth," and so forth. "In the abode of fire" means in the nature of fire; the sense is that it is the locus of the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). In the fourth...

By process of elimination, the fourteenth [letter] is the fourth; it should be understood as having the nature of space (*ākāśa*). By *citā*—that is, by the consciousness (*cit*) signified by the letter *ha*. Driven by the goad (*sṛṇi*) in the form of the letter *sa*, as in the word *sasṛṇi* and so forth—that is, by the hook (*aṅkuśa*)—the great beast (*mahāpaśu*), who is a supreme sacrificial animal (*caitya*), is indeed driven. Therefore...

The elephant is [like] a great beast; its dullness (*jaḍatvam*) is its manifestation apart from consciousness (*cidvyatirekeṇa*). That itself is the "sickness" (*ruk*), meaning disease; by that [disease], this is a qualification of the heart-consciousness (*hṛccit*). Just as a great beast, namely the elephant, is awakened by a goad, so too is the intellect (*caityam*) awakened by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Sadāśiva in the form of the letter *sa*.

It is awakened; it attains the state of being of the nature of pure consciousness (*cidekarūpatā*). Thus, the justification for the letter *sa* being the convention for the goad (*aṅkuśa*) is established.

The reflective awareness of non-duality (*abhedavimarśa*) is the letter *sa*, which, because it is a limb (*aṅga*) of the power of consciousness whose essence is the letter *ha*, is its attribute (*dharma*);

therefore, it possesses the nature of being its weapon. In this way, by the power whose form is *hasā* (the letter *ha*), which bears the goad of the letter *sa*, [the Lord] is "one-armed" (*ekabāhuḥ*).

Ekabāhumatī. Having thus visualized her as four-armed, she is the possessor of fourteen limbs (*caturdaśāṅgā*). She whose limbs are the four decades visualized by means of the four arms is the embodied one (*aṅginī*).
She is the embodied one whose form is the union of the syllables *kṣa* and *ma*; [she is formed] by the syllables *kṣa* and *ma* alone.

Regarding the phrase "presiding over the four decads": the correct logical conclusion is that the union of both [the vowels and consonants] constitutes the state of being the principal [deity], which is Tripureśvarī, whose essential nature is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Because the state of the fourth (*turīya*), which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), acts as the presiding authority by virtue of its centrality, the letter *kṣa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). As for the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)...
The letter *ma* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) because it constitutes the state of the "Middle" (*mādhyāmika*), which consists of the three states beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

He teaches that the very union of those two is the nature of that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*), because it is the root of all—stating, "in the middle state, the Transcendent Fourth. The supreme excellence of this very state is revealed by the word "Victorious" (*jayati*). 19
That which is the immersion of consciousness into the state of waking, following the manifestation of the Caityas arisen from the state of sleep and so forth;
And indeed, the fourth state (*turya*) therein is that portion of deep sleep which consists of consciousness;
that, being the very body of Śiva, is the supreme fourth.
Now, it might be argued that since the five elements and the five scriptures are the five faces of the Lord,
there ought to be ten states; and being characterized by the ten limbs such as deep sleep and the rest, He must be both identical with all that and yet other than it.
To the question, "How then is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*) said to be the principal (*aṅgin*)?", he replies:

"Beginning with sleep," and so forth. "Beginning with the state of sleep" means starting from the stage of deep sleep. "Of that which has arisen" refers to the manifestation of the object of cognition (*caitya*). "Beginning with the waking state" means starting from the stage of waking; "the immersion of consciousness" (*cidvinimajjana*) is the appearance of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmayatā*).

That indeed is the fourth state (*turya*). It is the state of non-dual manifestation (*abhedāvabhāsa*) that occurs through the sequence of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, for one who has emerged from the manifestation of duality through the sequence of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking.
That state of non-dual manifestation is indeed the fourth stage (*turyadaśā*). In that state—

That which is the portion of consciousness consisting of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is conceivable as a repose within the manifestation of consciousness during waking and dreaming, and which has the nature of deep sleep having become one with consciousness—this indeed is the state beyond the fourth (*atītaturya*), whose essential nature is that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*). It is the form of Śiva (*śivavapuḥ*), a body that is the very head of Śiva; it consists of consciousness.

The meaning is that waking and dreaming are the inferior bodies of Śiva, while his consciousness-nature (cinmayī) deep sleep is to be known as the state of his head. This is what is being said: for those who hold the view that there are only four states, the fourth state (turya)—designated as "beyond the fourth" (atītaturya) or "transcending the fourth" (atyuttīrṇaturīya)—is accepted by virtue of its transcendence of the consciousness-nature deep sleep.

Thus is their inclusion. For them, that which is called *turyātīta* (beyond the fourth) is not a separate state distinct from the others; rather, it is the presiding principle over all states, because the possibility of *turyātīta*—which is the object of the conception of the consciousness-filled deep sleep (*cinmayasuṣupti*)—is already contained within the *turya* itself. According to this view, [it is the basis] for the union of the letters *kṣa* and *a*.

The statement that the one who is the presiding lord of all ten states possesses the nature of the *turyātīta* (the state beyond the fourth) is made with the intention of referring to it as the *aṅgin* (the principal), and not merely as the ten states themselves; such is the intended meaning of the preceding sūtra.
Now, [one might ask]: "In this way, regarding the nature of the *turyātīta*, which is intended as the *aṅgin*..."
It should not be thought that it is only logical for [the Self] to be co-present with all ten limbs,
and not rather to have its fitness for association with the specific forms of the *kṣa* and *ka* syllables restricted to one part;
for just as [the soul], though co-present with the entire body, resides in the heart-lotus, which is but one part of the body.

Thus, the acceptance of its structural arrangement is likewise faultless; for it is only for that whose nature is beyond the fourth (turyātīta) and which possesses the integration of all states, that the arrangement of the central wheel (*madhyacakra*)—consisting of the union of the letters *kṣa* and *ma*—is indeed appropriate.
However, according to the view of those for whom the state beyond the fourth is merely the supreme consciousness-filled deep sleep (*cinmayasuṣupti*), it is only the fifth state [that is so].

In their view, the word (*pada*) consisting of the fusion of the phonemes *kṣa* and *a*, which is present in all states and is the Great Reality itself—the synonym for the life-force (*prāṇa*) of Tripureśvarī—is [the object of worship]; thus, there is no application of grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*). || 20 ||
The fourth state consists of two parts: the lower portion is the non-arising (abhava), and the head is the ultra-fourth (atiturya); the experience of these two is situated in the middle of the void.
This beast, whose head is waking while its body is sleeping, is in a state of inferior slumber; it is devoid of life-breath and possesses a perverted understanding.
He explains in detail what was stated generally in the previous sūtra—that the body of Śiva is "beyond the fourth" (atītaturya)—with the words beginning with "the fourth" (turyam).

"Two-part" (dvikhaṇḍa) means characterized by two sections; the sense is that it consists of the non-dual states of waking and dreaming. "The fourth" (turyam) refers to the lower portion of the unborn Śiva. "Beyond the fourth" (atītaturya) [refers to that which transcends even this].

The fourth state (*turya*) has the nature of non-dual deep sleep (*suṣupti*); it is a portion of the state of the fourth. "The head" (*mūrdhā*) refers to the "top" (*śiraḥ*). This is connected with the word *abhavasya* (of the unborn). The sense is that for Śiva, the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) is primary, whereas conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not primary. Between these two—the subordinate and the primary limbs—the "middle" (*madhya*) is that which takes the form of the letter *kṣa*.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) has its location in the *anubhū* (the throat). The meaning is that the vital breath indeed resides in the throat, which is situated between the two limbs in the form of the "lower head" (*jaghanya-śiras*). The intended sense is that it is logical for the presiding deity of both to reside in the middle of both.
In connection with Śiva, he describes the analysis of the limbs of the individual soul (*jīva*) as well: "that whose head is the waking state is 'waking-headed' (*jāgrac-chiraḥ*)."

The lowest stage of the state of sleeping is dream; that is, "dream" (svapna) refers to the lowest portion of the sleep of one who is sleeping. A "bound soul" (paśu) is one whose cognition is contrary to Śiva—that is, one who possesses knowledge opposite to that of Śiva.
The bound soul's contrariety to Śiva arises from the predominance of conceptual construction (vikalpa) and the non-predominance of non-conceptual awareness (nirvikalpa).

Such is the animal (paśu), which is without breath. The letter *ma*, situated between the two limbs (*a* and *ya*), is itself the locus of the animal's breath; this is the distinction, as explained previously. || 21 ||
The self is the sacrificial animal; it is indeed primordial nature (prakṛti), for by her it is swallowed.
Thus, the self is also nothing but the conscious primordial nature, which consists of the form of cessation.
Thus, the letter *kṣa* is Śambhu, the supreme ground of rest for the two-fold *prakṛti*; he exists as the absolute beyond even *prakṛti*.

Just as an animal in the form of the letter *ma* is bound by *prakṛti*, which brings about the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of duality, so too bondage is conceivable for Śiva in the form of the letter *kṣa*, who brings about the transmigratory existence of non-duality. How then can there be fixed bondage?
Regarding the fact that the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between the letter *ma* and the letter *kṣa* is accepted as the object of worship, he says:

"The self" (*mātmā*). The self (*mātmā*) is the essential nature of the letter *ma*. The bound soul (*paśu*), which is the individual life-force (*jīva*), is indeed *prakṛti*. He states the reason for this: "Swallowed by her" (*tayā nigīrṇaḥ*). This is because it is devoured by *prakṛti*. The sense is that [the self] is transcendent of *prakṛti* once it has emerged from it. Thus, even the self...
Consciousness is the letter *ha*. Consciousness is the form of *ha*. Nature (*prakṛti*) itself is the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*);

the intention is that this follows from the necessity of its association with that [consciousness]. But the letter *kṣa* is thus, in two ways, the ground of rest for nature. "Thus" means according to the aforementioned rule. "In two ways" means of dual form.

The resting place of *prakṛti*, which consists of both activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*), is the locus of repose. Because it is pure and introverted, it is untouched by even a fraction of the two-fold cycle of transmigratory existence;
thus, while it is not covered by *prakṛti*, the intention is that it is itself the concealer of *prakṛti*. For this very reason, the letter *kṣa* is the supreme Śambhu.
It is indeed beyond *prakṛti*, but it does not fall within it. Therefore, the letter *kṣa* is eternally liberated.

Of this very [letter], that which is its external form is the letter *ha*, and that which is its internal-yet-external form is the letter *ma*; it is these two alone that possess the nature of *prakṛti* through their dependence upon *prakṛti*, but not the letter *kṣa*.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that its status as an object of meditation is indeed appropriate. || 22 ||
Alternatively, here "kṣa" refers to Śiva; because it is devoid of any counter-correlative (pratiyogin), the very state of deep sleep is the supreme station of Śambhu, whose nature is consciousness.
That Śambhu occupies the center of the wheel and is its sovereign is due to his being worthy of worship because he possesses even a trace of the qualities associated with that [center]. || 23 ||

Because the letter *kṣa* stands in a state of opposition to the letter *ma*, the scent of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is difficult to avoid; therefore, for those who believe that the supreme reality is the pure non-conceptual state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) within consciousness, and that this alone is to be meditated upon, he says "or else" (*yadvā*) in order to refute that view. This is because of the state of opposition to *ma*; that is, because of the state of opposition to the letter *ma*, which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*).

Due to the relationship of mutual pervasion and being pervaded [between the letters], it is the letter *kṣa*, which is Śiva, but not Paramaśiva; the sense is that this is because of the persistence of even a trace of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). The "Self of Consciousness" (*cidātmā*) is the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*), which is indeed deep sleep itself, consisting of consciousness.
The "state of Supreme Śambhu" (*paraśambhupada*) is the reality of Paramaśiva. Or else—meaning in an alternative view—in this other position:

Even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the absolute cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is difficult to establish.
