If the absolute cessation of conceptual construction were established, it would ultimately entail insentience (*jaḍatva*). And that which is insentient cannot be an object of worship (*upāsya*). Therefore, whether in the state of conceptual construction or in the state of the "scent" (*gandha*), reality (*tattva*) is what must be worshipped; thus, by means of the letter *kṣa* abiding in the center of the wheel (*cakra*), it should be meditated upon.
He provides the resolution that the state of being worshipped as the presiding deity of the wheel (*cakrādhiṣṭhātṛ*) has become manifest, stating:

"That which is situated in the middle of the wheel," and so forth. The fact that the letter *kṣa* is situated in the middle of Śambhu’s wheel is traditional; its establishment in the center of the wheel is what awakens its status as the lord thereof—its status as the lord of the wheel (*cakrādhīśatā*).

And this very [attainment] of Śambhu is accomplished by the reason of his being "fragrant with qualities" (*guṇagandhitayā*); it is established because of his state of being worthy of worship (*arcyabhāvāt*), that is, because he is to be adored. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is brought about. The traditional position is that the letter *kṣa* resides in the center of Śambhu’s wheel precisely because he is to be worshipped through the imparting of the fragrance of qualities, and not because he is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). This is the realization itself.
The distinction is that it "renders capable. || 23 ||
(133) Moon, Fire-eater, Hare-marked, Moon-eater, Fire-vehicle, Equal-horse, and Sun— this triad [of syllables] occurs at every step at the beginning of the vowels.
Likewise, that undivided state consists of three parts; their resting place is at every ten, with these being equal in number.
Furthermore, time is established by means of the ten *daśās* (decades) alone, which revolve again and again.

And the lunar days (*tithis*)—fifteen in the bright fortnight and as many in the dark fortnight, totaling thirty—revolve repeatedly. From the perspective of the yogi, it is indeed these *daśās* that [constitute the cycle].
Regarding the nature of the lunar days (*tithi*), the fact that the ten [periods] possess a number equal to the lunar days is to be understood through traditional instruction;

thus, he teaches that very object of knowledge with the words beginning "The Moon is the fire-eater" (*candro 'gnibhuk*) and so forth. By means of two aphorisms, [he shows] that in each respective period (*daśā*), it takes on such and such a form.

Saṃsāra is constituted by the very aggregate of the five elements (*pañcabhūtātman*). Those elements, moreover, possess ten natures (*daśasvabhāva*). To illustrate: the moon, whose essence is the water-principle (*jalatattva*), is of the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupti*);

the sun, whose essence is the air-principle (*vāyutattva*), is of the nature of waking (*jāgrat*); and fire, whose essence is the fire-principle (*tejastattva*), is of the nature of dreaming (*svapna*).
Prakṛti, whose essence is the earth-element (pṛthvītattva), consists of the three qualities (guṇas) and serves as the seed for the triad of fires; it is the fourth state (turya).

Puruṣa, whose essence is the space-element (ākāśatattva), is the locus of rest for Prakṛti, which takes the form of the seed of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca); he is beyond the fourth (turyātīta). Although a multiplicity of kalās exists in states such as deep sleep, [the distinction remains].

Nevertheless, those *kalās* are included within these five very principles (*tattvas*). Thus, for each of the ten [states], there are exactly five *aṅgadaśās*: deep sleep within deep sleep is water; deep sleep within waking is air; deep sleep within dreaming is fire; deep sleep within the fourth (*turya*) is earth; and deep sleep within that which transcends the fourth is ether. It is thus.

The division of the five-fold state of limbs (aṅgadaśā) is to be understood even at the beginning of the waking state and so forth. Thus, when counting the groups of five-fold states of limbs for each state among the active forms of deep sleep, waking, and dreaming, the active form of saṃsāra consists of fifteen limbs. These are indeed those very limbs.

The distinction is that there are fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) for each of the two [fortnights] of the bright half (*śuklapakṣa*). Now, since all the members of the active cycle of existence (*pravṛttisaṃsāra*) take the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*) within the cycle of cessation (*nivṛttisaṃsāra*), there are fifteen lunar days for each of the two [fortnights] of the dark half (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) therein. In the active cycle of existence...
The waxing of the moon consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) constitutes its bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).

In the cycle of cessation (*nivṛtti-saṃsāra*), the waning of the moon of the object of knowledge constitutes its dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); such is the distinction. As for the literal meaning of the two aphorisms: the moon is the consumer of fire and the pervader of fire; it is the consumer of the hare-marked one (*śaśibhuk*).

Fire pervades the moon; thus, fire is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of both the moon and fire. However, it is not intended that there be a devouring of the moon by fire or a devouring of fire by the moon in all states.

For if that were the case, then during activity, deep sleep, and so forth, when the moon is devoured by fire, there would be a contradiction regarding its being the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣatva*).

Now, "equality": the equality of these two, the moon and the fire. "The sun" (bhānu): in the beginning of the vowels, that is, at the start of the class of vowels, this triad exists in every word; it must necessarily be accepted as being the very nature of the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra-kalāpa*). "In the same way" means like the moon and so forth; it consists of three parts, namely, the three parts represented by the moon, the fire, and the sun.
The manifestation in the form of the moon and so forth; the "indivisible state" (*akhaṇḍapada*) is the earth in its aspect of active manifestation (*pravṛttiparyāya*).

Indeed, the moon and the other [luminaries] consist of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and are of the nature of the manifestation of the earth in its aspect of active manifestation—this is the distinction. Because it is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three qualities, the nature of Prakṛti is that of the indivisible state.
And this word, like the words "moon" and so forth, has "form" (*saṃsthāna*) as its meaning;
and its resting place (*viśrama*) is the resting place—that is, the locus of repose—of that word which is the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
It is the nature of space; the meaning is that it is one's own essential self (*svātmatattva*). This word, too, is fixed for each decad.

The fixed periods (daśās) of the five limbs beginning with Aṅgada have been stated. The remainder [of the verse] is that it should be understood that these fixed periods of the limbs possess a number equal to that of the lunar days (tithis). || 24 ||
(135) By means of the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking— tripled through their forms of difference, non-difference, equality, and subtlety— ;

Indeed, the bright fortnight consists of the lunar days beginning with Earth (pṛthvī) and ending with Mind (manas), while the dark fortnight consists of those same [days] in reverse order, beginning with the state of waking (jāgara). || 25 ||

"By division," and so forth. By means of the subtle forms of division, differentiation, and equality—respectively having the natures of difference, non-difference, both, and their equilibrium—corresponding to the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking;
multiplied by three; [and] by the fifteen [units] beginning with earth and ending with ether.

By means of the ten forms beginning with Earth and ending with Space; by the five lunar days (tithis); and in the calculation of three groups, by fifteen—surely this constitutes the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa). This is the remainder [of the argument]. Through the cessation of that which begins with the state of waking (jāgarapada), then, in the state of the Fourth (turyadaśā)—

The first [of these states], waking and so forth, is the cessation of these lunar days (tithis) by means of accepting their cessation through the final [state]. This is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. Thus, for a person of arrogant vision regarding the yoga of discerning time according to the established tradition, there is the fivefold nature of time.
"It is established"—this is the instruction regarding the object of knowledge. || 25 ||
The supreme nature is indeed the body itself; it is that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which constitutes both engagement and withdrawal.
Its form is a mixture of speech and meaning, like the moon, fire, and the sun.
Each one is joined with a tripuṭikā; thus, there is one ninefold form. || 26 ||

Now, demonstrating that the Śrīcakra— which is the reflection of the power of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) whose nature is the Great Primordial Nature (*mahāprakṛti*)— consists of nine wheels because its constituent parts (*aṅga*), which take the form of specific states, are nine in number, he says:

"Consisting of the body," and so forth. "Consisting of the body" means having the form of the body; by this, it is demonstrated that the three bodies of Tripureśvarī alone constitute her primary form. Nature itself (prakṛti) is of the nature of the supreme speech (parāvāk), characterized by the grasping of its own essence. Thus, [she is] both "Nature" and "Supreme Speech."

Established and abiding as the foundation is *vimarśa*. This very power of *vimarśa* is the source of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) for Śiva. All of *saṃsāra*—whether it be the *saṃsāra* of engagement, the *saṃsāra* of withdrawal, or the mixed *saṃsāra*—has this as its cause.

In this context, the "root" is *prakṛti* itself, because it is the very form of manifestation; such is the meaning. Her body is a mixture of word and meaning (*vāgarthamiśravapuḥ*), for she is not merely of the nature of *parāvāk*. She is both of the nature of sound and of the nature of meaning, and a mixture of both, because the all-pervading reality has sound as its root and is thus included within sound. Such is the nature of Tripureśvarī.
The *tripuṭikā* (threefold sheath) is characterized by the union of each one of the triad consisting of the moon (*indu*), fire (*anala*), and the noble Āryaman (*āryaman*), joined with the triad;
that is, it is "joined with each one" (*ekaikayuk*), meaning that each one is joined individually. Thus, for each one...

That which is the triad consisting of the three cities— the objects of cognition and so forth— united with the Moon in the form of manifestation (*pravṛtti*), Fire in the form of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and Āryaman (the Sun) in the form of the equilibrium of both; though in reality it is of a single nature and non-dual in the state of rest, it possesses nine forms, that is, ninefold distinctions of its own nature.

This is the meaning: because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), the city of deep sleep (*suṣupti-pura*), which consists of the object of cognition (*prameya*) and comprises fourteen spokes, is divided into three types—by the predominance of emission (*visarga*), the predominance of the point (*bindu*), and the predominance of both.

Likewise, the city of waking (*jāgrat-pura*), which consists of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and comprises two sets of ten spokes, and the city of the subject (*pramātṛ-pura*) are also [divided] in that same way.

The city of dreams, consisting of eight spokes, is likewise; such is the discernment of the nine wheels. This wheel, through its various forms of ten spokes, constitutes a ninefold manifestation and becomes the image (*bimba*) of the Sovereign Lady of Tripura—this is the intention residing in the heart. (26)
Consciousness and insentience are equal in the two— reflective awareness (vimarśa) and consciousness (citi)— just as both [aspects] exist in the moon and the drop; that is will (icchā).
Karma may indeed be mutually inert due to its insentience, but knowledge is the common ground for both; thus it possesses a twofold nature. (27)

Thus, having elevated Prakṛti itself as the qualified form (*saguṇasvarūpa*) of Śiva and established the Navacakreśvarī through the possibility of her being an object of worship, and once her status as an object of cognition (*cetyatva*) is well-known, the potentiality for her to serve as a vessel for the doubt regarding the negation of her worshipability (i.e., her causality) [is addressed].
Refuting the common misconception, he says:

"Consciousness," and so forth. By stating that consciousness (*cit*) is non-inert (*ajaḍa*), he refutes its inertness while establishing the identity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) with consciousness. [This concerns] reflective awareness and consciousness.

In *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) and *prakāśa* (manifestation), consciousness and insentience are equal; for each of the two possesses both consciousness and insentience—this is the wonder (*camatkāra*). This wonder is based on mutual pervasion (*anyonyavyāpti*): consciousness alone is the pervader, and insentience alone is the pervaded.

The sense is that, since both possess the qualities of being pervasive and being pervaded, the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of the state of consciousness and non-consciousness must be realized without distinction. He states the reason for establishing that this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not insentient— namely, that both of these, light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness, possess will, knowledge, and action— with the words "because" (*yad yasmāt*).

Both [the moon and fire] are the two-fold [nature] of the Indu and Anala; that is their Will (icchā). Of those two, Light (prakāśa) and Reflection (vimarśa), the Will of Light is sometimes Fire when it is pervasive, and sometimes the Moon when it is the pervaded.
It is likewise for Reflection. One should not suspect that the Will of Reflection is exclusively the Moon, because of that Reflection...

In the state of pervasion (*vyāpakadaśā*), the attainment of the power of fire by the moon—that is, its very nature as fire—occurs through the will of that [light]; likewise, even for fire, through the "this-ness" (*idantā*) which is pervaded by that [will], the attainment of the dullness of the moon—that is, its very nature as the moon—occurs through the will of light.
Thus it is in the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahārapade*) regarding light and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Having stated that each of the two— the fire and the moon— which constitute its own nature, possesses both inertness and non-inertness by virtue of the mutual desire to be sought after,

he now describes their state of inertness and non-inertness as being mutually the agent and the object, beginning with the words "syāt" and so on. Indeed, the object is swallowed— that is, pervaded— by the agent.

It is pervaded; therefore, the meaning is that action both devours and is swallowed by one another, such that it becomes both the being (*bhūta*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). Their common ground is their mutual objectivity, and thus knowledge is of an identical form.
Likewise, as before, they are non-dual in form; the meaning is that each becomes both the knower and the knowledge of the other.

Thus, when there is no state of desire to be sought between the moon and the sun—between reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and light (*prakāśa*)—and when there is no distinction between them in terms of the relationship of agent and action, or knower and known, the insistence that the essence of light is insentient (*jaḍa*) brings about a state devoid of discrimination; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
In both cases, by virtue of the rotation [of the principles], there is the manifestation of the three—
desire and the other two— at each of the three abodes.
And among the six modes of activity, there is the relationship of cause and effect between the bindu and kṣaya, between m and bhava, and between the consonant groups pa and pha. || 28 ||
Now, regarding the great mantra of the Mātṛkā consisting of three parts, its constant repetition for the sake of both wings would not constitute a bond;
for there is no distinction between the beginning, middle, and end of these parts, and they possess the wonder of a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
This explains the secret that [the syllables] take on the form of a wheel with spokes:
"on both sides," and so forth. This refers to the three *dhāman*s, the *pada*s, and the segments of the mantra (*mantrakhaṇḍa*).
"On both sides" means on the right and on the left. "By way of revolution" means by way of circular rotation.

In every abode and at every step, through the state of the triad beginning with will (*icchā*), there arises the nature of will (*icchātva*), the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), and the nature of action (*kriyātva*).

The distinction is as follows: if any given part is accepted as being the first, it is the nature of will; if accepted as being the middle, it is the nature of knowledge; and if accepted as being the last, it is the nature of action. Herein—

In the three sections; according to the stated limits, in the six functions; in all [of them]; in the *bindu* (the vowel-group) and its destruction (*kṣa*), that is, the *bindu* and the letter *kṣa*; likewise, in *ma* and *bha*, that is, in *ma* which possesses the arrangement of the pervasive group, and in the group of the contact consonants (*sparśa*).

Between that pair of *bhakāra* and *bakāra*, which belong to the class of contact consonants (*sparśavarga*), and that very pair of *pakāra* and *phakāra*, as well as the *visarga* situated within the class of vowels, there exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect. This is the meaning.
At every moment, the emergence of the *āvarta* (whirl) from the region of the heart and the locus of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is to be contemplated;
and at every moment, within the region of the heart, the *bindu* and *visarga*, along with the groups of vowels,
are situated internally— thus the *bindu* and *visarga*, together with the groups of vowels, are established within the square wheel (*caturasracakra*).
The letters *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *bha* represent primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the mind (*manas*) respectively.
Among these, *pa* and *pha* correspond to the visarga, while *ba* and *bha* correspond to the bindu;
within the interior of the pervasive group [of consonants], the letters *ma* and *kṣa* (corresponding to the visarga and bindu) constitute the visarga.

In the location of the *bindu*. This being so, when one proceeds from the *bindu* through all [the letters] by revolving in reverse order (*pratiloma*) until reaching the end of the *kṣa*-letter within the immersion of the pervasive group (*vyāpakavarga*), then the *bindu* is the cause and the *kṣa*-letter is the effect; conversely, beginning from the *kṣa*-letter and revolving in direct order (*anuloma*) until reaching the *bindu*, the *kṣa*-letter [is the cause].

The cause is the *bindu*, and the effect is [the *visarga*]. Now, beginning with the *visarga* situated within the vowels (*svara*) and revolving in direct order (*anuloma*) until the *visarga* in the form of the letters *pa* and *pha* situated within the consonants (*sparśa*), the *visarga* is the cause and the *visarga* in the form of *pa* and *pha* is the effect; having commenced from the *visarga* in the form of *pa* and *pha*...

In the counter-clockwise rotation ending with the vowels and *visarga*, the *visarga* of *pa-pha* is the cause, while the *visarga* residing within the vowels is the effect. Then, beginning with the *bindu* in the form of the letter *ba* situated within the *sparśa* (consonant) group, and proceeding in clockwise order up to the *bindu* in the form of the letter *a* situated within the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) group, the *bindu* in the form of *bha* is the cause.

The *makāra*-bindu is the effect (*kārya*). Beginning from the *makāra*-bindu and revolving in reverse order up to the *ba-bha-ru* form-bindu, the *makāra*-bindu is the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the *ba-bha-ru* form-bindu is the effect; such is their distinction. In this context, the state of being a bindu belongs to both the bindu and the letter *kṣa*.

The traditional instruction is that the pair of letters *pa* and *pha* possess the nature of a pure *visarga*, while the pair of *ba* and *bha* letters, through their association with the letter *a*, possess the nature of both the *bindu* and the *visarga*. This applies to whichever [element] among the divisions of the object (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or the knower (*pramātṛ*).

The *mūlatvābhyupagama-siddhānta* (the doctrine of accepting [only] that which is fundamental) is established by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) in accordance with experience (*anubhava*). And experience is indeed as follows: when a jar or the like manifests, the manifestation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as the eye, and the manifestation of the perceiving subject (*pramātṛ*) endowed with eyes, are experienced without being perceived themselves, following a sequence. In that regard, someone [says]:

Some consider the manifestation of the jar to be primary, while others consider the manifestation of the sense organ to be primary, and still others the manifestation of the knower (*pramātṛ*). When there is a conflict regarding these three established doctrines determined by individual intuition, this is the "established settled doctrine" (*siddhasiddhānta*).
In the manifestations of jars and other objects, which consist of the wonder of light and reflective awareness, the synthesis of the three systems of doctrine alone remains established. || 28 ||

In the first word, there is consciousness (cit) within the two states of rest, namely the Moon and Fire, which are the abodes of the vowels and so forth, and which constitute the seed-state of the universe.
When the sun shines upon both, this entire [structure] is a *caitya* submerged in the city on one side and in the funeral pyre on the other. || 29 ||

Now, it may be objected that this has been established as the Siddhānta by the Śāktas, who primarily worship the Śākta *Svara-khaṇḍa*— which consists of the previously mentioned three sections, possesses the arrangement of fourteen spokes, and is of the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
[In contrast,] the nature of the object of consciousness submerged in consciousness (*cinnimagna-caitya-svarūpa*) possesses the arrangement of eight spokes and is of the nature of dream (*svapna*).
The Śaivas have established that the worship of the pervasive (vyāpaka) section is primary;

whereas for the undiscriminating person, the worship of the tactile section (sparśakhaṇḍa)— which consists of the ten-spoked [cakra] containing the square and belongs to the waking state— is primary due to the apprehension of the fettered condition (paśudaśā).

Or it may be in the sphere of equanimity (*upekṣā*); thus, by means of four sūtras beginning with "Candrāgni," he demonstrates that it is the traditional doctrine that the primary sacrifice (*pradhānayajana*) belongs specifically to that section. [The phrase] "of Candrāgni and Viśramaṇa" refers to the two abodes of *svarayā* and so forth.

The resting of the moon (*candra*) and the visarga within the two words—the word consisting of the pervasive class (*vyāpakavarga*) and the word consisting of the vowel class (*svaravarga*)—constitutes their state of rest (*viśrāntisthānatva*). In the word of the vowel class, there is the resting of fire (*agni*) and the bindu; and in the word of the pervasive class, within the vowel class, there is the swallowing of consciousness (*cinnigaraṇa*), resulting in the single parasol of the *caitya* throughout the pervasive class.

The sense is that through the swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) of the *caitya*, there is the single *citi* (consciousness), like a single umbrella. This refers to the two states of the seed of the universe (*viśvabīja*):

namely, the repose of the *caitya* and the repose of *citi*. Each possesses the nature of being the seed of the universe, because the universe is experienced as consisting of both reflective awareness (*vimarśamayatva*) and luminosity (*prakāśamayatva*). In the first word, which is the state of the vowels, it is *citi*.

In the City, the Caitya—the funeral pyre—submerges; the meaning is that there is no longer any perception of the Caitya. In "both shining forth" (*ubhayollasite*), it means shining forth as both Consciousness (*cic*) and the Caitya, in the form of a radiant manifestation (*ullāsa*). Regarding the Sun (*bhānau*): however, in the section on Touch (*sparśakhaṇḍe*), this pair of Consciousness and Caitya is entirely such that their respective natures have swallowed one another; both forms of Consciousness and Caitya are completely merged.

The reality (tattva) arises collectively in the locus of vision. Since both Śiva and Śakti are the locus of vision, the discernment is that the waking cycle itself, which is of the nature of the sun, is primarily to be worshipped. || 29 ||
And when there is a pair of wheels within the interior boundary of the moon and the fire-eater (the sun), which consists of the crushing of both consciousness and unconsciousness;
This pair of two images of the sun, indeed, exists entirely in a square form upon the surface of the solar orb. (30)

The deity couple who presides over these two wheels consists of the Caitya, whose essential nature is consciousness (citsvarūpa) encapsulated within the fourteen-spoked wheel, and Consciousness (cit) itself, whose essential nature is the Caitya encapsulated within the eight-spoked wheel; these two preside over the two ten-spoked wheels.
It is joined with a square wheel; for this very reason, he explains the square nature of this wheel with the words beginning with "indau ca" (and in the moon).
"In the moon" means in the fourteen-spoked wheel; "and in the fire-eater" means in the eight-spoked wheel.

Regarding "the secondary wheel" (*praticakra*): it is within the boundary of the belly, in the center of the circle of rays situated within the *bimba*. This is because of the suitability of the *bimba*-wheel.
The meaning is that as for the two wheels that exist, there are two wheels in each secondary wheel (*mandira*).
Within the interior of the fourteen-spoked wheel, there are two wheels consisting of eight petals and sixteen petals, which have the nature of consciousness (*citi*) and the *caitya*.

Within the interior of the eight-spoked [wheel], there are two wheels consisting of the nature of the *caitya* and *cit*, in the form of a triangle and a point (*bindu*). Of what nature are these two wheels? They are of the nature of the mutual sublation of the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). The sublation (*abhyavamarda*) of the conscious and the unconscious—that is, of the *cit* and the *caitya*—is their mutual penetration; they exist in that state. Within the fourteen-spoked [wheel], it exists by way of the sixteen-petaled [lotus].
By means of the *caityacakra*, there is the movement of the consciousness-wheel (*ciccakra*) consisting of eight petals;

for this very reason, that [eight-petaled wheel] is situated outside it in the form of sixteen-petaled rays. By means of the eight-spoked consciousness-wheel in the form of the *bindu* (point), there is the movement of the *caityacakra* in the form of a triangle; for this very reason, the triangle exists in the form of the rays of the *bindu*.
The external abiding. Thus, this pair of two-fold images is established:

consisting of the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled [lotuses], and the pair consisting of the triangle and the bindu, which together constitute four forms. Within the interior of the two ten-spoked [circles] at the location of the solar disc, there are eighty [petals].

By its squareness, it exists in a square form. It is "entirely" (samastam), meaning it exists as a unified whole. The four wheels, which consist of eight petals, sixteen petals, a triangle, and a bindu, exist in the form of four squares and four corners. Therefore, the square should be worshipped primarily.
The conclusion. || 30 ||
Therefore, this four-footed, square image is the confluence of the Yamunā and Nirjarasarit rivers at the *cic-caitya* Prayāga.
First, there should be worship; then follows the worship of the mental caitya-circle which constitutes its limb, as previously stated. || 31 ||
He concludes that the four-cornered wheel (*caturaśracakra*) is to be worshipped first by means of the reasoning already stated, beginning with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

"Therefore" means for that reason, namely, because of the cause consisting of the reasoning set forth in the preceding sūtra. It is "four-footed" (*catuṣpada*), meaning it is the locus of the assembly of the four deities who exist in the form of limbs and sub-limbs. This...

A square-shaped mound (*caturasrabimba*) [is seen] at the confluence of the *Cicacaitya* and the river Yamunā, and at the confluence of the Bhāgīrathī and the Yamunā. Due to its clarity, the mound possesses a resemblance to the Bhāgīrathī in terms of its color; and because the *caitya*, being of the nature of *saṃsāra*, is stained, it possesses a resemblance to the Yamunā by virtue of its dark hue. Prayāga is the name for the [confluence] of the Yamunā and the Bhāgīrathī.
The confluence is a most meritorious and distinguished sacred site (*tīrtha*).
Likewise, the square image of the deity is also most meritorious.
It has been described that by immersing oneself there, one immediately attains the state of the deity. Thus it is said.
First, in terms of the object of knowledge (*prameya*): it should be worthy of worship (*arcya*) and the object of worship (*arcanīya*).

Then, following the worship of the square (*caturaśra*), there is the worship of the mind (*cit*) and the *caitya*-wheel (*cakra*), which are its constituent parts, in the forms of the eight-spoked and fourteen-spoked [wheels].

That is the four-cornered wheel; the remainder of the sentence is that it is placed "in front," meaning at the beginning. This is for the purpose of instructing that within the Śrīcakra, which consists of three cities (puratraya), the four-cornered [wheel] alone is to be worshipped first—at the foremost position, the station of the Goddess.

In the case of the location pervading all wheels, the worship of the square [mandala] in its natural states takes the form of the fourteen-spoked and eight-spoked [wheels]; thus, that square wheel is positioned to the east,
precisely in the middle of the fourteen-spoked and eight-spoked [wheels], for the purpose of establishing that it is to be worshipped first.
The sense is that the arrangement of those two wheels in an external location, which is intended as their pervasion, is conceptual.

The four-cornered (caturaśra) wheel is also an elliptical indicator for the two ten-spoked wheels, because the existence of the Bimba-wheel within the Raśmi-wheel would otherwise be untenable. || 31 ||
This limb, situated within the square, consists of fire (Uṣarbudha) and the moon (Indu), has the sun as its essence, and is the source of both the conscious and the unconscious.

And this being so, since this [reality] consists of both the insentient and the sentient, it is worthy of worship even before [the manifestation]; thus it has been established in the state of plenitude (pūrṇapada). || 32 ||
Thus has the supreme secret, the essential nature of the meaning of the Mātṛkā,
been most clearly taught as it is manifested within the King of Wheels (cakrarāja). This meaning takes root when the inner self is pierced by Śakti.
But there is no further transgression elsewhere; that is not mine. // 33 //
[In this regard, this verse— which for the most part follows the sequence of the root verses— is found as an addition in the commentary within the manuscript.
Thus ends the supreme secret, the true nature of the meaning of the Mātṛkā.]
This has been taught most clearly through the practice of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).
Since this meaning applies when the inner self is pierced by *śakti*, there is no further obstacle for him in anything else. || 1 ||
Thus ends the fifth section, the Investigation of the Fourth State (*turyaviveka*), within the Investigation of the Wheel of the Mother-Syllables (*mātṛkācakraviveka*).
The Root Text on the Distinction of the Wheel of the Mātṛkās is complete.
The external arrangement of the waking wheel, characterized by its square shape,
is intended solely for the instruction of the disciple; however, from the perspective of one who has already attained proficiency, this conceptualization need not be followed,
as the primary focus is on the very square situated in the center.

Having established that it must be worshipped first, he dispels the objection regarding the fault of imagining a different arrangement of the wheel with the words "situated within" (*antaḥstha*) and so forth. [This refers to] the two [wheels] characterized by eight and fourteen spokes, belonging to Fire (*uṣarbudh*) and the Moon (*indu*), which consists of the Sun (*arka*).

It is square, with its arrangement fixed within the interior of the two ten-spoked [circles]. By the word "eva" (only/itself), its necessity is expressed; however, one should not suspect that its arrangement exists in the external region.
Indeed, it has the form of the sun, and the sun is a limb of both fire and the moon, because its establishment depends upon both of them.
Thus, although it is a limb (*aṅga*) of the square, this form of the square wheel—

which is the essence of the moon and fire principles (*tattva*), being the core of both the insentient and the sentient— is to be worshipped even before [the other limbs], precisely because it is the essential core of the limbs; for the purpose of establishing this, that square wheel is [placed] in the *pūrṇapada*.

In the place of pervasion (*vyāptisthala*), it is performed in the outer region; the phrase "by Śiva, who is established from the beginning" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the central wheel, which is characterized by its square shape: those practitioners who have understood the primacy of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) situated in the center—relative to the root-sprout—even though it is situated in the middle, [they perceive it as such].

They worship first the square (caturaśra), viewing it as primary like a seed. For those who are unacquainted with that [inner reality], this conceptualization of the arrangement outside the square is an explanatory form of the very same reality situated within the circle. The intended meaning is that it concerns a domain free from transgression.

The arrangement of the eight-petalled and sixteen-petalled [lotuses] occurs precisely within the center of the fourteen-spoked [wheel]. As for the arrangement of the square within the belly-region of those two squares: [it is as follows].
Immediately after the two ten-spoked [circles] which serve as indicators, the worship of the fourteen-spoked and eight-spoked [circles] must be performed;

thus, for the sake of instructing the disciple, the sixteen-petaled [lotus] serves as the indicator for the fourteen-spoked, and the eight-petaled [lotus] serves as the indicator for the eight-spoked, [all placed] on the outside.

It should be understood that [the deity] is "established. This is the meaning: each of the three wheels—consisting of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), waking (*jāgrat*), and dreaming (*svapna*)—is to be primarily worshipped. Among them, the predominance of the fourteen-spoked wheel of deep sleep is understood from its location in the external region at the site of pervasion (*vyāptisthala*).
According to the traditional reverse order, the predominance of the activity of the dream-wheel (*svapnacakra*) is also understood.

In comparison to those who understand the predominance of the waking-wheel (*jāgraccakra*), which falls between those two, by way of the arrangement of the seed-syllables (*bīja*), [the following is established].

The external arrangement of the square, sixteen-petaled, and eight-petaled [lotuses], which characterize the waking, deep sleep, and dreaming wheels respectively, should be followed according to the conceptual design. However, for those who are unskilled in this matter, the primacy of the waking wheel is intended with respect to them.
The arrangement of the external square and other wheels has been explained through the configuration of three lines.

That conceptualization, being intended solely for the instruction of the disciple, is a construction of arrangement; however, for the practitioner who possesses discernment and understanding, it extends only up to the fourteen-spoked wheel within the Śrīcakra.
Is it to be understood that each of the three wheels, beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), possesses predominance?
May there be auspiciousness.
|| 32 || 33 || (1) Thus ends the complete commentary on the *Mātṛkācakra*.
